abstract: Background: LDL-C, lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)], and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) represent complementary lipid and inflammatory dimensions of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk. Whether these biomarkers provide additive risk information across populations with different ethnic backgrounds and baseline risk profiles remains uncertain. Research Question: We studied whether LDL-C, Lp(a), and hsCRP were independently and jointly associated with incident ASCVD in a multi-ethnic primary prevention cohort, and whether these associations were modified by ethnicity. Methods: The analysis included 15,676 HELIUS participants free from prior myocardial infarction or ischemic stroke. ASCVD was defined as first nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, coronary revascularization, or cardiovascular death, ascertained through linkage to national registries. Biomarkers were analyzed across quintiles and as joint top-quintile elevations using Fine-Gray competing-risk models. Interaction was evaluated on multiplicative and additive scales. We also tested whether adding Lp(a) and hsCRP improved prediction beyond a PREVENT-ASCVD-based clinical model. Results: Participants had a mean age of 44.4±13.2 years; 56.0% were women; 45.8% were of African, 39.8% of European, and 14.4% of South Asian Surinamese descent. During a median follow-up of 8.9 years, 378 ASCVD events occurred. Compared with the lowest quintile, the highest quintile was associated with higher ASCVD risk for LDL-C (adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio [aSHR] 1.39; 95% CI, 1.09-1.79), Lp(a) (aSHR 1.86; 95% CI, 1.54-2.25), and hsCRP (aSHR 1.51; 95% CI, 1.34-1.71). Joint biomarker elevation conferred progressively higher risk, with an aSHR of 2.44 (95% CI, 1.46-4.09) for participants in the top quintile of all three biomarkers. There was no evidence of multiplicative or additive interaction, supporting independent contributions of the three pathways. Associations between cumulative biomarker burden and ASCVD were similar across ethnic groups (P interaction =0.75), but absolute 10-year risk was highest among South Asian Surinamese participants. Adding Lp(a) and hsCRP to the clinical model modestly improved 10-year discrimination (ΔAUC=0.006; P=0.030) and continuous net reclassification improvement (0.165; 95% CI, 0.050-0.289). Conclusions: In HELIUS, LDL-C, Lp(a), and hsCRP provided independent and cumulative information on ASCVD risk across ethnic groups. These findings support combined lipid and inflammatory biomarker assessment for pathway-oriented risk stratification in diverse primary prevention populations.
title: Abstract 10012: Combined LDL-C, Lp(a) and hsCRP Assessment Predicts ASCVD in the Multi-Ethnic HELIUS Cohort

abstract: Introduction: Williams syndrome is a multisystem disorder frequently involving the cardiovascular system, most often through elastin-mediated arterial stenoses. Although mitral valve (MV) abnormalities are reported, mitral regurgitation (MR) is usually mild; severe MR requiring surgical repair is rarely described, and optimal repair strategies remain poorly defined. We describe valve-sparing posterior leaflet extension for complex MV disease in a young adult woman with Williams syndrome. Case Presentation: A 24-year-old woman with Williams syndrome, characteristic facies and developmental delay, hypertension managed with metoprolol, and branch pulmonary artery stenoses treated with balloon angioplasty at 5 and 21 months of age, was followed for progressive MV disease. Preoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) demonstrated severe eccentric posteriorly directed MR with moderate mitral stenosis, a giant left atrium, and a markedly dilated mitral annulus. (Fig. 1) The valve was dysplastic, with a redundant, prolapsing anterior leaflet and a hypoplastic posterior leaflet with shortened chordae. Cardiac catheterization showed normal right heart pressures, mildly elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and no coronary ostial stenosis. Multidisciplinary consensus favored repair over replacement. Surgical Interventions: After median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass, left atriotomy via Waterson’s groove exposed the MV. Intraoperative inspection confirmed severe A2 prolapse due to elongated chordae, an A2-A3 pseudo-cleft, and a diminutive posterior leaflet tethered by restrictive secondary chordae. The pseudo-cleft was primarily repaired by suture re-approximation. The posterior leaflet was disarticulated from the annulus extending from anterolateral to posteromedial trigone. Secondary chordae were then divided to improve posterior leaflet mobility. The posterior leaflet was then augmented with a crescent-shaped patch to increase leaflet height and zone of coaptation. (Fig 2) A 32-mm flexible posterior annuloplasty band was placed, and left atrial appendage ligation was performed. Followup, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Cardiopulmonary bypass time was 146 minutes and cross-clamp time was 119 minutes. Intraoperative TEE demonstrated good biventricular function with trivial MR and no mitral stenosis. Postoperative acute kidney injury resolved over 4 days. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 7. At 1 year, echocardiography demonstrated trivial MR (Fig. 3). Discussion: To our knowledge, this is the first reported use of posterior leaflet extension for MV repair in Williams syndrome. By addressing posterior leaflet deficiency and annular dilation while preserving the native valve, this approach may expand repair options for selected patients with Williams syndrome and complex dysplastic MV disease.
title: Abstract 10026: Complex Mitral Valvuloplasty Using Posterior Leaflet Extension in a Patient with Williams Syndrome

abstract: Background: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is the most aggressive support for cardiogenic shock. Its rising use has made patient selection pivotal. Frailty is associated with worse cardiogenic shock outcomes, but frail patients often get less aggressive treatment, so this risk may partly reflect treatment rather than vulnerability alone. Whether frailty independently predicts outcomes on maximal support, as in VA-ECMO, has not been studied. Research Question: Among adults receiving VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock, is higher frailty, measured by the Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS), a validated claims-based measure, independently associated with worse in-hospital outcomes? Methods: Using the survey-weighted National Inpatient Sample (2016-2022), we identified adults (≥18 years) with any-etiology cardiogenic shock who received VA-ECMO. Post-cardiotomy shock, VV-ECMO, durable MCS, and prior heart transplant were excluded. The HFRS was dichotomized into low (<5, reference) and high (≥5). Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included major bleeding, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, vascular complications, durable LVAD, heart transplantation, discharge home, length of stay (LOS), and cost. Multivariable logistic/linear regression adjusted for 24 covariates spanning demographics, hospital characteristics, comorbidities, acute myocardial infarction, and cardiac arrest. Results: Among 34,260 hospitalizations (mean age 55.6 years), 82.0% had a high HFRS. In-hospital mortality was higher with high frailty (49.3% vs 45.6%), and the association strengthened after adjustment (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 1.10-1.43; p=0.001). High frailty was independently associated with greater odds of ischemic stroke (aOR 2.66; p<0.001), major bleeding (aOR 1.82; p<0.001), and hemorrhagic stroke (aOR 1.47; p=0.023), and lower odds of discharge home (aOR 0.79; p=0.006), with longer LOS and higher cost. Vascular complications, durable LVAD, and heart transplantation did not differ significantly. Conclusions: Among VA-ECMO recipients, higher frailty independently predicted higher mortality, stroke, bleeding, and worse discharge. Frailty remained prognostic even in this aggressively treated, selected population, with a more modest mortality association than broader cardiogenic shock cohorts. These associations emerged in a relatively young cohort, suggesting relevance beyond the older populations in which frailty is typically assessed. Despite this risk, roughly half of high-frailty recipients survived to discharge. Frailty should therefore inform, not preclude, VA-ECMO candidacy as part of individualized, shared decision-making.
title: Abstract 10030: Hospital Frailty Risk Score and In-Hospital Outcomes Among Adults Receiving Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Background: In cardiogenic shock requiring venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO), increased left ventricular afterload may aggravate pulmonary congestion. ECPELLA, combining VA-ECMO with a microaxial flow pump (mAFP), can maintain systemic perfusion while unloading the left ventricle. Optimal de-escalation may require preserving total systemic perfusion while shifting support from VA-ECMO to mAFP. Objective: To identify 72-hour flow-management phenotypes during ECPELLA support and evaluate their association with short-term outcomes. Methods: The UNLOADERS-PVAD Registry is a multicenter observational registry from three high-volume Impella centers. Among 501 patients receiving mAFP-based mechanical circulatory support (MCS) from April 2018 to December 2023, mAFP-alone patients were excluded. A 72-hour landmark cohort further excluded patients who died, were weaned from MCS, or lacked pulmonary artery catheter data before 72 hours. Estimated total systemic perfusion was derived from VA-ECMO flow and pulmonary artery catheter-derived cardiac output. Clustering used 24-, 48-, and 72-hour ECMO perfusion ratio, estimated total systemic perfusion index, VA-ECMO flow index, and mAFP flow index. Cox models were adjusted for age, E-CPR, baseline lactate, chronic kidney disease, and severity scores including APACHE II, SAPS II, and SAVE; center fixed-effect and inverse probability-weighted analyses were sensitivity analyses. Results: The analysis included 184 ECPELLA patients. Three phenotypes were identified: balanced de-escalation (n=40), early mAFP-dominant support (n=68), and ECMO-persistent support (n=76). Balanced de-escalation showed reduced VA-ECMO dependency from 24 to 72 hours, preserved total systemic perfusion, and increasing mAFP flow. Early mAFP-dominant support showed low VA-ECMO dependency and high mAFP flow from 24 hours onward, whereas ECMO-persistent support remained highly VA-ECMO dependent. Baseline severity scores and lactate levels did not substantially differ, although chronic kidney disease was more frequent in ECMO-persistent support. Thirty-day survival differed across groups (65.0%, 58.8%, and 40.8%; P=0.020). VA-ECMO weaning (87.5%, 85.3%, and 60.8%; P<0.001) and mAFP weaning (84.6%, 71.6%, and 48.6%; P<0.001) showed similar gradients. In adjusted Cox models, ECMO-persistent support was associated with higher 30-day mortality versus balanced de-escalation (HR 2.27, 95% CI 1.22-4.23; P=0.010), persisting after center fixed-effect adjustment (HR 1.99, 95% CI 1.04-3.82; P=0.037). Conclusions: In ECPELLA-supported cardiogenic shock, acute flow-management phenotypes were associated with short-term survival and MCS weaning. Persistent VA-ECMO dependency at 72 hours remained a high-risk phenotype after adjustment for baseline severity and center differences.

register_verdicts.note: Small registry phenotype analysis of flow management does not provide comparative randomised evidence.

title: Abstract 10032: Acute Flow Management Phenotypes and Outcomes in Cardiogenic Shock Supported by Combined Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation and Microaxial Flow Pump

abstract: Background: Residual cardiovascular risk persists in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) despite intensive lipid-lowering therapy. We investigated whether extended biomarker profiling, including a 9-plex apolipoprotein panel (with apoE phenotyping) and 11 CE-marked emerging Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) parameters, improves prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and death beyond conventional demographic and lipid parameters in the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial. Methods: The trial was randomized, double-blind, and compared the PCSK9 inhibitor alirocumab to placebo in patients with recent ACS receiving optimized statin treatment. Over a median follow-up of 2.8 years, the primary MACE endpoint comprised coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal and nonfatal ischemic stroke, and hospitalization for unstable angina; all-cause death was a secondary endpoint. In 11,843 trial participants (placebo n=5926; alirocumab n=5917) apolipoproteins and apoE phenotype were measured by mass spectrometry and CKM parameters were measured using a Roche Cobas analyzer. CKM parameters included cystatin C, high-sensitivity troponin T (hs cTnT) , NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, small-dense low-density lipoprotein, GDF-15, sFlt, interleukin 6, insulin, homocysteine, and the NAFLD fibrosis score (Angulo et al . Hepatology . 2007;45:846-54). Incremental multivariable logistic regression models with natural cubic splines were constructed with demographics, diseases and standard lipid parameters (Model 1), apolipoprotein panel (Model 2), and CKM parameters (Model 3). Model performance was assessed using area under the curve (AUC) statistics, DeLong tests and generalized likelihood ratio tests. Due to lower event counts, penalized regression (ridge-type penalty) was applied for death analyses. Results: The baseline model yielded AUCs of 0.66 (0.64 - 0.68) for prediction of MACE and 0.71 (0.68 - 0.74) for death (Figure 1). Addition of apolipoproteins improved the AUCs to 0.69 (0.67 - 0.71) for MACE and 0.76 (0.72 - 0.79) for death. Further addition of CKM parameters improved the AUCs to 0.72 (0.70 - 0.75) and 0.82 (0.79 - 0.85), respectively. For MACE, the five strongest predictors were hs cTnT, apolipoprotein(a), NT-proBNP, diabetes, and cystatin C. For death, the five strongest predictors included NT-proBNP, sex, total cholesterol, age and small dense LDL-C. Conclusion: In statin-treated patients with recent ACS, comprehensive biomarker profiling with a multiplex apolipoprotein panel including apoE phenotypes and emerging CKM tests each provides clinically meaningful improvement in the prediction of MACE and death beyond conventional demographics, disease state and standard lipid profile. These findings support the conclusion that residual risk in ACS is multidimensional.
title: Abstract 10036: Apolipoproteins and Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic-Biomarkers Each Add to Prediction of Residual Cardiovascular Disease Risk After Acute Coronary Syndrome: Insights from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES Trial

abstract: Introduction: Cardiovascular (CV) inflammation is associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Inhibition of interleukin-6 (IL-6), which is upstream to C-reactive protein (CRP), is a promising target for attenuating CV inflammation and may reduce MACE in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Methods: The ARTEMIS study (Effects of ziltivekimab versus placebo on CV outcomes in patients with AMI) is evaluating the impact of ziltivekimab, a human monoclonal antibody targeting the IL-6 ligand, versus placebo in patients with an AMI enrolled across 24 countries (Figure). This double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 CV outcomes study randomized patients within 36 hours of ST-elevation MI (STEMI) or within 72 hours of non-STEMI (NSTEMI) 1:1 to ziltivekimab or placebo, with an initial loading dose of 30 mg subcutaneously and then 15 mg subcutaneously once monthly, on top of standard of care. Participants were required to have angiographic evidence of a type 1 AMI. The primary endpoint of MACE is defined as a composite of CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke, and ischemia-driven coronary revascularization. The study was designed using an unstratified Cox model and a power of 90% to confirm superiority using a type I error rate of 2.5% (one-sided) for the primary endpoint, assuming a hazard ratio of 0.77, requiring a total of 616 primary endpoint events. Results: A total of 8584 participants with AMI were screened, and 8346 participants were randomized to ziltivekimab or placebo, administered on top of standard of care. The median age was 62 years (interquartile range [IQR] 54-70), and 20.7% were female. Major comorbidities included hypertension (63.5%), type 2 diabetes (36.0%), heart failure (12.3%), chronic kidney disease (6.3%), prior AMI (15.1%), and prior coronary revascularization (12.5%). A total of 50.4% of participants presented with NSTEMI, and 76.0% had multivessel coronary artery disease during the index AMI. The median time from first hospital contact to study randomization and administration of ziltivekimab or placebo was 28.2 hours (STEMI, 23.9; NSTEMI, 40.4). The baseline median serum high-sensitivity CRP concentration was 10.3 mg/L, serum IL-6 concentration was 17.2 pg/ml, and serum low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentration was 105 mg/dL. At index AMI discharge, 90.1% were on aspirin, 94.4% on a P2Y12 inhibitor, and 94.0% on a statin. The table describes participant demographics, comorbidities, medications at index AMI discharge, and inflammatory markers, both overall and stratified by NSTEMI versus STEMI presentation. Conclusions: The ARTEMIS study, the largest study of an IL-6 inhibitor in AMI, will determine the safety and efficacy of a novel IL-6 inhibitor, ziltivekimab, in patients with AMI. Participants enrolled in the ARTEMIS study are representative of real-world, high-risk patients with AMI.
title: Abstract 10037: Ziltivekimab in Acute Myocardial Infarction: Rationale, Design and Baseline Clinical Characteristics of the ARTEMIS Study

abstract: Introduction: Obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) and angina without obstructive coronary arteries (ANOCA) caused by coronary vasomotor dysfunction (CVDys) are distinct ischemic entities within chronic coronary syndrome (CCS). Comparative data on their cardiovascular risk are limited. Understanding potential differences may improve risk stratification and inform tailored preventive strategies in patients with ischemic symptoms. Research Question: What are the differences in cardiovascular risk profile and prognosis between patients with obstructive CAD and CVDys? Methods: This study included CCS patients from two prospective, multicenter registries in the Netherlands: the south-east Netherlands Heart Registry (ZON-HR), containing patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for obstructive CAD, and the NetherLands registry of invasive Coronary vasomotor Function Testing (NL-CFT), including ANOCA patients undergoing a clinically indicated coronary function test (CFT). From the latter registry, only patients with CVDys, defined as an abnormal CFT, were included. Prevalence of risk factors and major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) -including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, unplanned coronary revascularization, and ischemic stroke- within one year after the index PCI or CFT were assessed. Results: 3542 patients with CCS due to obstructive CAD and 1066 patients with CVDys were included. Baseline characteristics are presented in table 1. After 1 year follow-up, 9.0% of the obstructive CAD patients had experienced MACCE, compared to 1.2% of the ANOCA patients (p<0.001) (figure 1). All MACCE components occurred more frequently in patients with obstructive CAD (cardiovascular death 1.6% vs. 0%, p<0.001; myocardial infarction 3.3% vs. 0.6%, p<0.001; unplanned coronary revascularisation 6.8% vs. 0.6%, p<0.001, ischemic stroke 0.9% vs. 0.1%, p=0.009). Sex, diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease, prior revascularization, and severe renal insufficiency were identified as independent predictors of MACCE in the obstructive CAD population, whereas only prior myocardial infarction independently predicted MACCE in the CVDys population. Conclusion: Patients with obstructive CAD have a worse risk profile and prognosis compared to CVDys patients. While cardiovascular risk factors and established atherosclerotic disease were determinants for outcomes in obstructive CAD, only prior myocardial infarction was predictive for outcomes in CVDys.
title: Abstract 10044: One-Year Outcomes of Obstructive Coronary Artery Disease and Coronary Vasomotor Dysfunction in Chronic Coronary Syndrome: Insights from Two Multicenter Registries

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic and mixed cardiogenic-septic shock carry some of the highest mortality in critical care, despite advances in vasoactive therapy and mechanical circulatory support. At the bedside, clinicians read the rise and fall of vasopressor and inotrope doses as a signal of who is improving, however this signal has not been rigorously quantified as a predictor of death. The vasoactive inotropic score (VIS) captures this support in a single number, and its early trajectory may hold prognostic information beyond established severity scores. Hypothesis: Higher maximum VIS and slower VIS reduction over the first 24 hours of ICU admission are independently associated with in-hospital mortality, beyond established severity scores. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adults aged 18 years or older with cardiogenic or mixed shock in MIMIC-IV v2.2, identified by ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes and confirmed by at least one vasoactive infusion within 24 hours of ICU admission. We analyzed the first ICU stay per hospitalization. Hourly VIS was computed from time-weighted infusion rates of six agents (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine, milrinone, and vasopressin). We derived the maximum VIS and the VIS reduction rate (VRR), the proportional fall in VIS from peak to hours 18 to 24. Multivariable logistic regression for in-hospital mortality compared a baseline model (age, sex, comorbidities, first-day Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, first-day lactate, shock type) with models adding maximum VIS as a restricted cubic spline and then adding VRR. Discrimination was compared by C-statistic and DeLong tests. Results: Among 1,458 patients (1,080 cardiogenic, 378 mixed), in-hospital mortality was 40.3%, and nearly double in mixed shock (60.1% vs 33.4%). Mortality rose steeply across maximum VIS quartiles, from 22.5% in the lowest to 65.9% in the highest. After adjustment (complete-case analysis, n=1,284), both measures independently predicted death. Across the interquartile range, a higher maximum VIS raised the odds of death by about 60% (adjusted OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.17), as did a smaller reduction in VIS over the first day (adjusted OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.28). The fall in VIS added prognostic value beyond maximum VIS alone (P=0.001), and including both measures improved discrimination (C-statistic 0.796 to 0.808, DeLong P=0.007). Conclusions: Both the peak and the early trajectory of vasoactive support independently predicted in-hospital mortality in cardiogenic and mixed shock, beyond traditional markers of shock severity. Because VIS is already in the medication record and needs no additional testing, these trajectory metrics could sharpen bedside risk assessment and warrant prospective, multicenter validation.

title: Abstract 10109: Early Vasoactive Inotropic Score Trajectories and In-Hospital Mortality in Cardiogenic and Mixed Shock

abstract: Background: Advances in primary percutaneous coronary intervention have substantially improved in-hospital survival after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, contemporary real-world data on post-discharge outcomes in Japanese patients remain limited, particularly regarding temporal changes in heart failure hospitalization (HFH) and its prognostic significance. Purpose: To evaluate 2-year post-discharge outcomes after AMI in a contemporary Japanese cohort, focusing on temporal trends in all-cause death, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), and HFH. Methods: This study included 6,394 consecutive patients with AMI enrolled in the Mie ACS Registry between January 2013 and December 2022 who survived to hospital discharge. Endpoints were all-cause death, MACCE, and HFH within 2 years after discharge. MACCE was defined as cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, or non-fatal stroke. Cumulative event rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared between the early (2013-2017) and late (2018-2022) periods. Outcomes were also compared between the first and second years after discharge. The prognostic impact of HFH on 2-year all-cause mortality was assessed using multivariable Cox regression analysis. Results: The 2-year cumulative incidence of all-cause death was similar between the early and late periods (7.0% vs. 6.3%, log-rank P=0.58, Figure 1A), as was that of MACCE (5.2% vs. 5.3%, P=0.95, Figure 1B). Most all-cause deaths and MACCE events occurred during the first year after discharge. In contrast, the incidence of HFH was significantly lower in the late period than in the early period (2.8% vs. 4.0%, log-rank P<0.01, Figure 2). This reduction was primarily attributable to a lower incidence of first-year HFH in the late period (2.2% vs. 3.2%, P<0.001, Figure 2), whereas the incidence of second-year HFH was similar between the two periods (0.6% vs. 0.8%, P=0.33, Figure 2). Patients who experienced HFH within the first year after discharge had a substantially higher 2-year all-cause mortality than those without HFH (30.8% vs. 6.0%, P<0.01, Figure 3). Moreover, first-year HFH was the strongest independent predictor of 2-year all-cause mortality (HR 2.38, 95% CI 1.70-3.30, P<0.001). Conclusions: In this contemporary Japanese AMI cohort, the 2-year post-discharge risks of all-cause death and MACCE remained unchanged between the study periods, whereas HFH declined significantly, particularly within the first year after discharge. Nevertheless, early HFH remained a strong independent predictor of subsequent mortality. These findings identify the first year after discharge as a particularly vulnerable period and underscore the importance of intensive follow-up and secondary prevention during this phase.
title: Abstract 10114: Temporal Trends in 2-Year Post-Discharge Outcomes After Acute Myocardial Infarction: Insights from the Mie ACS Registry

abstract: Background: Coronary microvascular and vasomotor dysfunction (CMVD) is the earliest stage of coronary atherosclerosis and has been associated with female sex and with increased mortality risk. We previously introduced integrated myocardial flow reserve (iMFR) as a noninvasive marker to distinguish focally impaired from diffusely impaired perfusion (reflecting epicardial stenosis and CMVD, respectively) and showed that the extent of diffusely impaired iMFR is a strong, independent predictor of mortality. We sought to evaluate the role of female sex in CMVD using iMFR. Methods: We analyzed a single-center registry of patients referred for rest-stress PET myocardial perfusion imaging (March 2011 to December 2024). iMFR combines perfusion defect and quantitative perfusion to classify the left ventricle into normal (MFR≥2.0 outside regional defects), diffusely impaired (MFR<2.0 outside defects), focally impaired (MFR<2.0 within defects), and focally preserved regions, each reported as percent myocardium. CMVD, demographics, risk factors, cardiac history, global MFR, and ischemic total perfusion deficit (TPD) were compared by sex using Wilcoxon rank-sum and chi-squared tests, and linear regression was used to measure sex as a predictor of log(diffuse iMFR+1). Results: Among 11,669 patients (43% women, 57% men, median age 64 years in both), women had a lower burden of CAD (history of MI, PCI, and CABG) and hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and hypercholesteremia (all p<0.001). Despite a lower prevalence of risk factors and recognized CAD, women had a similar burden of CMVD as men (median diffuse iMFR in women 35.9% [IQR 7.2, 74.4] vs men 34.8% [6.7, 72.2], p=0.288). Women had greater extent of normal perfusion (55.2% [12.6, 88.7] vs 49.6% [8.7, 86.1], p<0.001) and lower ischemic TPD (0.6% [0.1, 2.3] vs 1.0% [0.1, 4.4], p<0.001). Global MFR differed only slightly (2.1 in both, p=0.003). Women had similar diffuse iMFR extent reflecting CMVD even after adjusting for age, risk factors, and prior CAD (β=0.039, p=0.153). Conclusion: In this large, quantitative perfusion registry of 11,669 patients, women had a comparable burden of CMVD despite a notably lower burden of risk factors and overall CAD than men. These findings implicate a more complex relationship between CMVD, sex, and CVD risk factors than suggested by prior studies.
title: Abstract 10116: Coronary Microvascular and Vasomotor Dysfunction in 11,669 Women and Men

abstract: Background: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients are at increased risk of contrast-induced acute kidney injury, periprocedural myocardial infarction and dialysis requirement following standard contrast percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Zero or ultra-low contrast PCI has emerged as a potential strategy to overcome these risks. Methodology: We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane Library till January 2026. We included studies that evaluates zero-contrast or ultra-low contrast PCI in CKD patients. Pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) are calculated by using random-effects models. Heterogeneity and statistical significance are estimated. Certainty of evidence is evaluated by using the GRADE framework. Results: A total of 21,882 patients with advanced chronic kidney disease undergoing zero or ultra-low contrast percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) were included. The pooled overall event rate was 2% (95% CI 0.00-0.04) with considerable heterogeneity (I 2 = 99.2%). Periprocedural myocardial infarction across 8 studies (n = 10,062) was exceedingly rare (0.0%, 95% CI 0.00-0.00; I 2 = 0%). In-hospital mortality (4 studies, n = 21,574) was low at 0-2% (95% CI 0.00-0.02) but with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.4%), while 30-day mortality (6 studies, n = 223) remained low at 1% (95% CI 0.00-0.03; I 2 = 19.9%). The incidence of requirement for new dialysis post-PCI across 14 studies (n = 21,900) was negligible (0.0%, 95% CI 0.00-0.00; I 2 = 83.1%). Procedural success was high, ranging from 91% (95% CI 0.79-0.97) in smaller cohorts to nearly 100% (95% CI 0.99-1.00) in larger analyses (I 2 = 0%). Conversion to standard PCI was infrequent at 2% (95% CI 0.00-0.07; I 2 = 64.9%). Renal outcomes showed minimal change in serum creatinine (0.09, 95% CI 0.04-0.13; I 2 = 25.4%) and no significant change in eGFR (0.48, 95% CI –0.29 to 1.25; I 2 = 0%). Target vessel revascularization incidence was rare (0.0%, 95% CI 0.00-0.01; I 2 = 0%), and incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events was in 1% of patients (95% CI 0.00-0.05; I 2 = 63.5%). Overall, zero or ultra-low contrast PCI shows high procedural success rate with very low complication and mortality, that support its safety and feasibility in CKD patients despite variability across studies. Conclusion: Zero or ultra-low contrast PCI is associated with near-zero risks of developing periprocedural MI and need for new dialysis, very low in-hospital and 30-day mortality, and high procedural success rate in patients with chronic kidney disease. In advanced CKD, 2% composite event rate is uncertain due to definitional heterogeneity. A consistent 9% incidence of MRAW was observed across 16 studies with low heterogeneity. All these findings support zero or ultra-low contrast PCI as a safe and effective strategy for CKD patients, also included patients with advanced disease.
title: Abstract 10135: Clinical Outcomes of Zero and Ultra-Low Contrast IN Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) frequently coexists with coronary artery disease (CAD), requiring both valve replacement and coronary revascularization. While transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is increasingly utilized, comparative real-world outcomes versus surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) with coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) remain limited. We compared short and long term outcomes between these treatment strategies in patients with severe AS and concomitant CAD. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network. Adults with severe AS and CAD who underwent SAVR plus CABG or TAVR plus PCI between January 2015 and December 2022 were identified. Patients undergoing PCI within 90 days before or after TAVR were included in the TAVR plus PCI cohort. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using demographics, cardiovascular comorbidities, laboratory variables, and clinical risk factors. The 30-day outcomes included all-cause mortality, stroke, and permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality at 1 and 3 years. Additionally, a subgroup analysis was performed evaluating 3-year mortality among patients aged ≥80 years. Results: Among 11,211 patients identified (6,811 SAVR+CABG and 4,400 TAVR+PCI), propensity score matching yielded 2,483 patients per cohort. At 30 days, SAVR+CABG was associated with higher all-cause mortality (4.2% vs 2.7%; HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14-2.11; p=0.005) and stroke (5.5% vs 3.8%; HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.14-1.94; p=0.003) compared with TAVR+PCI. However, PPM implantation occurred less frequently following SAVR+CABG (5.2% vs 8.4%; HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.47-0.74; p<0.001). At 1 year, all-cause mortality was similar between groups (10.4% vs 11.1%; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.77-1.09; p=0.70). At 3 years, SAVR+CABG was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality than TAVR+PCI (18.7% vs 26.2%; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.80; p<0.001). In a matched octogenarian subgroup (n=664 per group), SAVR+CABG remained associated with lower 3-year mortality (19.3% vs 26.2%; HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56-0.91; p=0.006). Conclusions: In patients with severe AS and concomitant CAD, TAVR+PCI was associated with superior short-term procedural safety, demonstrating lower 30-day mortality and stroke, whereas SAVR+CABG was associated with lower rates of PPM implantation and improved long-term survival at 3 years. Notably, the long-term survival benefit of SAVR+CABG persisted among patients aged ≥80 years. These findings suggest an important tradeoff between early procedural risk and long-term survival when selecting a treatment strategy for patients requiring both valve replacement and coronary revascularization.
title: Abstract 10153: Outcomes of Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement with Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting versus Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement with Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

abstract: Introduction: Mavacamten is a cardiac myosin inhibitor approved for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) with obstruction that carries a known risk of systolic dysfunction and requires strict Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) program guided transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) surveillance. We present a case of fulminant biventricular failure in an HCM patient receiving mavacamten. Patient Information: 53-year-old man with obstructive HCM on mavacamten for three months presented with one week of progressive dyspnea following a viral prodrome. Prior cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) demonstrated asymmetric septal hypertrophy with preserved systolic function and no late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). Genetic testing identified a clinically silent pathogenic transthyretin mutation (Val142Ile) with PYP scan and CMR not suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis. REMS surveillance TTEs after mavacamten initiation showed improved obstructive gradients with preserved systolic function up until one month prior to presentation. Clinical Findings: He was tachycardic and hypervolemic, with elevated lactate, NT-proBNP, acute kidney injury, and mildly elevated troponin with no significant delta. TTE demonstrated new, severe biventricular systolic dysfunction with global hypokinesis (LVEF 16%, RVFAC 8%). Right heart catheterization showed cardiogenic shock (RA 23 mmHg, PCWP 28 mmHg, CI 1.5 L/min/m^2), requiring dobutamine and prolonged intra-aortic balloon pump support for 14 days. Diagnostic Assessment: Coronary angiography revealed a significant proximal LAD lesion (iFR 0.74). However, biventricular dysfunction and distribution were disproportionate to the CAD. Endomyocardial biopsy showed mild lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates without amyloid deposition. CMR demonstrated decreased LV mass, severe global hypokinesis, myocardial edema, hyperemia, and nonischemic pattern of LGE, consistent with inflammatory cardiomyopathy. Therapeutic Interventions: Due to possible myocarditis, he received three days of pulse dose steroids, followed by maintenance steroids. Coronary intervention was deferred due to lack of anginal symptoms and disproportionate cardiomyopathy. On discharge, TTE showed LVEF improvement to 35% and RV recovery. Discussion: This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of acute biventricular failure in patients with HCM receiving mavacamten. Although transient systolic reduction is a recognized effect of mavacamten therapy, the patient’s viral prodrome, fulminant presentation, biopsy findings, and CMR features favored inflammatory cardiomyopathy as the likely cause of cardiogenic shock. The case also supports current recommendations to evaluate for stressors, CYP450-mediated drug interactions, and interval systemic or myocardial illnesses that may potentiate systolic dysfunction during myosin inhibition.
title: Abstract 10156: Mavacamten Induced Toxicity: A Diagnosis of Exclusion in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Patients with Acute Biventricular Failure?

abstract: Background: Catheter-based renal denervation (RDN) has regained interest as an adjunctive therapy for difficult-to-control hypertension following newer sham-controlled trials using improved devices and more rigorous trial designs. However, the magnitude and consistency of its blood pressure-lowering effect in resistant and treatment-resistant populations remain uncertain. Methods: We followed the PRISMA guidelines and searched the databases - PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL - up to May 2026. We also manually checked the references from eligible trials and recent systematic reviews to supplement our search. The primary analysis included sham-controlled catheter-based RDN trials enrolling resistant, treatment-resistant, or difficult-to-control treated hypertension populations. Strict resistant-hypertension trials and broader uncontrolled-hypertension trials were evaluated separately in sensitivity analyses. Ambulatory systolic blood pressure (SBP) was pooled using random-effects generic inverse-variance models, reporting mean differences (MDs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 framework. Results: Among 51 screened records, 7 randomized sham-controlled trials involving 1,555 participants met criteria for the primary analysis. Included trials evaluated radiofrequency, ultrasound, and alcohol-mediated RDN platforms. Compared with sham control, RDN significantly reduced ambulatory SBP in resistant/difficult-to-control treated hypertension (MD –3.54 mmHg; 95% CI –5.99 to –1.09; I 2 =60.1%). The results showed a moderate level of heterogeneity, which likely reflected the differences in the devices used, the medication protocols, and the enrolled hypertension phenotype. In a strict resistant-hypertension sensitivity analysis excluding Iberis-HTN and TARGET BP I, the effect remained significant but smaller (MD –2.30 mmHg; 95% CI –4.22 to –0.38; I 2 =0%). In a broader sensitivity analysis of 14 catheter-based sham-controlled trials across resistant and uncontrolled hypertension populations (n=2,872), RDN reduced ambulatory SBP by MD –3.68 mmHg (95% CI –5.24 to –2.11; I 2 =64.6%). Major adverse events, renal artery stenosis, and clinically significant renal function decline were uncommon, with no consistent excess signal observed with RDN versus sham. Conclusions: In randomized sham-controlled trials, catheter-based RDN produced a clinically modest but statistically significant reduction in ambulatory SBP among patients with resistant or difficult-to-control treated hypertension. These findings support RDN as an adjunctive blood pressure-lowering strategy in carefully selected patients, while emphasizing the importance of patient selection, medication protocol, and device platform when interpreting treatment effects.
title: Abstract 10159: Renal Denervation versus Sham Control for Resistant and Difficult-to-Control Treated Hypertension: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials

abstract: Background: Left atrial (LA) myopathy is increasingly recognized as driving adverse outcomes in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). The molecular mechanisms mediating these effects are poorly understood, partly due to a lack of access to relevant tissue. Hypothesis: We consider the interatrial septum (IAS) as an LA reporter tissue: IAS derives from atrial precursors and is continuously exposed to LA pressure. Spatial transcriptomics may characterize IAS cells relevant to HFpEF and identify novel therapeutic targets and biomarkers through cell-type specific gene expression of LA myopathy traits. Methods: ALLAY-HF is a randomized trial enrolling patients with HFpEF. In patients randomized to intervention, a portion of the IAS is excised to create an interatrial shunt. Samples were profiled using 10x Genomics’ Visium HD platform. After segmentation, cells were clustered and annotated. Cell-type proportions were compared across clinical and LA phenotypes (age, sex, BMI, LA volume index [LAVI] and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure [PCWP]). Differential expression analyses were performed within cell types using DESeq2. Results: Spatial transcriptomics was performed on 14K cells from 4 IAS samples from subjects consenting to a tissue substudy. The resulting 18 clusters showed robust cellular composition representative of the LA including cardiomyocytes, macrophages, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) (Figure). Cell composition varied across samples with the largest proportion of cardiomyocytes in a histopathologically normal sample (62%) and the lowest in the most fibrotic sample (25%). Two samples with normal LAVI (mean 25.2 mL/m 2 ) had lower proportions of macrophages, SMCs and fibroblasts and higher cardiomyocytes compared to samples with elevated LAVI (mean 37.1 mL/m 2 ). Samples with normal and elevated PCWP gave consistent results. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs, FDR<0.05) were identified within cell types, including PDK4 with lower expression in myocytes in individuals with high PCWP. PDK4 regulates cardiac metabolic fuel substrate selection. NPPA encodes atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP); its expression was higher in macrophages of high BMI samples, which may represent macrophages engulfing apoptotic or other damaged cardiomyocytes. Of nominally significant DEGs (p<0.05), the normal vs. elevated LAVI comparison revealed activated fibrosis genes ( AEBP1 , IGFBP7 , USF2 ) in fibroblasts, suggesting stromal remodeling and ECM fibro-inflammatory signaling, as well as stress activation ( FOSB , SAT1 ) and macrophage remodeling ( F13A1 ). Conclusions: IAS tissue contains a diverse cellular population relevant to LA myopathy; its cell composition and differential expression correlate with clinical LA phenotypes. These preliminary data suggest IAS may therefore offer a rare and clinically tractable window into LA myopathy biology in HFpEF.
title: Abstract 10180: Spatial Transcriptomics of the Interatrial Septum Reveals Cellular Composition and Biologic Targets Relevant to Left Atrial Myopathy in HFpEF: An ALLAY-HF Substudy

abstract: Background: Drug-coated balloons (DCBs) have emerged as an important treatment strategy for coronary in-stent restenosis (ISR) and de novo small-vessel coronary artery disease. Paclitaxel-coated balloons (PCB) and sirolimus-coated balloons (SCB) differ in pharmacologic properties and drug-delivery mechanisms, but their comparative clinical effectiveness remains uncertain. We evaluated the safety and efficacy of PCB versus SCB in patients with coronary artery lesions. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that sirolimus-coated balloons would be non-inferior to paclitaxel-coated balloons with respect to clinical and angiographic outcomes in coronary artery lesions. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL was performed through August 2025 for randomized controlled trials and observational studies comparing PCB and SCB. The primary outcomes were major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), myocardial infarction (MI), and cardiac death. Secondary outcomes included target lesion revascularization (TLR), target lesion failure (TLF), stent thrombosis, mortality, and procedural and angiographic characteristics. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed, and pooled effect estimates were reported as odds ratios (OR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: Eleven studies comprising 4,528 patients (SCB: n=2,909; PCB: n=1,619) were included. No significant differences were observed between PCB and SCB for MACE (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.76-1.17; P=0.59), MI (OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.70-1.84; P=0.61), cardiac death (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.10-5.32; P=0.77), TLR (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.75-1.18; P=0.59), TLF (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.68-1.21; P=0.49), all-cause mortality (OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.40-1.79; P=0.66), or stent thrombosis (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.22-4.24; P=0.96). Compared with SCB, PCB was associated with shorter DCB length (MD –1.86, 95% CI –3.14 to –0.57; P=0.005) and shorter lesion length (MD –1.09, 95% CI –2.07 to –0.11; P=0.03). No significant differences were observed in DCB diameter, final diameter stenosis, predilation, balloon pressure, dissection, or unscheduled angiography. Conclusion: In patients undergoing DCB-based treatment of coronary artery lesions, paclitaxel-coated and sirolimus-coated balloons demonstrated comparable safety and efficacy, with no significant differences in major cardiovascular outcomes, repeat revascularization, or mortality. Although minor procedural and angiographic differences were observed, these did not translate into clinically meaningful outcome differences. Further large-scale randomized trials with longer follow-up are warranted to identify potential benefits in specific patient subgroups.
title: Abstract 10187: Comparative Performance of Paclitaxel- and Sirolimus-Coated Balloons in Coronary Artery Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in Japan are often hospitalized longer than those in Western countries despite successful revascularization. Identification of low-risk patients suitable for early discharge may improve healthcare resource utilization; however, validation of risk stratification tools in Japanese populations remains limited. We evaluated the prognostic performance of the Zwolle Risk Score (ZRS) in Japanese AMI patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods: We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients with AMI who underwent PCI at our institution between 1999 and 2015. Patients with incomplete clinical data required for ZRS calculation were excluded. Low-risk status was defined as ZRS ≤3. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. Discriminative performance of ZRS for predicting 30-day mortality was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Results: Among 1,915 eligible patients, 1,103 (57.6%) were classified as low-risk and 812 (42.4%) as high-risk. Median ZRS was 3 (interquartile range 2-5). Thirty-day mortality was significantly lower in low-risk versus high-risk patients (1.6% vs 11.7%, p<0.001). ZRS demonstrated good discriminative performance for 30-day mortality with a C-statistic of 0.84. Low-risk patients were younger and had lower prevalence of cardiogenic shock and renal dysfunction compared with high-risk patients (all p<0.001). Median length of hospital stay was shorter in the low-risk group; however, hospitalization remained prolonged compared with contemporary Western practice, with a median stay of 15 days. Conclusions: The Zwolle Risk Score demonstrated good prognostic performance for short-term mortality in Japanese AMI patients undergoing PCI. Identification of low-risk patients using ZRS may support implementation of earlier discharge strategies and optimization of healthcare resource utilization in Japan.
title: Abstract 10189: Utility of Zwolle Risk Score in Guiding Low-Risk Acute Myocardial Infarction Following Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

abstract: Background: Platelet-mediated thrombosis is a major contributor to myocardial infarction and other cardiovascular diseases. Reperfusion following ischemia can further exacerbate tissue injury, in part through platelet activation and inflammatory signaling. Platelet 12(S)-lipoxygenase (12-LOX), an oxygenase that promotes platelet activation through the generation of bioactive oxylipins including 12-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (12-HETE), has also been implicated in ischemia-reperfusion injury. Our laboratory previously developed ML355, a selective 12-LOX inhibitor that demonstrates antiplatelet and antithrombotic efficacy without increasing bleeding risk. Two second-generation inhibitors, SLUG001 and CCG263719, were subsequently identified. SLUG001 exhibited 7.2-fold greater potency and improved selectivity in enzymatic assays, while CCG263719 demonstrated improved antiplatelet activity. Here, we compared the efficacy of SLUG001 and CCG263719 to ML355 in human platelets and in vivo models of thrombosis and myocardial reperfusion injury. Methods: Isolated human platelets and human whole blood were incubated with 12-LOX inhibitors prior to assessment of platelet activation by aggregation, integrin activation, and granule secretion. Further, Ex vivo thrombus formation was evaluated using the Total Thrombus Formation Analysis System. In vivo efficacy was assessed using laser-induced cremaster arteriole thrombosis and myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury models. Results: Both second-generation compounds inhibited collagen- and thrombin-induced platelet aggregation in a dose-dependent manner. CCG263719 demonstrated greater potency than ML355 and SLUG001 in collagen-stimulated aggregation, integrin activation, and granule secretion, whereas SLUG001 and ML355 exhibited similar activity. Among the inhibitors tested, only CCG263719 significantly reduced ex vivo thrombus formation. Both CCG263719 and SLUG001 inhibited thrombus formation in vivo following intravenous administration, although SLUG001 exhibited a delayed onset of activity. SLUG001 and CCG263719 demonstrated antithrombotic efficacy following oral administration and were bioavailable. In a myocardial ischemic-reperfusion injury model, both second-generation inhibitors reduced infarct size following transient occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery. Conclusions: Although SLUG001 exhibited superior potency in enzymatic assays, CCG263719 produced the most robust antiplatelet effects. Together, these data support continued development of next-generation 12-LOX inhibitors as a novel therapeutic strategy for thrombotic cardiovascular diseases, including myocardial infarction and ischemia-reperfusion injury, while potentially avoiding the bleeding liabilities associated with current antiplatelet therapies.
title: Abstract 10195: Comparing the Antiplatelet and Antithrombotic Effects of CCG263719 and SLUG001, Second Generation 12-Lipoxygenase Inhibitors, to ML355

abstract: Background: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] and coronary artery disease (CAD) polygenic risk scores (PRS) are heritable markers of CAD risk. Lp(a) measurement is recommended at least once in adulthood, and PRS is increasingly being considered for clinical risk refinement. However, when elevated Lp(a) or PRS is found in an index individual, it remains unclear whether this information can be used to identify first-degree relatives (FDRs) at higher clinical risk and support cascade screening for these common inherited risk markers. Research Question: We assessed whether Lp(a) and PRS measured in index individuals independently and jointly predict incident CAD in FDRs. Methods: We studied 26,914 genetically inferred FDR pairs from the UK Biobank. Index participants and FDRs were free of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at baseline. Exposures were Lp(a) and GPS Mult , a CAD PRS, measured in index participants. Incident FDR CAD was defined as myocardial infarction or coronary revascularization. Cox models with robust standard errors clustered by FDR identifier estimated associations between index exposures and FDR CAD, adjusted for established cardiovascular risk factors. Results: The cohort included 25,106 unique index participants and 24,706 unique FDRs; 78.4% of pairs were siblings. During 13.9 years median follow-up, 973 CAD events occurred in FDRs. Index and FDR values correlated for Lp(a) and GPS Mult , with correlation coefficients of 0.37 and 0.52, respectively. Compared with FDRs whose index participant had Lp(a) in the bottom half of the distribution, FDRs whose index participant had Lp(a) in the highest decile had higher CAD risk (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.42; 95% CI, 1.15-1.74; P trend =0.002). Each SD increase in index Lp(a) was associated with higher FDR CAD risk (aHR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.04-1.18; P=0.002), with no evidence of nonlinearity (P nonlinearity =0.48). Compared with FDRs whose index participant had GPS Mult in the bottom half, FDRs whose index participant had GPS Mult in the highest decile had an aHR of 1.69 (95% CI, 1.38-2.08; P trend <0.001). Each SD increase in index GPS Mult was associated with higher FDR CAD risk (aHR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.15-1.32; P<0.001), with no evidence of nonlinearity (P nonlinearity =0.68). Associations did not differ by FDR sex for either marker. Index GPS Mult was more strongly associated with CAD in younger versus older FDRs (P interaction =0.01). FDRs whose index participant had both Lp(a) and GPS Mult at or above the 80 th percentile had more than double the CAD risk compared with FDRs whose index participant had both markers below the 80 th percentile (aHR, 2.34; 95% CI, 1.56-3.52). Conclusions: Lp(a) and PRS measured in index individuals independently and additively predict CAD in their FDRs. These findings support extending cascade screening beyond monogenic lipid disorders to include common inherited cardiovascular risk markers.
title: Abstract 10198: Index Lipoprotein(a) and Polygenic Risk Score Identify Coronary Artery Disease Risk in First-Degree Relatives

abstract: Background: Peri-procedural bleeding requiring red blood cell transfusion is common during transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), yet whether transfusion itself worsens clinical outcomes remains uncertain. Hypothesis: Peri-procedural red blood cell transfusion is associated with worse clinical outcomes in patients undergoing TAVR. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception through April 2026 for studies comparing transfused versus non-transfused TAVR patients. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were pooled using random-effects models; heterogeneity was assessed with the I 2 statistic. Pre-specified subgroups were stratified by age (≥82 versus <82 years) and baseline hemoglobin (≤11 versus >11 g/dL). Publication bias was assessed using Egger regression, and robustness was assessed using a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Results: A total of 14 retrospective cohorts were included. Transfusion was associated with significantly higher risks of 30-day mortality (RR 3.34, 95% CI 2.19-5.09; p<0.00001; I 2 =84%), 1-year mortality (RR 2.44, 95% CI 1.80-3.31; p<0.00001; I 2 =80%), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; RR 2.17, 95% CI 1.25-3.75; p=0.006; I 2 =91%), stroke (RR 1.90, 95% CI 1.49-2.43; p<0.00001; I 2 =51%), and life-threatening bleeding (RR 8.59, 95% CI 4.65-15.89; p<0.00001; I 2 =76%). Risks were also elevated for major (RR 4.21, 95% CI 2.87-6.16; p<0.00001) and minor (RR 1.66, 95% CI 1.17-2.36; p=0.004) vascular complications, and acute kidney injury (AKI) stage 1 (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.17-1.64; p=0.0002) and stage 2-3 (RR 2.82, 95% CI 2.26-3.52; p<0.00001). No significant association was observed with non-fatal myocardial infarction (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.59-1.04; p=0.09) or in-hospital mortality (RR 3.93, 95% CI 0.37-41.70; p=0.26). Age modified the 1-year mortality association (interaction p<0.0001), with greater risk in younger patients (<82 years: RR 5.73 versus ≥82 years: RR 2.12). Egger regression showed no evidence of publication bias for 30-day mortality (p=0.321). Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness for mortality, stroke, AKI, and major vascular outcomes; minor vascular complications and in-hospital mortality depended on single studies. Conclusions: Peri-procedural red blood cell transfusion in TAVR is associated with significantly increased mortality, MACE, stroke, bleeding, vascular complications, and acute kidney injury. Because these data are observational, associations may partly reflect confounding by indication, and causation cannot be inferred. The findings support bleeding-avoidance and restrictive transfusion strategies and underscore the need for randomized trials.
title: Abstract 10201: Association Between Peri-Procedural Red Blood Cell Transfusion and Clinical Outcomes in Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement:A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Coronary angiography, the gold-standard test for coronary artery disease (CAD), has provided key insights into atherosclerosis biology and therapeutic development. However, coronary angiogram reports are stored as free-text and registry development is resource-intensive, limiting use of these data for research and clinical care. Objectives: We used large language models (LLMs) to transform coronary angiogram reports into a structured registry for the Mass General Brigham (MGB) healthcare system to understand regional trends in cardiovascular disease and improve operational efficiencies and research efforts. Methods: We identified individuals who underwent cardiology studies in MGB from 1986 to 2025 and developed an LLM pipeline to 1) identify coronary angiogram reports and 2) extract variables into a structured database. Using GPT-5.2, we extracted procedural data, native anatomy, high-risk phenotypes, and non-obstructive pathologies. We validated extraction accuracy with a double-blinded review and against an internal database for a subset. We used the registry to characterize trends in coronary angiogram practice and risk stratify patients. Results: Our coronary angiogram registry includes 197,309 reports from 124,253 patients, spanning nearly 40 years of practice across Massachusetts General Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Salem Hospital, and Faulkner Hospital. The LLM pipeline processed 309,292 cardiology reports, averaged 0.65 seconds/report for variable extraction (>500x faster than manual input), and cost $4,166 ($0.02/report). Validation accuracy ranged from 96-100% across variables. We observed substantial temporal variation in coronary angiogram volume and indication. Procedures performed for non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) have increased, with more complex CAD (3-vessel and/or left main disease) at presentation. Percutaneous coronary interventions are performed more frequently in low vs high complexity CAD (P<0.001); overall rates of complex intervention have increased. Higher Gensini score on index angiogram was associated with increased relative risk and cumulative incidence of repeat angiogram and all-cause mortality. Our registry is enriched for participants meeting interventional clinical trial enrollment criteria compared to real-world recruitment (55 vs 9 participants/site for DISRUPT CAD III, 106 vs 15 participants/site for AGENT-IDE). Conclusions: We developed an efficient and accurate LLM-powered pipeline to create a coronary angiogram registry for a healthcare system. We observed a rise in complex CAD, likely reflecting evolving biology in response to contemporary medical therapies. Using the registry for risk stratification showed promise, highlighting the potential of using LLMs to improve clinical and research efforts across healthcare systems.
title: Abstract 10217: Large Language Models Enable Scalable Coronary Angiography Registry Development and Capture Four Decades of Cardiac Catheterization Practice in Greater Boston

abstract: Introduction: Infective endocarditis (IE) caused by Capnocytophaga canimorsus is remarkably rare, with fewer than 35 cases reported. Cases involving TAVR bioprostheses are even less well described. To our knowledge, we report the first case of C. canimorsus IE of a TAVR bioprosthesis, complicated by septic shock and multifocal cardioembolic stroke. Patient Information: An 81-year-old man with prior TAVR, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented after three to four weeks of progressive diaphoresis, generalized weakness, and fever. Social history was significant for recent adoption of a puppy with frequent face licking, bed-sharing, and direct saliva exposure to an open leg wound. No formal animal bite was reported. Clinical Findings and Timeline: On presentation, the patient was febrile, tachycardic, and hypotensive, requiring ICU admission. Following initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluid resuscitation, he developed acute mental status changes. Brain MRI demonstrated multifocal acute infarcts bilaterally, consistent with cardioembolic etiology. Diagnostics: TTE was unrevealing. TEE identified a 1 cm filamentous-like mobile vegetation on the bioprosthetic aortic valve, consistent with prosthetic valve endocarditis. Blood cultures yielded C. canimorsus after 12 days of extended incubation. Modified Duke criteria were met. Treatment: He received IV ceftriaxone with metronidazole for empirical anaerobic coverage given the wound exposure, then transitioned to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and metronidazole for a six-week course. Surgery was deferred as he improved clinically. Follow-up and Outcomes: Fever resolved and mental status improved. The patient was discharged home in stable condition to complete outpatient therapy. Repeat blood cultures remained negative. Follow-up echocardiography demonstrated reduction in ejection fraction to 35-40%, worsened intra- and paravalvular regurgitation suggesting bioprosthetic valve destruction. Patient Perspective: At 81, he is still an active outdoorsman who prides himself on his independence. When his symptoms began to slow him down, it was this evident change from his baseline that ultimately brought him to care. Discussion: Thorough animal contact history, including non-bite exposures, is essential in septic patients with prosthetic valves. TEE must be pursued promptly when prosthetic valve IE is suspected regardless of TTE findings. C. canimorsus should be considered in IE with any dog or cat contact, even without a documented bite. Reduced ejection fraction and worsened paravalvular regurgitation suggest bioprosthetic valve destruction, highlighting that TAVR-IE can leave lasting cardiac risk even after clinical recovery and warrants close follow-up. Multidisciplinary coordination was central to both diagnosis and management.
title: Abstract 10246: Man's Best Friend, Valve's Worst Enemy: Capnocytophaga canimorsus Endocarditis of a Transcatheter Bioprosthetic Aortic Valve

abstract: Introduction: Preoperative management of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients requiring urgent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) while receiving antiplatelet therapy remains challenging because of the competing risks of surgical bleeding and myocardial ischemic events due to antiplatelet discontinuation. Hypothesis: We aimed to evaluate the current state of the art, as well as the clinical outcomes and the rate of major bleeding events related to CABG surgery in ACS patients on a multicenter basis. Methods: Data from 3,364 ACS patients undergoing CABG between January 2010 and December 2025 were analyzed from an ongoing national multicenter surgical myocardial infarction registry. The primary endpoint was CABG-related bleeding according to Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) type 4 criteria. Secondary endpoints included in-hospital mortality (IHM) and major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE). Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression models. Results: Mean age was 68±11 years, and 78% were male. ACS presentation included unstable angina (24.5%), NSTEMI (50.0%), and STEMI (25.4%) presenting a logistic EuroSCORE-I of 15.1±15.1% in UAP, 20.3±20.1% in NSTEMI and 23.5±20.0% in STEMI. At admission, 93% of the patients received aspirin, 54.7% dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors, and 13.4% glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors. BARC-4 major bleeding occurred in 18.1% overall, with rates of 17.2% in unstable angina, 15.0% in NSTEMI, and 25.1% in STEMI patients. IHM and MACCE increased across ACS severity, reaching 12.6% and 28.5%, respectively, in NSTEMI and STEMI patients. DAPT independently predicted BARC-4 bleeding in the overall cohort (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.21-3.02; P=0.02), with the highest risk observed in STEMI patients undergoing CABG within 24 hours (OR 3.83, 95% CI 1.98-5.45; P<0.0001). Conclusions: Continued preoperative DAPT is associated with increased BARC-4 bleeding, which in turn is linked to higher risks of IHM and MACCE. STEMI patients receiving DAPT and undergoing non-deferrable CABG within 24 hours represent the highest-risk subgroup.
title: Abstract 10251: Impact of Preoperative Antiplatelet Therapy and Major Bleeding Complications Following CABG in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndromes: A Current Report of the North-Rhine-Westphalia Surgical Myocardial Infarction Registry

abstract: Background: Transcatheter therapies for severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) have rapidly expanded, with transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) and transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) emerging as major treatment strategies. Comparative real-world outcome data between these approaches remain limited. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network including 171 healthcare organizations. Adult patients undergoing T-TEER or TTVR were identified using CPT and ICD-10-PCS procedural codes. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using 48 variables, including demographics, comorbidities, medications, and laboratory characteristics including left ventricular ejection fraction. The primary outcome was heart failure hospitalization (HFH). Secondary outcomes included stroke, permanent pacemaker implantation, infective endocarditis, and new dialysis requirement after the index procedure. Kaplan-Meier and risk analyses were performed. Results: A total of 2,351 patients were identified, including 1,337 undergoing T-TEER and 1,014 undergoing TTVR. After propensity score matching, 901 patients remained in each cohort. Mean follow-up duration after matching was 851 days for T-TEER and 866 days for TTVR. The primary outcome of HFH occurred less frequently among patients undergoing T-TEER than TTVR (54 [19.1%] vs 72 [24.6%]), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51-1.03; p=0.069). Similarly, stroke rates were not significantly different between groups (54 [6.9%] vs 63 [7.7%]; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.61-1.26; p=0.479). However, T-TEER was associated with significantly lower risks of permanent pacemaker implantation (27 [3.5%] vs 81 [11.4%]; HR 0.29, 95% CI 0.19-0.45; p=0.014) and infective endocarditis (21 [2.4%] vs 61 [7.4%]; HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.19-0.52; p<0.001). Rates of new dialysis requirement were similar between groups (24 [2.8%] vs 28 [3.2%]; HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.49-1.46; p=0.135). Conclusions: In this large propensity-matched real-world analysis, T-TEER and TTVR demonstrated comparable risks of HF hospitalization, stroke, and dialysis. However, T-TEER was associated with lower risks of permanent pacemaker implantation and infective endocarditis. These findings may help inform procedural selection and patient counseling as transcatheter tricuspid interventions continue to expand.

title: Abstract 10298: Comparative Outcomes of Transcatheter Tricuspid Edge-to-Edge Repair versus Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Introduction/Background: Mavacamten has expanded treatment options for patients with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM). However, the contemporary role of septal myectomy in the post-mavacamten era remains incompletely understood. Research Questions: To characterize patients undergoing septal myectomy following mavacamten approval and compare outcomes among patients eligible for either treatment strategy. Methods: We performed a retrospective single-center study of patients with symptomatic oHCM who were eligible for septal reduction therapy and were treated with either mavacamten or septal myectomy between 2022-2025. Baseline clinical and echocardiographic characteristics were compared between treatment groups. Patients undergoing septal myectomy were further classified according to whether they were eligible for either treatment strategy or had an alternative primary surgical indication. Clinical and echocardiographic outcomes at approximately 1 year were evaluated among patients eligible for either treatment strategy. Results: A total of 56 patients underwent treatment with mavacamten and 36 patients underwent septal myectomy during the study period. Compared with patients treated with mavacamten, patients undergoing septal myectomy were younger (60±14 vs 67±13 years, p=0.02), were more symptomatic (19% vs 0% with NYHA class IV symptoms, p<0.001), and more often had at least moderate mitral regurgitation (36% vs 16%, p=0.03) ( Table 1 ). LVOT gradients, LVEF, and septal thickness were comparable between the two groups. Among the 36 patients undergoing septal myectomy, only 19 (53%) were eligible for either mavacamten or myectomy, while 17 (47%) had other primary surgical indications including mitral or aortic valve disease requiring repair/replacement, apical hypertrophy/complex anatomy, or coronary artery disease requiring CABG ( Figure 1 ). Among patients eligible for either treatment strategy, both therapies resulted in substantial symptomatic and hemodynamic improvement at approximately 1 year of follow up. LVOT gradient with Valsalva decreased from a mean of 81 to 12 mmHg following mavacamten and from 82 to 3 mmHg following myectomy (β=-9.2, p=0.005) (Figure 2a) . NYHA class improved following both treatments, with 74% of patients becoming asymptomatic (NYHA class I) after septal myectomy and 50% after mavacamten treatment, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.11) ( Figure 2b ). Conclusions: In the post-mavacamten era, septal myectomy continues to play an essential role in the management of oHCM, particularly among patients with complex anatomy or other concomitant cardiac conditions requiring surgery. Among patients eligible for either treatment strategy, both mavacamten and septal myectomy provided substantial symptomatic and hemodynamic improvement.
title: Abstract 10317: Characteristics and Outcomes of Patients Selected for Mavacamten versus Septal Myectomy in Contemporary Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Practice

abstract: Background: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) requires rapid post-arrest intervention, often including coronary angiography, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), targeted temperature management (TTM), and mechanical circulatory support (MCS). While sex-based disparities in post-arrest care have been documented in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, very few studies have examined whether similar gaps exist in IHCA. This study aims to evaluate sex-based differences in post-arrest procedural utilization and in-hospital mortality among IHCA patients nationally. Hypothesis: Based on trends observed in other cardiac diseases, we hypothesize that women with IHCA are less likely to receive post-arrest interventional procedures and therefore experience higher in-hospital mortality compared to men. Methods: We analyzed the National Inpatient Sample database from 2016 to 2022, identifying adult IHCA hospitalizations using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision codes. Primary outcomes included utilization of coronary angiography, PCI, TTM, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and MCS, as well as in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression models were created to estimate odds ratios, adjusted for age, Elixhauser comorbidity index, race/ethnicity, insurance type, income quartile, illness severity, hospital teaching status, weekend admission, and year. Results: Out of the 347,034 IHCA hospitalizations sampled, 41.9% were female. Compared to men, women were slightly older (65.5 vs. 63.5 years) with similar comorbidity burden and lower procedural utilization across all interventions. After adjustment, women had 32% lower odds of coronary angiography (OR: 0.68; 95% CI: 0.667-0.696), 41% lower odds of PCI (OR: 0.59; 95% CI: 0.572-0.615), 15% lower odds of ECMO (OR: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.775-0.921), and 29% lower odds of MCS (OR: 0.71; 95% CI: 0.585-0.871). TTM was modestly more common in women (OR: 1.22; 95% CI: 1.083-1.384). Women had 11% higher adjusted odds of in-hospital mortality (OR: 1.11; 95% CI: 1.089-1.121). The sex gap in angiography persisted across all racial groups but was attenuated in Black patients (interaction OR: 1.19; p<0.001). All values were statistically significant (p-value <0.05). Conclusion: This study showed that women with IHCA, despite similar comorbidity burden to men, are consistently less likely to receive post-arrest interventional procedures, contributing to higher in-hospital mortality even after adjusting for socioeconomic and clinical factors. Combined with documented sex-specific disparities in other cardiac diseases, these findings highlight a strong necessity for investigating possible barriers to post-arrest care at both the individual and system level.
title: Abstract 10344: Sex-Based Disparities in Post-Arrest Procedural Utilization and In-Hospital Mortality Among Patients with In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: Intermittent prosthetic aortic valve dysfunction causing episodic acute severe aortic regurgitation (AR) is rare and may mimic acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Dynamic prosthetic valve dysfunction may produce global subendocardial ischemia with left-main-equivalent electrocardiographic changes despite angiographically normal coronary arteries. Case: A 41-year-old male with prior rheumatic heart disease underwent double valve replacement nearly two decades earlier with mechanical mitral and aortic prostheses. He presented with recurrent episodes of chest pain, dyspnea, pulmonary edema, and hemoptysis over several years. Previous coronary angiography and fluoroscopy performed during asymptomatic periods were normal. During an acute hospitalization, he developed respiratory distress, hypotension, bilateral pulmonary crackles, and intermittent absence of prosthetic aortic valve clicks. Electrocardiography demonstrated diffuse ST-segment depression with ST elevation in lead aVR suggestive of left main coronary artery occlusion. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography during symptoms revealed acute severe AR with restricted prosthetic leaflet motion. Cine-fluoroscopy confirmed intermittent fixation of the tilting-disc prosthesis in a semi-open position, while repeat coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries. Discussion: The patient underwent emergency redo aortic valve replacement. Intraoperative findings confirmed centripetal pannus ingrowth interfering with the hinge mechanism and intermittently fixing the prosthetic disc in the open position without associated thrombus. The dysfunctional valve was replaced with a mechanical prosthesis, with complete postoperative symptom resolution. This case highlights a rare “hemodynamic ACS” phenotype in which acute severe AR produced diffuse subendocardial ischemia and lead aVR ST elevation despite normal coronary arteries. Resting imaging may appear deceptively normal between symptomatic episodes, making symptom-triggered multimodality imaging essential. Recognition of this entity is critical to avoid misdiagnosis and delays in surgical intervention
title: Abstract 10348: Intermittent Mechanical Aortic Valve Dysfunction Mimicking Left Main Coronary Artery Occlusion on ECG

abstract: Background: Watchman endocarditis is a rare phenomenon with only case series described in the literature. There are no guidelines on how to best manage Watchman endocarditis. Management can prove challenging given the uncertainty of the diagnosis and balancing the risks of potential surgical/percutaneous interventions. Case: A 74-year-old male with a remote history of pacemaker extraction due to lead-associated endocarditis underwent an uncomplicated Watchman device placement for stroke prevention, due to frequent falls and a CHA 2 DS 2- VASC score of 6. Six weeks later, he presented with diabetic ketoacidosis and sepsis and was ultimately diagnosed with MSSA bacteremia. Decision-Making: Initial transthoracic echocardiogram did not demonstrate any abnormalities and blood cultures cleared after 4 days. Despite improvement in inflammatory markers, a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was obtained to further evaluate for potential endocarditis. This demonstrated two small mobile echo-genetic masses on the Watchman device (0.87cm x 0.48cm and 0.78cm x 0.66cm) (Figure 1) without evidence of valvular endocarditis. Watchman endocarditis was considered, however given his improved clinical picture, thrombus was favored and conservative treatment with anticoagulation and intravenous antibiotic therapy was undertaken. During his hospitalization, he complained of back pain and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging revealed pre-vertebral and ventral cervical epidural abscesses. TEE was repeated which demonstrated three echo-dense Watchman masses (16x5.7mm, 9.2x7.4 mm, and 6.7 mm) (Figure 2). Cardiothoracic surgery was consulted, however the patient suffered a stroke and subsequently died. Conclusion: Watchman infections are rare and its diagnosis and management prove challenging. There is high mortality with both conservative and surgical/percutaneous interventions with both approaches lacking evidence. We present a difficult case of watchman endocarditis where conservative therapy did not yield a successful outcome. Further research is required to define optimal management and timing of removal.
title: Abstract 10379: An Unlikely Culprit: A Rare Case of Watchman Endocarditis

abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is prevalent among patients with acute mesenteric ischemia and may reflect embolic etiology, underlying cardiovascular disease, or both.
