Statistical analyses were conducted with RevMan 5.4, using pooled risk ratios and a random-effects model, with heterogeneity evaluated through the Cochran Q test and I 2 statistic. Results: Twenty-one randomized controlled trials were included. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor (GPI) therapy did not significantly reduce 30-day all-cause mortality (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-1.05; P=0.11) or 6-month mortality (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-1.05; P=0.10) compared with control. GPI use was associated with a significant reduction in heart failure (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.40-0.89; P=0.01). Favorable but non-significant trends were observed for recurrent myocardial infarction (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.49-1.02; P=0.06) and target vessel revascularization (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.71-1.01; P=0.07). No significant differences were observed in TIMI flow <3, stroke, or thrombocytopenia. Subgroup analyses demonstrated a significant reduction in 30-day mortality with tirofiban (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.34-0.94; P=0.03), while abciximab, eptifibatide, and zalunfiban showed no mortality benefit. Heart failure reduction was most pronounced with abciximab (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.20-0.87) and tirofiban (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.93). Zalunfiban was associated with a higher risk of TIMI flow <3 (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.05-1.26; P=0.003). Trial sequential analysis indicated that the available evidence remains underpowered to establish definitive mortality benefits. Conclusion: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, particularly tirofiban, show potential in reducing 30-day mortality and heart failure in STEMI patients, with modest benefits observed for recurrent myocardial infarction and target vessel revascularization. However, further studies with lower heterogeneity are needed to confirm these findings and optimize treatment strategies.
title: Abstract 11085: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa Inhibitors in ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction: A Grade Assessed Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a causal risk factor for native calcific aortic stenosis, which shares pathobiology with bioprosthetic structural valve degeneration (SVD). Whether elevated Lp(a) predicts adverse outcomes after surgical or transcatheter bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement is uncertain. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing elevated serum Lp(a) measured by any validated assay with lower Lp(a) concentrations in patients with bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. Hypothesis: Elevated Lp(a) is associated with higher rates of SVD, all-cause mortality, and subclinical leaflet thrombosis/hypoattenuated leaflet thickening (SLT/HALT) after bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane were searched through May 2026 for studies using prespecified elevated Lp(a) thresholds (predominantly ≥30 mg/dL) vs lower Lp(a) and (i) SVD, (ii) all-cause mortality, or (iii) SLT/HALT after bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. Hazard ratios (HR) and odds ratios (OR) were pooled separately by outcome using inverse-variance random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed by I 2 . Results: Six studies were included, encompassing 1,548 patients. Compared with lower Lp(a) concentrations, elevated serum Lp(a) was associated with a significantly higher risk of SVD (pooled HR 2.91; 95% CI 1.76-4.83; p<0.0001; I 2 =7%; three studies; Figure 1) and all-cause mortality (pooled HR 1.53; 95% CI 1.13-2.08; p=0.006; I 2 =16%; four studies; Figure 2). For SLT/HALT, there was no significant difference between groups (pooled OR 2.77; 95% CI 0.75-10.22; p=0.13; I 2 =37%; two studies; Figure 3). Conclusions: Elevated Lp(a) was associated with significantly increased risks of SVD and all-cause mortality following bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. Although no significant association was observed for SLT/HALT, the direction of effect was consistent with increased risk.
title: Abstract 11096: Elevated Lipoprotein(a) and Bioprosthetic Valve Outcomes: A Sytematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Transcatheter tricuspid replacement (TTVR) is an emerging, minimally invasive intervention for tricuspid regurgitation. The risks associated with post-procedural permanent pacemaker (PPM) placement after TTVR are unclear. We evaluated whether presence of conduction disturbances including an epsilon-like wave, “e-wave,” was associated with requiring PPM. Methods: Patients who underwent TTVR at Columbia University 2017-2024 were included in this retrospective study. Exclusion criteria included: PPM prior to TTVR, no electrocardiogram (EKG) within 1 week prior to TTVR, and no EKG within 1 week after TTVR. EKGs were adjudicated by 3 reviewers for rhythm, presence of bundle branch block, and “e-wave”, defined as notching of the QRS and/or the presence of an additional low amplitude wave, either positive or negative, after isoelectric phase within 55msec of the QRS and occurring before the T wave in any lead (Fig. 1). Fisher’s exact test was used for statistical analysis. Results: 80 patients underwent TTVR. Three were excluded due to EKGs outside the designated timeframe or having missing data; 20 were excluded due to the presence of a PPM prior to TTVR. The mean age of patients was 76.6 years (SD=10 years); 34 (60%) were female. 13 patients (22.8%) required PPM post-procedurally. At baseline, 5 (38.4%) patients who required PPM had RBBB & 6 (46.1%) had an e-wave , among patients who did not require PPM 17 (38.6%) had RBBB & 7 (15.9%) had an e-wave. Post procedurally, 11 of the patients requiring PPM (84.6%) had RBBB. Among the patients who required PPM post procedurally 10 (76.9%) had an e-wave post-procedure. Of the 44 patients who did not require a PPM, 22 (50%) had a RBBB (p=0.07); 11 (25%) had an e-wave post-procedure (p-value=0.002). Conclusion: Odds of post-procedure e-waves were 7.1 times higher in patients requiring PPM after TTVR, than those who did not, indicating this novel marker may be useful in identifying patients who will require PPM after TTVR. Odds of post-procedure RBBB was 3.6 times higher in patients requiring PPM after TTVR. More research is needed to understand the pathophysiological significance of specific morphologies of RBBB such as the e- wave in conduction disease.
title: Abstract 11097: Novel Electrocardiographic Marker, Right Bundle Branch Block & the “e-wave,” Associated with Increased Risk for Permanent Pacemaker After Transcatheter Tricuspid Replacement

abstract: Background: Cerebral embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to reduce periprocedural stroke risk during transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Despite regulatory approval of the Sentinel Cerebral Protection System, real-world utilization remains low and observational evidence on clinical effectiveness is limited. Methods: We analyzed consecutive TAVR procedures from a prospective institutional registry (D1-D3 cohort). Patients with documented EPD status were included. The primary outcome was a composite of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA). Secondary outcomes included ischemic stroke, permanent pacemaker implantation, major and minor vascular complications, and access-site bleeding. Unadjusted comparisons used Fisher's exact test. Adjusted analyses applied Firth penalized logistic regression (age, sex, STS score, LVEF, creatinine). A 1:3 propensity score-matched (nearest-neighbor, logit) cohort was constructed to further control for confounding. Results: Of 1,410 patients with documented EPD status, 59 (4.2%) received an EPD (all Sentinel Cerebral Protection System) and 1,351 did not. EPD recipients were younger (77.2 ± 8.7 vs. 82.6 ± 8.8 years; p<0.001) and less often female (25% vs. 41%; p=0.019). After 1:3 propensity score matching (59 EPD vs. 177 controls), the composite stroke/TIA rate was 0% vs. 1.7% (p=0.58). There were zero strokes in the EPD group in both the full and matched cohorts. Permanent pacemaker rates were numerically lower with EPD (6.8% vs. 11.9%; p=0.34), as were major vascular complications (0% vs. 3.4%; p=0.34). Access-site bleeding was numerically higher in the EPD group (5.1% vs. 1.1%; p=0.10). On Firth-adjusted logistic regression, EPD was associated with a non-significant reduction in stroke/TIA (OR 0.63; 95% CI 0.00-4.80; p=0.73) and a borderline increase in access-site bleeding (OR 3.45; 95% CI 0.89-10.08; p=0.07). Conclusions: In this propensity score-matched real-world analysis, EPD use during TAVR was associated with zero periprocedural strokes, though the difference was not statistically significant given the small EPD cohort. A trend toward higher access-site bleeding warrants further investigation. Larger prospective studies are needed to define the role of cerebral embolic protection in contemporary TAVR practice.
title: Abstract 11113: Periprocedural Stroke with Cerebral Embolic Protection in Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Propensity Score-Matched Real-World Registry Analysis

abstract: Introduction/Background: Mild paravalvular leak (PVL) is common following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), affecting approximately 25-30% of contemporary recipients. While moderate-to-severe PVL is an established predictor of adverse outcomes, the long-term prognostic significance of mild PVL remains debated. Prior meta-analyses are dominated by earlier-generation valves and higher-surgical-risk populations, limiting applicability to contemporary practice as TAVR expands to younger, lower-risk patients with longer post-procedural survival. Research Questions/Hypothesis: In contemporary cohorts undergoing TAVR, is mild PVL associated with increased long-term all-cause mortality compared with none/trace PVL? We hypothesized that incorporating recently published large cohort studies would refine prior estimates of the mortality risk attributable to mild PVL. Methods/Approach: A PRISMA-guided systematic search of PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov was conducted through March 2026. Eligible studies were observational cohorts or registries comparing mild PVL with none/trace PVL post-TAVR and reporting adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for all-cause mortality. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data. Adjusted HRs were pooled using inverse-variance weighted random-effects meta-analysis in RevMan Web. Heterogeneity was assessed via the I 2 statistic. Quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was performed. Results/Data: Five observational studies published 2022-2026 met inclusion criteria (n = 13,801; 3,467 mild PVL [25.1%]; 10,261 none/trace [74.3%]; 73 moderate-to-severe [0.5%]). All studies were rated high-quality (Newcastle-Ottawa 8-9). Mild PVL was associated with increased long-term all-cause mortality (pooled adjusted HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.26; p = 0.01) with moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 42%; χ 2 = 6.91; p = 0.14). Individual HRs ranged 1.01-1.41 with consistent direction. In leave-one-out analysis, pooled HRs ranged 1.10-1.18; significance was retained when Rosenzveig, Warraich, or Yokoyama were excluded but became borderline when Watanabe (HR 1.18; p = 0.06) or Okuno (HR 1.10; p = 0.07) were excluded. Conclusions: In this updated meta-analysis of contemporary TAVR cohorts, mild PVL was associated with a modest but statistically significant increase in long-term all-cause mortality compared with none/trace PVL. As TAVR expands to younger, lower-risk populations, these findings support continued efforts to minimize residual PVL at implantation and structured echocardiographic surveillance of patients with mild PVL at discharge.
title: Abstract 11120: Mild Paravalvular Leak Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement and Long-Term All-Cause Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Patients requiring oral anticoagulation (OAC) who have undergone percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or experienced acute coronary syndrome (ACS) face complex antithrombotic management decisions. While guidelines increasingly recommend discontinuation of aspirin within 1 to 12 months after the index event, real-world practice often extends aspirin use indefinitely. Whether continued aspirin confers benefit or harm beyond 1 year remains a critical clinical question. Research Question: Does the addition of aspirin to OAC beyond one year after ACS or PCI confer benefit or harm in terms of recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, bleeding, or all-cause mortality? Methods: Using the TriNetX federated research network at Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center, we identified adult patients with a history of ACS or PCI prescribed oral anticoagulation (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban). Patients were stratified into Aspirin + OAC (n = 17,680) and OAC Alone (n = 4,160). Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed on 25 baseline characteristics, yielding 4,160 matched patients per group. Outcomes were assessed 365 through 1,825 days (1-5 years) after the index event. Measures of association (Hazard ratio [HR]) and time-to-event analyses (Kaplan-Meier survival with log-rank testing and hazard ratios) were calculated for all-cause death, recurrent MI, stroke, and bleeding. Results: After matching, baseline characteristics were well balanced (mean age 72.3 years; 38-41% female). Compared with OAC alone, aspirin + OAC was associated with significantly higher rates of recurrent MI (5.8% vs. 2.2%; HR 2.54, 95% CI 1.98-3.27, p < 0.001), stroke (4.3% vs. 2.6%; HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.13-1.82, p = 0.003), and bleeding (7.0% vs. 5.0%; HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.01-1.45, p = 0.041). All-cause mortality risk was similar (15.1% vs. 15.4%; risk difference -0.002, p = 0.760). Conclusions: Continuation of aspirin alongside OAC beyond 1 year after ACS or PCI was associated with higher risks of recurrent MI, stroke, and bleeding without clear mortality benefit on risk analysis. The mortality benefit seen on hazard ratio analysis is likely not clinically significant given the small risk deference (-0.002) and survivorship bias in the aspirin + OAC cohort. These findings support recent data favoring OAC monotherapy in stabilized post-ACS/PCI patients.
title: Abstract 11124: Outcomes of Aspirin Addition to Oral Anticoagulation Beyond One Year After Acute Coronary Syndrome or Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

abstract: Introduction: A 70-year-old man with advanced malignancy receiving 6 months of ipilimumab, nivolumab, and relatlimab, was found during a routine infusion visit to have markedly elevated high-sensitivity troponin I (1236 ng/L, rising to 1936 ng/L). He remained minimally symptomatic, reporting only chronic dyspnea, and electrocardiogram showed chronic repolarization abnormalities, with no dynamic changes. Diagnostic Assessment: CMR (Figure 1A) showed patchy mid-septal late gadolinium enhancement in a nonischemic subepicardial distribution, with T1 and T2 prolongation, newly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 37%, and global hypokinesis, supporting myocarditis. Immunosuppressive therapy was started after CMR. Because the initial rapid rise in cardiac enzymes raised a concern for an alternative diagnosis despite limited symptoms, coronary CT angiography (Figure 1B) was completed and demonstrated chronic total occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery with mixed calcified and noncalcified plaques and retrograde filling from the right coronary artery. Therapeutic Intervention and Clinical Course: The patient received methylprednisolone (1g IV, daily x 3 doses), along with abatacept (10mg/kg IV, daily x 2 doses) and ruxolitinib (10mg PO twice daily), for suspected immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis. Cardiac enzymes then declined slowly (Figure 1C). Given the LAD chronic total occlusion and viable myocardium at risk, multidisciplinary discussion supported coronary angiography (Figure 1D) with PCI and drug-eluting stent placement, achieving full reperfusion on day 2. After a slight rise around catheterization, cardiac enzymes declined steadily, and the patient reported improvement in dyspnea. Management required treating myocarditis while evaluating and revascularizing clinically silent but high-risk coronary occlusion. The patient was discharged on a prednisone taper, guideline-directed medical therapy, dual antiplatelet therapy, and follow-up with serial biomarkers, electrocardiograms, and plan for repeat CMR. Conclusion: Myocarditis and obstructive coronary disease may co-occur during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, even in minimally symptomatic patients. Findings consistent with myocarditis should not preclude further evaluation for ischemia when the biomarker trajectory is discordant. Multimodality imaging and multidisciplinary management informed immunosuppression, revascularization, and follow-up.
title: Abstract 11160: Steroids and Stents: Myocarditis and Coronary Occlusion with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy

abstract: Background: People with HIV face 1.5- to 2-fold higher atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk compared with the general population, even with effective antiretroviral therapy (ART). Whether this excess risk persists in people with HIV achieving sustained HIV-1 RNA ≤20 copies/mL without any viral blips (21–200 copies/mL) remains unknown. We examined cardiovascular outcomes in this cohort compared with healthcare-engaged controls without HIV. Methods: Using the TriNetX federated deidentified healthcare database, we identified adults ≥18 years with HIV on continuous ART (2015–2023) with sustained viral suppression (≤20 copies/mL on ≥ 2 measurements) and no viral blips, free of prior ASCVD events (including acute myocardial infarction [AMI], stroke, heart failure, and prior revascularization). The comparator cohort comprised adults without HIV who had serial lipid/HbA1c screening, ≥10 ambulatory visits spanning ≥1 year, and no prevalent ASCVD. Propensity score matching (1:1) was done on key covariates including demographics, comorbidities, and medications. The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; AMI, cerebral infarction, and all-cause mortality). Secondary outcomes included stroke and AMI individually. Urinary tract infection (UTI) and acute upper respiratory infection (URI) served as negative control outcomes. Outcomes were assessed from 1 to 10 years post-index using Kaplan-Meier analysis with Cox proportional hazards regression. Results: After matching, cohorts were well-balanced (standardized mean difference < 0.1 for covariates; n=1,978 in each group). Adults with HIV had higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.80, 95% CI 1.20 –2.70, p=0.004) and MACE outcomes (HR 1.52, 95% CI 1.12–2.06, p=0.007). Stroke was similar between groups (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.62–1.54, p=0.93). AMI events were too few for analysis. Both negative controls showed null results (UTI: HR 1.04, p=0.80; URI: HR 1.00, p=0.98). Conclusions: People with HIV with sustained viral suppression without viral blips had significantly higher all-cause mortality and composite MACE compared with healthcare-engaged controls, with MACE findings likely driven by all-cause mortality. These findings may suggest persistent residual cardiovascular risk despite durable viral suppression and highlight the need for further investigation and continued attention to cardiovascular prevention strategies in people with HIV.
title: Abstract 11169: Residual Cardiovascular Risk in People with HIV with Sustained Viral Suppression Without Viral Blips: A Propensity Score-Matched Retrospective Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is associated with residual atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk despite lipid-lowering therapy. High-intensity statins effectively reduce LDL-C; they may modestly increase Lp(a). In contrast, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors (PCSK9i) reduce both LDL-C and Lp(a), although comparative outcome data in patients with elevated Lp(a) remain limited. Research Question: Among patients with elevated baseline Lp(a), is initiation of PCSK9i monotherapy, compared with high-intensity statin monotherapy, associated with lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)? Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using a target-trial emulation framework using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, including adults with hyperlipidemia and elevated Lp(a) (≥75 nmol/L or ≥30 mg/dL) from January 2015 to December 2025. Patients initiating PCSK9i monotherapy meeting eligibility criteria (Time 0) were compared with those initiating high-intensity statin monotherapy during the same window, using an intention-to-treat framework. Propensity score matching (1:1) was used to balance standardized mean differences to <0.1 across demographics, comorbidities, laboratory values, cardiovascular risk factors, and baseline medications. The primary outcome was MACE (all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, TIA). Secondary outcomes included major adverse limb events (MALE), acute myocardial infarction, the composite of stroke, TIA, or intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), coronary revascularization, peripheral revascularization, all-cause mortality, and ICH as a standalone outcome. Follow-up began at Time 0 up to 1 year. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate HRs and 95% CIs. Results: Among 10,934 eligible patients, 4,146 propensity score–matched patients were included (2,073 per group; mean age 61.5±11.4 years; 53.1% women). Median follow-up was 365 days in both cohorts. MACE occurred less frequently with PCSK9i monotherapy compared with high-intensity statin monotherapy at 1 year (8.3% vs. 12.2%; HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63–0.92; p=0.005). PCSK9i monotherapy was also associated with significantly lower rates of MALE (0.8% vs. 1.9%; HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.27–0.84; p=0.009). Acute myocardial infarction (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59–1.02; p=0.065) and the composite of stroke, TIA, or ICH (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.61–1.04; p=0.093) numerically favored PCSK9i without statistical significance. The falsification endpoint of gastritis did not differ between groups (HR 1.14; p=0.569). Conclusions: In patients with elevated Lp(a), PCSK9i monotherapy was associated with lower rates of MACE and MALE compared with high-intensity statin monotherapy at 1-year follow-up, suggesting a potential strategy to reduce residual ASCVD risk in this high-risk population.
title: Abstract 11178: Efficacy of Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin Kexin Type 9 Inhibitor versus Statin Monotherapy in Patients with Elevated Lipoprotein(a): A Target Trial Emulation

abstract: Introduction: Cardiac metastasis from a neuroendocrine tumor (NET) is rare, occurring in fewer than 5% of metastatic cases, typically involving the right heart via hematogenous spread. Epicardial metastasis in the territory of the left anterior descending artery (LAD) is exceedingly rare with only single-digit cases globally. We present a DOTATATE-confirmed epicardial NET deposit in the LAD territory, presenting as chest pain with coronary vasospasm involving LAD. Clinical Findings and Timeline: An 81-year-old man with metastatic small bowel NET on lanreotide, coronary artery disease with previous percutaneous intervention, deep vein thrombosis, COPD, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm presented with chest pain and hypotension. Electrocardiography was unremarkable and troponin elevated with a downtrending pattern, interpreted as type 2 NSTEMI in the setting of recent gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Echocardiography showed preserved ejection fraction, no wall motion abnormality, and severe aortic stenosis. On day three, crushing substernal chest pain with anterior ST elevation (Fig 1) and troponin rise developed, resolving within minutes. Coronary angiography revealed non-obstructive disease and also incidental aortocaval fistula. Patient subsequently died due to pulseless electrical activity. Diagnostic Assessment: Autopsy confirmed epicardial NET metastasis adjacent to the LAD (Fig 2). Chart review revealed a prior computed tomography identified an indeterminate anterior cardiac mass. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a 2.1 x 2.1 x 1.1 cm oval mass at the anterior cardiac margin adjacent to the interventricular groove in the LAD distribution, extrinsic to the heart.(Fig 3). DOTATATE positron emission tomography confirmed focal epicardial uptake and an avid mesenteric mass, establishing metastatic small bowel NET with epicardial involvement. Patient was not considered to be a surgical candidate, he was started on lanreotide; serial DOTATATE imaging confirmed stability including even two months prior to this admission. Discussion: This case highlights a rare epicardial NET metastasis adjacent to LAD . The nature of spread is unclear as hematogenous spread involving venous system would be mechanistically not possible and through arterial spread is difficult to postulate. We propose transient anterior ST elevation resulted from serotonin-mediated LAD vasospasm from the adjacent deposit — a mechanism not previously described. Cardiac NET involvement should remain an active consideration in such cases; acute coronary presentations may represent carcinoid manifestations rather than just conventional ischemic events.
title: Abstract 11205: A Rare Destination, a Rarer Presentation: Epicardial Carcinoid Metastasis Adjacent to Left Anterior Descending Coronary Artery

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock (CS) complicates approximately 10% of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) cases. End-stage renal disease (ESRD) patients represent a high-risk subgroup with accelerated atherosclerosis, excess comorbidities, and underutilization of evidence-based therapies. Prior studies have demonstrated that ESRD is an independent predictor of mortality in acute myocardial infarction complicated by CS, yet contemporary national data on temporal trends in incidence, mechanical circulatory support (MCS) utilization, and outcomes in this population remain limited. Methods: Adult hospitalizations with a principal diagnosis of STEMI and secondary diagnoses of ESRD and CS were identified from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database (2016-2023) utilizing ICD-10 codes. Outcomes studied were in-hospital mortality, coronary revascularization procedures, and use of percutaneous MCS (pMCS). Temporal trends were assessed using survey logistic regression, and multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of in-hospital mortality. Results: Of a total of 23,205 hospitalizations for STEMI in ESRD patients, 6,515 (28%) developed CS (mean age 66.4 ±11.3 years, 64.2% male). Prevalent comorbidities included hypertension (91.6%), diabetes mellitus (69.1%), and dyslipidemia (50.4%). In-hospital mortality was 41%, with no significant change over the period studied (p trend 0.173). Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) were performed in 60.7% and 10.2% of patients, respectively (p trend 0.343 and 0.238, respectively). Overall pMCS use was 48.1% (p trend 0.417). Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) use decreased over the study period (31.6% to 21.4%, p trend 0.0008) while percutaneous ventricular assist device (pVAD) use increased (12% to 27.3%, p trend 0.0017). Age (OR 1.04, CI 1.02-1.05) and diabetes mellitus (OR 1.60, CI 1.16-2.19) were independent predictors of mortality, while PCI and CABG were associated with lower mortality (OR 0.41, CI 0.33-0.55; OR 0.28, CI 0.16-0.48, respectively). Conclusions: CS complicates a high percentage of STEMI in ESRD patients with a high in-hospital mortality. Despite increasing use of pVAD and most patients undergoing revascularization, mortality remains high. These findings call for further investigation into strategies to improve outcomes in this high-risk population.
title: Abstract 11209: Incidence, Management and Outcomes of Cardiogenic Shock in Patients with End-Stage Renal Disease Presenting with ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Background: The optimal use of left ventricular (LV) unloading with Impella in patients receiving venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for cardiogenic shock (CS) remains an active area of clinical debate. Although observational data suggest a possible mortality benefit with combined Impella plus VA-ECMO (ECPELLA), concerns that the added device may increase infection risk have limited its adoption. We compared infection and mortality outcomes between ECPELLA and VA-ECMO alone in a contemporary cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of adult CS patients receiving ECMO-based mechanical circulatory support (MCS), comparing ECPELLA to VA-ECMO alone. Outcomes were time to first chart-reviewed, clinically diagnosed infection and 60 day all-cause mortality, both assessed within 60 days of MCS placement. For the infection analysis, death, bridging to durable therapy, and discharge were treated as competing events. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression compared ECPELLA with VA-ECMO alone, adjusting for pre-specified baseline covariates: age, female sex, diabetes, lactate at MCS placement, acute myocardial infarction (AMI) etiology, cardiac arrest on admission, and Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) stage >3 at MCS placement. Results: The cohort included 150 patients (76 VA-ECMO alone, 74 ECPELLA); median age was 56 vs 57 years. ECPELLA patients more often had SCAI stage >3 at MCS placement (77% vs 54%), with similar lactate at MCS placement (median 6.0 vs 5.0 mmol/L). Infection within 60 days occurred in 32 (42%) VA-ECMO and 29 (39%) ECPELLA patients. In multivariable Cox regression, ECPELLA was not associated with infection hazard compared with VA-ECMO alone (adjusted HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39-1.17, p=0.16); findings were consistent by Fine-Gray competing-risks analysis (subdistribution HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.48-1.35, p=0.40) and Gray's test (p=0.70). Sixty-day mortality was 50% (VA-ECMO) vs 36% (ECPELLA; log-rank p=0.07); in multivariable Cox regression, ECPELLA showed a non-significant trend toward lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.36-1.09, p=0.10), while higher lactate (HR 1.10 per mmol/L, p<0.001) and older age (HR 1.03 per year, p=0.002) were independently associated with mortality. Conclusions: In patients receiving ECMO-based mechanical circulatory support for cardiogenic shock, adding LV unloading with Impella (ECPELLA) was not associated with increased infection risk compared with VA-ECMO alone, with a non-significant trend toward lower 60-day mortality. These findings address a key safety concern about ECPELLA and warrant prospective evaluation.
title: Abstract 11213: Adding Left Ventricular Unloading with Impella to Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Cardiogenic Shock: Infection Risk and Mortality

abstract: Background: Assessment of aortic valve stenosis can be fraught with error due to inadequate signal, beam-width artifact, or beam angulation. Case: A 91-year-old female with a history of coronary artery bypass grafting, pacemaker implantation, mitral stenosis, and severe pulmonary hypertension underwent transcarotid transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) three weeks prior to admission for a right acetabular fracture. TTE revealed severe eccentric tricuspid regurgitation (TR) with a peak velocity of 4.4 m/s (Figure A). Color Doppler across the TAVI was aliased, and peak velocity was 4.4 m/s with a mean gradient of 46 mmHg, concerning for TAVI obstruction or patient-prosthesis mismatch. Orthopedic surgery was paused given concern for severe aortic valve stenosis. Decision-Making: In the absence of symptoms since TAVI, the TTE hemodynamic data were considered questionable. Re-examination of the images revealed the aorta in the apical 5-chamber view (Figure B) overlying the eccentric TR jet; the aliasing, elevated velocity, and increased gradient may have reflected Doppler sampling of TR velocities (beam-width artifact). Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) (Figure C), performed in the transgastric position to allow parallel Doppler beam interrogation of the TAVI away from regurgitant jets, revealed a velocity of 3.4 m/s and a mean gradient of 25 mmHg, within the upper limits of normal for a small TAVI valve. The patient subsequently underwent uneventful surgery. Conclusion: It is important to consider potential sources of error when evaluating prosthetic valves to avoid inaccurate assessment of stenosis severity, which may negatively impact patient care and clinical decision-making.
title: Abstract 11215: Stenotic TAVI or Not? Examine the Neighborhood!

abstract: Introduction: Surgical aortic valve closure during left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation can prevent aortic insufficiency and backflow but may eliminate native left ventricular egress, creating complete LVAD dependence. This physiology may become maladaptive when LVAD preload is limited. Case Presentation: A 59-year-old man with sarcoid cardiomyopathy and destination-therapy HeartMate 3 LVAD support had undergone LVAD implantation with atrial septal defect closure and Park stitch closure of the aortic valve. After implantation at an outside center, he was unable to rehabilitate, became progressively weaker, and grew dependent on family for activities of daily living. After relocating for family support, he presented with recurrent exertional syncope, low-flow alarms, and an inability to ambulate. LVAD interrogation showed flow 2.6 L/min at 4900 rpm and multiple alarms. Echocardiography showed ejection fraction 30% to 35%, LV end-diastolic dimension 3.5 cm, right ventricular dysfunction, and a surgically closed aortic valve that did not open. LVAD speed was reduced to 4700 rpm because of the small LV cavity and suspected inflow limitation. Low-output syncope was attributed to recurrent suction physiology and LVAD inflow limitation. With complete aortic valve closure, compensatory native forward flow was unavailable during exertion or low preload. Management: Redo surgery was high risk given destination-therapy LVAD support, frailty, and right ventricular dysfunction. Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation-supported transcatheter electrosurgery-assisted TAVR was performed to restore controlled aortic outflow. Aortic root angiography and transvenous pacing were performed. An AL1 guide, Quick-Cross catheter, piggyback system, and Astato wire were used to traverse the surgically closed valve. Balloon dilation created space for valve deployment, followed by implantation of a 26-mm Edwards SAPIEN 3 valve. Outcomes: Postprocedure echocardiography showed a well-seated valve, peak gradient 3 mmHg, mean gradient 1 mmHg, no significant aortic regurgitation, and no perivalvular leak. No immediate complication was documented. After return to 4900 rpm, LVAD interrogation showed a flow of 3.2 L/min and no recurrent low-flow alarms during inpatient observation. He completed inpatient rehabilitation with improved strength and ability to perform ADLs and IADLs, then relocated home. Discussion: This case highlights maladaptive complete LVAD dependence. In patients with small LV cavities, recurrent suction and low-flow episodes may cause exertional syncope, progressive frailty, and poor quality of life when native flow is blocked by complete aortic valve closure. Transcatheter electrosurgery-assisted TAVR may restore controlled aortic outflow when redo surgery is prohibitive.
title: Abstract 11222: When Complete LVAD Dependence Becomes Maladaptive: Transcatheter Electrosurgery-Assisted Restoration of Aortic Valve Opening After Surgical Closure

abstract: Keywords: Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension, Coronary Circulation, Collateral Circulation Introduction: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is a rare but potentially curable cause of pulmonary hypertension due to persistent organized thromboemboli leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular dysfunction. It may follow pulmonary embolism, though many patients lack a documented venous thromboembolism history. Pathophysiology involves fibrotic vascular obstruction and microvascular remodeling. Chronic hypoperfusion promotes systemic collateral formation, most commonly bronchial; coronary-pulmonary collaterals are rare (10-18%) and seen in severe disease. We report a case of bilateral coronary collaterals and its clinical implications. Case: Patient Information- A 54-year-old woman with CTEPH, pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular dysfunction, mixed lung disease, heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, and atrial flutter presented with chest pain and palpitations three days after elective cardioversion. Clinical Findings and Timeline: She was hypotensive, with elevated NT-proBNP and normal troponins; ECG showed atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response. Her medical history is notable for CTEPH developed after DVT/PE in 1992, treated with pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (1992, 2009) and later balloon pulmonary angioplasty (2024), with recurrent right heart failure. Diagnostic Assessment and Therapeutic Interventions: On this admission, TTE showed new mild LV dysfunction with apical hypokinesis and severe pulmonary hypertension (RVSP 62 mmHg, PVR 13.4 WU). CT angiography suggested an aberrant pulmonary artery vessel. Symptoms improved with rate control. Coronary angiography revealed normal coronaries with extensive bilateral atrial branch collaterals to the pulmonary vasculature. Given the absence of obstruction in the collaterals, no further intervention was done for these collaterals. Discussion and Conclusion: Coronary-pulmonary collaterals represent a rare adaptation to chronic pulmonary artery obstruction and may cause coronary steal, leading to ischemic symptoms without obstructive coronary disease. In this case, symptoms were likely due to demand ischemia from coronary steal in the setting of tachyarrhythmia. Recognition is important as these collaterals may mimic fistulas and influence surgical or interventional planning. Although management was unchanged acutely in the above case, identification explained the symptoms and has implications for future pulmonary vascular interventions.
title: Abstract 11233: Coronary Artery Collateralization to the Pulmonary Circulation in Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension: A Case Report

abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is associated with an increased risk of stroke and systemic thromboembolism. Although left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an established alternative for patients unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation, its role in patients who remain eligible for anticoagulation remains uncertain. Recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have reported conflicting results. Therefore, we performed an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of five RCTs comparing LAAC with anticoagulation in this population. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases were systematically searched through April 2026. A random-effects model was used to calculate risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical analyses were conducted using Review Manager software, version 5.4.1. Results: Five RCTs comprising 5,404 patients were included, with a mean follow-up of 3.4 years. Among trials reporting CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc scores, the weighted mean score was approximately 4.0, consistent with a population at moderate-to-high thromboembolic risk. Compared with anticoagulation, LAAC was associated with significantly lower risks of clinically relevant non-major bleeding (CRNMB) (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.41-0.64; p < 0.001; I 2 = 0%) and non-procedure related bleeding (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.49-0.71; p < 0.001; I 2 = 0%), but a higher risk of ischemic stroke (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.09-2.02; p = 0.01; I 2 = 0%). No significant differences were observed in cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.62-1.26; p = 0.49; I 2 = 58%), all-cause stroke (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.81-1.50; p = 0.55; I 2 = 25%), systemic embolism (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.34-4.38; p = 0.76; I 2 = 0%), or major bleeding (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.80-1.19; p = 0.82; I 2 = 0%). In subgroup analyses by anticoagulation strategy, LAAC was associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.58-0.99; p = 0.05; I 2 = 0%) and hemorrhagic stroke (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.07-0.58; p = 0.003; I 2 = 0%) compared with warfarin. Conclusions: Among anticoagulation-eligible patients with AF, LAAC showed similar risks of cardiovascular mortality, all-cause stroke, systemic embolism and major bleeding compared with anticoagulation, but was associated with significantly lower clinically relevant non-major and non-procedure related bleeding and a higher risk of ischemic stroke. These findings highlight the need for individualized selection of LAAC versus continued anticoagulation based on thromboembolic and bleeding risk.
title: Abstract 11235: Left Atrial Appendage Closure versus Oral Anticoagulation in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

abstract: Introduction: Cardiogenic shock (CS) unrelated to acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is increasingly managed with advanced mechanical circulatory support (MCS), including Impella and venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO). However, contemporary data examining sex-based differences in outcomes among these patients remain limited. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) from 2018 to 2023. Adult patients (≥18 years) with non-AMI cardiogenic shock supported with Impella, VA-ECMO, or both (ECPELLA) were identified using ICD-10-CM codes. Patients with acute myocardial infarction or COVID-19 were excluded. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included acute kidney injury (AKI), dialysis-requiring AKI, stroke, sepsis, bleeding complications, thromboembolic events, mechanical ventilation, and vascular complications. Multivariable logistic regression with adjustment for NIS survey weights, clustering, and strata was used to evaluate adjusted outcomes. Results: A total of 33,585 weighted hospitalizations met study criteria, including 23,405 males and 10,180 females. Females were younger than males (57.1 vs 58.8 years, p<0.001) and had a lower comorbidity burden (Charlson Comorbidity Index 2.82 vs 3.21, p<0.001). Females were more likely to receive VA-ECMO alone (38% vs 27%) and less likely to receive Impella alone (56% vs 65%), while ECPELLA was used in 6% of females and 8% of males. After adjustment, females had higher in-hospital mortality compared with males (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 1.11-1.39, p<0.001). Females also had higher odds of pulmonary embolism (aOR 1.39, 95% CI 1.17-1.66, p<0.001), vascular injury (aOR 1.62, 95% CI 1.17-2.26, p=0.004), intracranial bleeding (aOR 1.43, 95% CI 1.08-1.91, p=0.013), device-related thromboembolism (aOR 1.40, 95% CI 1.06-1.84, p=0.019), and mechanical ventilation (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 1.12-1.39, p<0.001). Conversely, females had lower odds of AKI (aOR 0.61, 95% CI 0.54-0.69, p<0.001), dialysis-requiring AKI (aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.90, p=0.001), and sepsis (aOR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.00, p=0.049). Males had longer length of stay (21.7 vs 18.6 days, p<0.001) and higher total hospital charges ($930,520 vs $838,238, p=0.001). Conclusion: Among patients with non-AMI CS receiving advanced MCS, females experienced significantly higher in-hospital mortality despite a lower baseline comorbidity burden. Female sex was independently associated with increased thrombotic, bleeding, and vascular complications. These findings highlight important sex-based disparities in outcomes and underscore the need for improved risk stratification and sex-specific management strategies in females with CS requiring advanced circulatory support.
title: Abstract 11263: Sex-Based Differences in Outcomes Among Patients with Non-Acute Myocardial Infarction-Related Cardiogenic Shock Supported with Advanced Mechanical Circulatory Support

abstract: Background: Percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (pLAAO) has emerged as a non-pharmacologic alternative to oral anticoagulation (OAC) for stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (AF). However, individual randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remain underpowered to detect meaningful differences in ischemic outcomes. We sought to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of pLAAO versus OAC using complementary statistical frameworks. Methods: We included RCTs comparing pLAAO versus OAC. Two analytical frameworks were applied to assess non-inferiority of pLAAO versus OAC. Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis utilized a normal-normal hierarchical model with a weakly informative prior, with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of Relative Risk (RR) = 1.40, consistent with the established margin used in the largest trial, CHAMPION-AF. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) with O'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending boundaries (α = 0.05, β = 0.20) determined whether the accrued sample size was sufficient to reliably establish or refute non-inferiority. The primary efficacy endpoint was ischemic stroke or systemic embolism; the primary safety endpoint was major bleeding. Results: For ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (4 RCTs, n = 5,714 patients), the Bayesian pooled RR was 1.44 (95% credible interval = 0.69 - 2.72; Figure 1 ). The posterior probability that pLAAO met the non-inferiority margin (RR < 1.40) was only 45.3%, with a 54.7% probability of exceeding it; thus, non-inferiority was not established. On TSA, the cumulative Z-curve for ischemic stroke or systemic embolism trended below zero, favoring OAC, without crossing the O'Brien-Fleming non-inferiority boundary ( Figure 2A). The accrued sample size (n = 5,714) remained below the required information size (RIS = 11,538). For major bleeding (6 RCTs, n = 6,951 patients), the TSA Z-curve entered the futility zone, indicating that a prespecified 20% relative risk reduction with pLAAO is unlikely to be demonstrated even with further evidence accumulation ( Figure 2B ). Conclusions: In this Bayesian meta-analysis and TSA synthesis of contemporary RCTs, pLAAO failed to establish non-inferiority compared to OAC for ischemic outcomes. Furthermore, TSA confirmed that current evidence remains insufficient to establish non-inferiority under prespecified margins, and that a meaningful reduction in major bleeding with pLAAO is unlikely with further evidence accumulation. These findings challenge the adequacy of current evidence supporting pLAAO as a non-inferior stroke-prevention strategy and underscore the need for larger, adequately powered trials before broader adoption.
title: Abstract 11268: Bayesian Meta Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion in Atrial Fibrillation

abstract: Introduction: Kidney transplant recipients have an increased risk of major adverse cardiac events (MACE). Ticagrelor has demonstrated benefit over clopidogrel in broader patient populations with acute coronary syndrome (ACS); however, outcomes among kidney transplant recipients remain unclear. Identifying optimal P2Y12 inhibitor treatment in these patients may help guide clinical decision-making. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that cardiovascular outcomes differ among kidney transplant recipients with acute coronary syndrome prescribed clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using TriNetX to identify kidney transplant recipients with a history of ACS who were prescribed either clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor post-transplant. Following pairwise propensity score matching, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was performed, and hazard ratios (HR) with log-rank P-values were calculated. Outcomes were assessed at 30, 180, and 365 days after the P2Y12 inhibitor was prescribed. The primary outcome was MACE, which was defined as myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure, cardiac arrest, or cerebral infarction. Secondary outcomes included MI, bleeding, acute kidney injury, and electrolyte imbalance. Results: In 421 matched pairs comparing ticagrelor to clopidogrel, ticagrelor was associated with a higher 1-year MACE risk of 65.1%, whereas clopidogrel had a 56.1% risk (HR, 1.526; 95% CI, 1.281-1.817). This difference held true in MI, where ticagrelor had a 50.8% risk, compared with 32.1% for clopidogrel (HR, 2.061; 95% CI, 1.660-2.558). These significant findings were also observed at 30 and 180 days. In 104 matched patients per group, prasugrel and ticagrelor did not significantly differ in MACE or MI at any of the three time points. Among 105 matched patients per group, prasugrel and clopidogrel did not significantly differ in MACE; although MI risk was higher with prasugrel at 1 month (30.5% vs 18.1%; HR, 1.807; 95% CI, 1.024-3.189) and 1 year (44.8% vs 31.4%; HR, 1.606; 95% CI, 1.029-2.508). Secondary outcomes, including bleeding, acute kidney injury, and electrolyte imbalance, showed no consistent differences across comparisons and time points. Conclusion: In this retrospective cohort study, ticagrelor was associated with significantly higher MI and MACE risk than clopidogrel in kidney transplant recipients with ACS. These findings are consistent with emerging evidence of worse ticagrelor outcomes in dialysis patients but differ from the PLATO trial findings for the general ACS population. Together, these results suggest potential differences among P2Y12 inhibitors for preventing adverse cardiac outcomes in certain high-risk patient populations and highlight the importance of future investigation to confirm these results.
title: Abstract 11269: Ticagrelor is Associated with Higher Major Adverse Cardiac Event Risk Than Clopidogrel in Kidney Transplant Recipients with Acute Coronary Syndrome: A TriNetX Retrospective Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Concomitant cardiac amyloidosis is increasingly recognized in patients with aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, its impact on in-hospital outcomes, particularly conduction abnormalities and device utilization, remains incompletely defined. We hypothesized that, despite a greater arrhythmia burden, patients with amyloidosis would not have higher rates of pacemaker implantation or in-hospital mortality after TAVR. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample. Adult hospitalizations with primary or secondary diagnoses of aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR were identified and stratified by the presence of amyloidosis. Baseline characteristics, comorbidities, and in-hospital outcomes were compared. Survey-weighted multivariable regression analyses evaluated the independent association of amyloidosis with mortality, conduction abnormalities, pacemaker implantation, length of stay, and hospitalization costs. Results: Among 396,090 weighted hospitalizations undergoing TAVR, 580 (0.1%) had concomitant amyloidosis. Patients with amyloidosis were older (81.4 vs. 78.9 years, p<0.01) and had a higher burden of heart failure (83.6% vs. 70.6%) and arrhythmias (76.7% vs. 51.9%) (both p<0.01). Unadjusted rates of third-degree atrioventricular block were higher in amyloidosis (12.9% vs. 8.7%, p=0.10), whereas pacemaker implantation was numerically lower (2.6% vs. 6.4%, p=0.09). After adjustment, amyloidosis was not associated with increased in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.1-4.8, p=0.70) or high-grade AV block (adjusted OR 1.1, 95% CI 0.6-1.9, p=0.71). However, it was associated with significantly lower odds of pacemaker implantation (adjusted OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.1-0.9, p=0.03) and reduced hospitalization costs (beta -$32,080, p<0.01), with no difference in length of stay. Conclusions: Among patients undergoing TAVR, concomitant amyloidosis was associated with a higher arrhythmia burden but lower rates of pacemaker implantation, without increased mortality. These findings are hypothesis-generating and may reflect differences in the recognition or management of conduction disease in this population, warranting prospective investigation.
title: Abstract 11329: Impact of Concomitant Cardiac Amyloidosis on Conduction Outcomes and Device Utilization After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Introduction: Pregnancy in patients with established pulmonary hypertension (PH) is associated with high maternal morbidity and mortality. Although guidelines have traditionally advised against pregnancy, they increasingly emphasize individualized risk assessment and shared decision-making. Most prior studies, focusing on pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), report maternal mortality rates of 11-25%. Recent studies, some of which include all World Health Organization (WHO) PH Groups in aggregate, report lower mortality (0.5-11.5%) but are limited by small sample size, a lack of racial and ethnic diversity or limited follow-up. Research question/hypothesis: We sought to characterize cardiovascular and obstetric outcomes among pregnant patients with established PH in a contemporary and diverse cohort, with outcomes stratified by WHO PH Group and followed up to 1 year postpartum. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study within an integrated healthcare system (Kaiser Permanente Northern California), including individuals with PH during pregnancy or with a prior PH diagnosis who subsequently became pregnant between 2010 and 2024. PH was defined by ICD diagnosis codes or by enrollment in a clinical Kaiser PAH database. For individuals with multiple pregnancies, the first pregnancy after PH diagnosis was included. Patients were classified according to WHO PH Group. Maternal cardiovascular outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, intensive care unit admission heart failure hospitalization, cardiogenic shock and need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Obstetric outcomes included pre-term delivery, spontaneous and therapeutic abortion, and mode of delivery. Results:Among 45 pregnancies, WHO Group 2 PH (left heart disease, 53%) and Group 1 (PAH, 33%) predominated. The cohort included patients with a mean age of 33 years (ranging 29-38 years), was racially/ethnically diverse (31% Asian, 15% Black, 27% Hispanic, 20% White),and 39% were primigravida pregnancies. Moderate or severe right ventricular enlargement by echocardiography was present in 19%, PH-specific medical therapy was utilized in 36% and loop diuretics in 60% of pregnancies. There was one maternal death which occurred in a Group 1 PAH patient (overall maternal mortality 2%). ICU admission (27%) and cardiogenic shock (20%) were more common in Group 1 PAH, whereas heart failure hospitalization (50%) was more common in Group 2 PH (see Table 1). Adverse obstetric outcomes were more common in Group 1 PAH, including preterm birth (33%) and spontaneous abortion (20%); cesarean delivery occurred in 46% of pregnancies. Conclusion: Despite low material mortality in pregnant patients with PH, cardiovascular morbidity remains substantial. Group 2 PH may represent a growing, underappreciated risk factor for material CV morbidity among pregnant patients.
title: Abstract 11337: Cardiovascular and Obstetric Outcomes Among Pregnant Patients with Pulmonary Hypertension Stratified by WHO Pulmonary Hypertension Group

abstract: Background: Renal denervation (RDN) reduces blood pressure in resistant hypertension, yet approximately one-third of patients show minimal response. Sham-controlled randomized trials demonstrate modest average systolic blood pressure (SBP) reductions of approximately 5.9 mmHg, raising the question of whether baseline sympathetic nervous system (SNS) activity can identify patients most likely to benefit from RDN. Objectives: (1) Quantify SBP reduction in sympathetically phenotyped patients versus unselected RCT populations; (2) rank SNS markers—including muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA), baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), heart rate variability (HRV), resting heart rate, and orthostatic blood pressure response—by predictive strength; (3) assess whether device generation or medication status modifies the SNS-response relationship; (4) define an evidence-based clinical phenotype for ideal RDN candidates. Methods: A systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane databases (inception through January 2026) identified 50 studies (N=5,113) reporting baseline sympathetic measures and blood pressure outcomes after RDN. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed using the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method. Subgroup analyses were conducted by device generation, medication status, and predictor category. Results: Patients phenotyped by elevated baseline MSNA achieved a pooled SBP reduction of –15.79 mmHg (95% CI: –19.33 to –12.25), a 3-fold greater response versus –5.94 mmHg in unselected sham-controlled trial populations. Heterogeneity among MSNA-phenotyped studies was absent (I 2 =0%, p=0.90), confirming robust consistency across global centers. Impaired BRS and orthostatic hypertension emerged as the strongest clinical predictors, while resting heart rate and pulse wave velocity (PWV) provided modest value. Predictive power was independent of device generation (1st vs. 2nd generation, p=0.67) and medication status (on vs. off medication, p=0.40). A tiered selection algorithm was developed: Tier 1 (bedside screening: heart rate >70 bpm, orthostatic BP), Tier 2 (office assessment: HRV, PWV), Tier 3 (specialized testing: BRS, MSNA), with ≥2 positive markers identifying ideal candidates (expected response ~16 vs. ~6 mmHg). Conclusions: Sympathetic phenotyping identifies high-responders achieving 3-fold greater blood pressure reduction after RDN. Incorporating markers such as BRS, orthostatic BP response, and resting heart rate into a tiered selection algorithm transforms RDN from a modest population-level intervention into a highly effective precision-medicine therapy, supporting a paradigm shift toward individualized patient selection.
title: Abstract 11342: Baseline Sympathetic Nervous System Activity and Blood Pressure Response to Renal Denervation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Coronary artery embolism accounts for approximately 5% of all myocardial infarction (MI) cases. Infective endocarditis (IE) can be culture-negative in up to 30% of cases, posing significant diagnostic challenges. Case: A 40-year-old male with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation status post ablation and a recent gout flare treated with oral steroids and indomethacin presented with acute chest pain. Electrocardiogram showed ST-elevation in the precordial leads. Bedside echocardiography revealed an aortic valve mass. He subsequently developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and was taken emergently for cardiac catheterization. Coronary angiography demonstrated high-grade stenosis in the mid left anterior descending (LAD) artery, suspected to be embolic given the known aortic mass and a characteristic “railroad-track” appearance. Successful thrombectomy and stenting of the mid-LAD were performed; however, distal embolization persisted despite multiple balloon inflations and attempted thrombectomy. Transesophageal echocardiography further characterized the mass as a mobile, bulky, echodense lesion measuring 18 х 12 mm on the ventricular side of the anterior cusp of a bicuspid aortic valve. Empiric intravenous antibiotics were initiated for presumed infective endocarditis; however, blood cultures remained negative. Due to high thromboembolic risk, he underwent aortic valve replacement. Pathology confirmed active native valve endocarditis, though no organisms were identified on routine stains. Notably, foamy macrophages with bubbly cytoplasmic material were seen on specialized staining, with PCR confirming Tropheryma whipplei. He was initiated on long-term antibiotic therapy. Discussion: Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis is a rare and underrecognized cause of culture-negative IE. It typically presents without fever or positive blood cultures, often leading to delayed diagnosis. Furthermore, the organism may not be identified on routine histologic stains, highlighting the importance of maintaining clinical suspicion. Cardiac involvement can occur in isolation, without classic gastrointestinal manifestations of Whipple’s disease. This case illustrates an unusual presentation with coronary embolization leading to STEMI. The presence of an aortic valve mass, absence of significant atherosclerosis, and angiographic “rail road-track” appearance suggested an embolic etiology. Recognition of these features is critical for appropriate diagnosis and management. Conclusion: This case underscores the importance of considering rare causes of culture-negative endocarditis, such as Tropheryma whipplei, particularly in patients with valvular masses and embolic complications.
title: Abstract 11345: Coronary Embolism Causing STEMI as the Initial Presentation of Tropheryma whipplei Endocarditis

abstract: Introduction: Although low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) remains the primary lipid target after percutaneous coronary intervention, prior studies have shown that triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (non-HDL-C), and diabetic atherogenic dyslipidemia may identify residual cardiovascular risk despite controlled LDL-C. Research Question: We hypothesized that residual dyslipidemia would remain common among post-percutaneous coronary intervention patients achieving LDL-C <70 mg/dL and would be more prevalent among patients with diabetes. Methods: We performed a single-center retrospective cohort study of 406 adults undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention at Loyola University Medical Center. Lipid values and clinical characteristics were collected at baseline and up to 24 months. Among patients achieving LDL-C <70 mg/dL at latest post-baseline follow-up, residual dyslipidemia was defined as triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, non-HDL-C ≥100 mg/dL, or low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, defined as <40 mg/dL in men and <50 mg/dL in women. Residual dyslipidemia was compared by diabetes status. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, Black race, body mass index, and latest LDL-C. Results: Among 175 patients who achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL at latest follow-up, 159 had complete lipid data for residual dyslipidemia assessment. Residual dyslipidemia was present in 86 patients, 54.1%. Low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol was most common, present in 76 patients, 47.8%, followed by triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL in 33 patients, 20.8%, triglycerides ≥200 mg/dL in 17 patients, 10.7%, and non-HDL-C ≥100 mg/dL in 8 patients, 5.0%. Patients with diabetes were more likely to have residual dyslipidemia than patients without diabetes, 67.1% versus 42.2%, p=0.002, driven by higher rates of triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, 28.9% versus 13.3%, p=0.019, and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, 59.2% versus 37.3%, p=0.007. Despite lower achieved LDL-C among patients with diabetes, 48.4 ± 11.6 versus 52.2 ± 11.1 mg/dL, p=0.039, diabetes remained independently associated with residual dyslipidemia, adjusted odds ratio 3.08, 95% confidence interval 1.51-6.26, p=0.002. Conclusion(s): In this single-center percutaneous coronary intervention cohort, more than half of patients who achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL had residual dyslipidemia, most commonly low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and hypertriglyceridemia. Diabetes was independently associated with a threefold higher odds of residual dyslipidemia despite LDL-C goal achievement. LDL-C control alone may not fully characterize residual lipid risk after percutaneous coronary intervention, particularly among patients with diabetes.
title: Abstract 11360: Diabetes and Residual Dyslipidemia After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Despite Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Control

abstract: Background: Right ventricular-pulmonary arterial (RV-PA) coupling, measured by the TAPSE/RVSP ratio, reflects right-sided contractile reserve under afterload stress. Its prognostic value in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is not well established. Hypothesis: Pre-procedural RV-PA uncoupling (TAPSE/RVSP ≤0.51 mm/mmHg) independently predicts long-term all-cause mortality and outperforms TAPSE alone in patients undergoing TAVR. Methods: We studied 1,597 TAVR patients (March 2011-December 2025) at Mayo Clinic, categorized as coupled (TAPSE/RVSP >0.51 mm/mmHg; n=749) or uncoupled (≤0.51 mm/mmHg; n=848). Baseline characteristics, echocardiographic parameters, and survival were compared. Unadjusted and adjusted Cox proportional hazards models evaluated the risk of death from TAPSE/RVSP and TAPSE, both modeled as continuous predictors using restricted cubic splines and adjusted for age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, LVEF, and AVA. Median follow-up was 3.8 years (IQR: 1.6-6.4), during which 643 deaths occurred. Results: TAVR utilization increased steadily from 2011 to 2021. Uncoupled patients had lower TAPSE (16 vs. 22 mm; p<0.001) and higher RVSP (51 vs. 32 mmHg; p<0.001). Survival was significantly worse in uncoupled versus coupled patients (p<0.001); 1-, 3-, and 5-year estimates were 85.9%, 64.0%, and 42.1% versus 94.1%, 83.7%, and 63.5%, respectively. ( Figure 1 ) Similarly, patients with abnormal TAPSE (≤1.7 cm) had lower survival (84.6%, 64.6%, 41.1%) than those with normal TAPSE (>1.7 cm; 92.9%, 78.0%, 58.4%; p<0.001). ( Figure 2 ) TAPSE/RVSP added significant predictive value over TAPSE alone (partial χ 2 =58.3; p<0.001) with superior discrimination (C-index: 0.678 vs. 0.655; adequacy: 0.98 vs. 0.79). In adjusted models, TAPSE/RVSP remained independently associated with mortality (HR per IQR decrease: 1.94 [95% CI: 1.54-2.45]; p<0.001), and uncoupled patients carried a 75% higher adjusted mortality risk (HR: 1.75 [95% CI: 1.47-2.10]; p<0.001). Conclusions: RV-PA uncoupling is common in TAVR candidates and is a strong, independent predictor of long-term mortality. TAPSE/RVSP outperforms TAPSE alone and should be incorporated into routine pre-TAVR risk assessment.
title: Abstract 11361: Right Ventricular-Pulmonary Arterial Coupling as a Predictor of Mortality After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Introduction: The 2025 AHA guidelines recommend a first shock energy of 200J for electrical cardioversion energy for atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, despite acknowledging that current, not energy, is what depolarizes the myocardium. It is unclear whether this recommendation leads to delivery of a consistent therapeutic dose of current. We measured the delivered current using a 200J setting in four globally marketed defibrillators (ZOLL, Stryker, Mindray and Corpuls) across a range of test impedances. Methods: Defibrillators delivered a biphasic truncated exponential (Stryker, Mindray) or a rectilinear biphasic (ZOLL and Corpuls) waveform and were evaluated in a bench test using 50, 100, and 150 Ω test loads. A 200 J shock was delivered into an Impulse7000DP and Impulse7010 load box (Fluke Corporation) connected in parallel. The delivered current waveform from all defibrillators for each test were recorded on an oscilloscope using a current probe. The load impedance, delivered energy, peak and average voltage, peak and average current, and waveform duration for both phases were recorded for all tests using the Impulse-7000DP device. Results: Figure 1 shows the delivered average current as a function of device manufacturer and test load. Patient impedance has a significant impact on the delivered current, with the current delivered into 50 Ohms resistance being 40-150% higher than the current delivered into 150 Ohms resistance. For low impedance (50 Ohm) loads, the highest current delivered 20% more amperes than the lowest current. Similarly, for high impedance (150 Ohm) loads, the highest current delivered 70% more amperes than the lowest current. Conclusions: In these experiments, delivered average currents fell in the range of 8.3 - 24.6 amperes depending on device manufacturer and test load despite being set at a uniform 200 J. For a given test load, the delivered current varied by 20 - 70%. The wide variation in delivered current is driven by both manufacturer design specifications and the patient’s transthoracic impedance. While guidelines emphasize that current is the key factor in achieving myocardial reset, standardizing the initial energy setting may result in the delivery of unnecessarily high currents, potentially increasing the risk of myocardial injury, even though equivalent currents can often be achieved at lower energy levels.
title: Abstract 11367: Exploring the Relationship Between Energy Setting and the Dose of Delivered Cardioversion Current for Atrial Fibrillation and Flutter

abstract: Background: PCI of severely calcified, tortuous coronary arteries may be limited by poor device deliverability and complicated by dissection, no-reflow, and hemodynamic deterioration. RCA compromise may cause severe RV dysfunction despite preserved LV systolic function. Here we present a novel method of preserving distal perfusion during a case of coronary dissection. Case: A 75-year-old man with coronary artery disease underwent elective angiography for exertional symptoms and abnormal coronary CTA. Angiography demonstrated severe, calcified RCA stenosis. RCA PCI was technically challenging because of severe calcification, tortuosity, and prior proximal stents. After multiple attempts and calcium modification, a single drug-eluting stent was deployed; however, the procedure was complicated by distal edge dissection and no-reflow despite repeated balloon angioplasty, with inferior ST-segment elevation and hemodynamic deterioration. The patient was initially stabilized with mechanical circulatory support. A microcatheter was advanced across the dissected segment and connected to the radial arterial sheath, allowing perfusion of the RCA distal to the dissection. Once distal coronary perfusion was established, the patient’s hemodynamics improved and the ST-segment elevation resolved. Mechanical circulatory support combined with microcatheter-mediated distal perfusion provided sufficient time for transfer to a tertiary care center for urgent CABG. Conclusion: Complex RCA PCI in a calcified, tortuous, previously stented vessel can progress from elective intervention to surgical bailout when dissection and no-reflow cannot be corrected percutaneously. In this case, microcatheter-mediated distal coronary perfusion served as a temporary bridge to definitive surgical revascularization.
title: Abstract 11368: Novel Method of Maintaining Distal Perfusion During Coronary Intervention Complicated by Coronary Dissection

abstract: Introduction: Severe bilateral renal artery stenosis (sBRAS) Is relatively uncommon and often discovered incidentally on imaging or as a workup for work up for hypertension or progressive renal insufficiency. Its diagnosis creates anxiety for the patients and even physicians as management practice is not well defined. Benefits of revascularization of one or both renal arteries well as risks are not well defined. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that intervention for sBRAS is safe with low peri-procedural risks and preservation of renal function with a low recurrence of admission for HTN crisis or heart failure. Methods: This is a single center, retrospective study. sBRAS patients were identified from computed tomography angiogram reports using a natural language processing software (Illuminate Insight. Findings were confirmed by manual review of images by an experienced vascular physician. Patients with fibromuscular dysplasia or dialysis dependence were excluded. Clinical characteristics, revascularization strategy, renal function, and longitudinal cardiovascular outcomes were analyzed. Results: sBRAS, was identified in 72 patients. Of these17 (23.6%) underwent renal artery revascularization (mean age 73.5±7.88 years; 70.6% female). Comorbidities included: HTN in 96%, DM, Active smoking in 31%, DM in 39.5%, CAD in 69% and PAD in 44%. Indications for revascularization were: uncontrolled hypertension in 12 patients, worsening renal function in 6 % and during AAA surgery in 2 (in 2 patients’ indication was both HTN and renal dysfunction). 9 (52.9% underwent unilateral stenting, 6 (35.3%) underwent B/L stenting and 2 had surgical revascularization during AAA repair. There were no procedural deaths of major complications. Mean follow-up was 5.65±4.98 years. Mean estimated glomerular filtration rate declined from 46.5±18.1 to 42.5±16.3 mL/min/1.73m 2 , consistent with age-expected progression (mean creatinine change was 0.38±0.91 mg/dL). Cardiovascular morbidity was substantial: 23.5% hospitalized for heart failure, 23.5% experienced hypertensive crisis, 5.9% sustained myocardial infarction, and 11.8% had stroke and 58.8% of patients died during follow-up. Conclusion: Revascularization for sBRAS is safe and does not contribute to decline in renal function. However, its effect on BP control and reduction in HF or HTN related admissions is unclear and since these patients have a high risk of death due to comorbidities, decision to revascularize should be made with due thought and shared decision making about benefits expected.
title: Abstract 11384: Outcomes of Renal Artery Revascularization in Severe Bilateral Renal Artery Stenosis

abstract: Introduction: Electrical storm is uncommon in young patients without structural heart disease. Left ventricular false tendons (LVFTs), though generally benign, may rarely serve as arrhythmogenic substrates due to embedded Purkinje fibers. We present a rare case of refractory polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PMVT) storm originating from an LVFT in an otherwise healthy young adult requiring VA-ECMO and catheter ablation despite maximal medical therapy. Patient Information and Clinical Findings: An 18-year-old previously healthy female underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. On postoperative day one, she developed sudden cardiac arrest with pulseless PMVT requiring 10 defibrillation shocks and intubation. Initial evaluation demonstrated QTc prolongation and hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L) after receiving intravenous ondansetron. Despite aggressive management with electrolyte replacement, amiodarone, lidocaine, esmolol, quinidine, propranolol, deep sedation, and stellate ganglion blockade, she developed recurrent PMVT triggered by short-coupled PVCs with R-on-T phenomenon, requiring more than 50 external defibrillation shocks within 48 hours. Diagnostic Assessment and Therapeutic Intervention: Coronary angiography, CT angiography, and infectious evaluation were unrevealing. Echocardiography demonstrated transient reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction to 32%, likely secondary to myocardial stunning. Due to refractory electrical storm and hemodynamic instability, VA-ECMO was initiated. Electrophysiology study with CARTO mapping localized the triggering PVCs to a false tendon between the papillary muscles, demonstrating earliest activation 30 ms pre-QRS. Radiofrequency ablation targeting the false tendon eliminated the PVCs and rendered VT noninducible despite isoproterenol infusion and programmed stimulation. Follow-Up and Discussion: Following ablation, ventricular ectopy immediately ceased and no further ventricular arrhythmias occurred. The patient was successfully decannulated from ECMO, extubated, and discharged with a subcutaneous ICD and quinidine therapy. Cardiac MRI demonstrated complete recovery of ventricular function without scar, infiltrative disease, or structural heart disease. Genetic testing was performed and identified variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in ALMS1 and RBM20, without a clearly pathogenic arrhythmogenic mutation.Although hypokalemia and ondansetron-associated QT prolongation likely served as the initial trigger, persistence of PMVT despite correction suggested an underlying arrhythmogenic substrate. This case highlights LVFTs as a rare but important cause of malignant ventricular arrhythmias and demonstrates the lifesaving role of early electrophysiologic evaluation, mechanical circulatory support, and early catheter ablation in refractory electrical storm.
title: Abstract 11386: Refractory Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia Storm from an Arrhythmogenic Left Ventricular False Tendon Requiring VA-ECMO and Catheter Ablation

abstract: Background: . End-stage renal disease (ESRD) accelerates vascular and valvular calcification, yet patients with ESRD have historically been excluded or underrepresented in major transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) trials. Higher mortality after TAVR is well established in this population, but bioprosthetic valve durability itself remains understudied. Methods: . Using the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR from 2016 onward and divided them by pre-existing ESRD (dialysis dependence or stage 5 disease before TAVR) versus no ESRD. Cohorts underwent 1:1 propensity score matching on demographics, comorbidities, and cardiovascular medications. Outcomes within 1 year of TAVR (30-day landmark) were a bioprosthetic valve failure composite (mechanical-complication codes plus repeat aortic valve intervention), all-cause mortality, and stroke. Aalen-Johansen estimation modeled valve failure and death as competing events, and a multivariable Cox model assessed independent predictors of valve failure. Results: . Matching yielded 2,791 well-balanced patients per group. Early valve failure did not differ between ESRD and non-ESRD patients (2.7% vs 3.4%; risk ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.58-1.06; P = .12). ESRD patients died nearly twice as often (17.5% vs 9.4%; risk ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.63-2.16; P < .001), while stroke was similar (3.5% vs 3.2%; P = .59). When death was modeled as a competing event, valve failure incidence remained low in both cohorts (<4% at 1 year), confirming the null was not an artifact of higher ESRD mortality. In the multivariable model, ESRD was not an independent predictor of valve failure (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.77-1.21; P = .75), whereas markers of structural heart disease (tricuspid and mitral valve disease, cardiomyopathy, thoracic aortic aneurysm) and chronic kidney disease stage 4 (HR 1.22; P = .048) were, confirming the model detected risk where present. Conclusion: . ESRD did not independently increase early bioprosthetic valve failure after TAVR. The nearly two-fold higher mortality, without a corresponding rise in valve failure, indicates that these patients often die before degeneration can manifest; this finding likely reflects the competing risk of death rather than equivalent valve durability. Consistent with this, the renal effect on durability was evident at pre-dialysis (stage 4) disease but eclipsed by mortality in ESRD. Procedural and technical factors not captured here may play a larger role in early failure, and ESRD alone may not warrant withholding TAVR on early durability grounds.
title: Abstract 11399: Pre-existing End-Stage Renal Disease and Early Valve Failure After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Introduction: Polycythemia Vera (PV) is a JAK2-mutated myeloproliferative neoplasm in which thrombosis is the leading cause of morbidity. Acute coronary syndrome as the initial manifestation is rare, and prior reports of multi-vessel involvement describe sequential or occlusive disease treated percutaneously.
