To validate the regulatory relationship between IRF9 and thrombospondin 1 (THBS1), IRF9 overexpression and THBS1 knockdown was simultaneously performed in cardiomyocytes, the expressions of proptosis effectors were examined. Results: Compared with controls, impaired cardiac systolic function and elevated myocardial injury markers occurred in TRZ-treated mice. Morphological staining revealed increased fibrosis and cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in the TRZ group. IRF9 expression was significantly increased in the myocardium after TRZ treatment. Cardiomyocyte-specific IRF9 overexpression aggravated TRZ-induced cardiac dysfunction, myocardial injury, and cardiomyocyte pyroptosis, whereas cardiomyocyte-specific IRF9 knockdown attenuated these effects. Mechanistically, IRF9 overexpression could increase the expression of THBS1 in myocardium and cardiomyocytes, whereas IRF9 knockdown reduced the expression of THBS1. THBS1 knockdown attenuated TRZ-induced cardiomyocyte pyroptosis mediated by IRF9 overexpression, whereas THBS1 overexpression abrogated the protective effect of IRF9 knockdown against pyroptosis. Conclusions: This study is the first to define the critical role of IRF9 in TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity. IRF9 overexpression aggravates TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity through the increased cardiomyocyte pyroptosis in a THBS1-dependent manner. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity and suggest potential therapeutic targets to mitigate TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity.
title: Abstract 13853: Interferon Regulatory Factor 9 Aggravates Trastuzumab-Induced Cardiotoxicity Through Promoting Pyroptosis of Cardiomyocytes via the Positive Regulation of Thrombospondin 1

abstract: Background: Oral anticoagulation (OAC) remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF), but its use is limited by bleeding risk. Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) devices offer a nonpharmacological alternative; however, recent randomized trials have reported inconsistent efficacy compared with OAC. Research question: To compare the safety and efficacy of LAAO and OAC in adults with AF. Methods: We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane CENTRAL to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) through April 1, 2026. We included adult patients (≥18 years) with all subtypes of AF on OAC or LAAO devices. Primary outcome was ischemic stroke; secondary outcomes included major bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke, and all-cause mortality. We pooled aggregate data using risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs; random-effects models were applied when heterogeneity was substantial (I 2 >60%). As a sensitivity analysis, individual patient-level data (IPD) were reconstructed from published Kaplan-Meier curves and analyzed as time-to-event outcomes (hazard ratios, HR). Results: Among six included RCTs (total n= 7,004), the weighted mean age was 72 years, CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score 3.9, HAS-BLED score 1.7, and follow-up duration 38 months. Aggregate analysis showed no significant difference in ischemic stroke (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.83-1.78), major bleeding (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.50-1.10), or all-cause mortality (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.66-1.21). LAAO was associated with a significantly lower risk of hemorrhagic stroke (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.07-0.74). Reconstructed IPD from available trials demonstrated no significant differences in all-stroke (3 studies; HR 1.24, 95% CI 0.79-1.94) or major bleeding (2 studies; HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.65-1.07), while showing lower all-cause mortality with LAAO (2 studies; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52-0.95). Conclusion: LAAO provided similar protection against ischemic stroke and reduced the risk of hemorrhagic stroke compared with OAC. Reconstructed IPD suggested a potential mortality benefit, although evidence was limited by the small number of contributing trials. Further studies with contemporary devices and post-ablation populations are needed.
title: Abstract 13895: Comparison of Left Atrial Appendage Closure Devices with Oral Anticoagulation Therapy on Clinical Outcomes in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation: A Reconstructed Individual-Patient Data Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Coronary angiography reports harbor rich, but complex information on coronary anatomy, atherosclerotic lesion characteristics and results of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, their free-text format limits scalability and usability in cardiovascular research. Traditional, single-agent large language models (LLMs) transform free text into structured, readily analyzable data, but are limited by suboptimal precision. Recently, multi-agent LLM frameworks have shown improved accuracy. The objective of this study was to develop a multi-agent LLM framework for detailed extraction of coronary angiography reports. Methods: We compiled coronary angiography reports of patients undergoing major vascular surgery from the University of Maryland Medical System (UMMS, 1/1/2016-1/1/2026) that includes 8 cardiac catheterization laboratories. We established an iterative development and validation framework using GPT-4 to achieve three goals: a) assess clinical indication; b) extract detailed coronary vessel findings; and c) describe PCI if performed. Two pipelines were evaluated: 1) a single-agent for end-to-end extraction and 2) a multi-agent sequential framework using six specialized agents with intermediate validation checkpoints and rule-based gating. The LLM results were compared to manually curated ground truth by two independent expert physicians. LLM errors were categorized as non-critical or critical if the error correction changed diagnosis and/or would likely have affected clinical care. Results: The final multi-agent framework was tested on 50 cases and achieved greater overall accuracy compared to the single-agent LLM (98.0% vs 95.9%), and was, therefore, deployed to the full cohort. From N=1,015 angiography reports, additional N=50 cases were randomly chosen, across hospitals and years, for validation. The overall accuracy of the multi-agent LLM after deployment to the full cohort was 98.5% and ranged from 94% to 100% (Table 1). The accuracy to identify lesion quantity and characteristics was 99.4%, 99.0%, 98.1% and 97.4% for left-main, left anterior descending, left circumflex and right coronary arteries, respectively. The accuracy of PCI identification and referral for coronary artery bypass graft was 100% and 98%, respectively. Overall, the rate of critical errors was low (0.9%), and included false reporting of vessel stenosis severity and presence of coronary artery disease in 3.4% and 1.3%, respectively. Non-critical errors were rare (0.6%). Conclusion: The multi-agent LLM framework achieved excellent accuracy when transforming free-text coronary angiography reports into readily analyzable data and outperformed the single-agent model. The rate of critical errors was low, further highlighting the role of this tool for large-scale deployment across medical systems and in cardiovascular research.
title: Abstract 13929: Development and Validation of a Multi-Agent Large Language Model Pipeline for Coronary Angiography Report Extraction and Evaluation of Errors

abstract: Background: Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy with historically poor inpatient outcomes. The 2019 FDA approval of tafamidis for transthyretin CA (ATTR-CM), the first disease-modifying therapy shown to reduce mortality in the ATTR-ACT trial, alongside broader adoption of bone scan, has transformed the diagnostic and therapeutic landscape. National hospitalisation rates for CA have risen substantially in the ICD-10 era, yet whether these advances have translated into improved inpatient outcomes at a population level remains unknown. Methods: Using the National Inpatient Sample 2016-2022, we identified hospitalizations with CA as the principal discharge diagnosis. Three clinical eras were defined: pre-tafamidis (2016-2017), early approval (2018-2019), and contemporary (2020-2022). Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included nonhome discharge, acute kidney injury (AKI), cardiogenic shock, LOS, and inflation-adjusted charges and costs. Survey-weighted logistic and linear regression adjusted for demographics, hospital characteristics, and comorbidities. Results: We identified approximately 219,500 weighted hospitalizations nationally over the study period, with annual volume growing 83% from 24,575 in 2016 to 44,875 in 2022. Era-specific weighted hospitalizations were 46,625 (Era 1: 2016-2017), 58,175 (Era 2: 2018-2019), and 114,700 (Era 3: 2020-2022). Mean age was 72.5 years (95% CI 72.2-72.9); prevalent comorbidities included heart failure (75.5%), cardiomyopathy (63.2%), atrial fibrillation (57.7%), and chronic kidney disease (49.5%). Overall in-hospital mortality was 5.9% (95% CI 5.4-6.4%). Contemporary-era hospitalizations were associated with lower odds of in-hospital death compared to the pre-tafamidis era (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56-0.90); no significant difference was observed in the early approval era (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.71-1.19). Nonhome discharge declined in the contemporary era (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75-0.97). CS increased (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.12-1.86), while AKI and LOS did not change significantly. Inflation-adjusted total charges and costs each rose approximately 17% in the contemporary era (both p<0.001). No significant change between era and race on in-hospital mortality. Conclusions: CA hospitalizations increased markedly from 2016 to 2022. Adjusted in-hospital mortality was lower in the contemporary era, though rising hospitalization volume and the likelihood of earlier diagnosis of less severe disease limit causal interpretation. The concurrent increase in cardiogenic shock likely reflects greater care intensity rather than worsening disease. Healthcare charges and costs rose substantially. These findings provide population-level benchmarks for CA inpatient outcomes and highlight the need for future prospective studies to better understand drivers of these trends.
title: Abstract 13931: Rising Diagnoses, Falling Mortality: A National Analysis of Cardiac Amyloidosis Hospitalizations Across the Tafamidis Era

abstract: Background: Although prasugrel and ticagrelor are preferred P2Y 12 inhibitors for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), comparative real-world data on their effectiveness and safety are limited. To fill this gap in evidence, we aimed to compare real-world risks of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), bleeding and dyspnea among ACS patients treated with prasugrel versus ticagrelor after PCI. Methods: This retrospective cohort study used MarketScan ® research databases (2017-2023) to identify patients aged 18 years or older with ACS who underwent PCI and initiated either prasugrel or ticagrelor within 30 days of discharge. The index date was the first date of drug fill following PCI discharge. Primary outcomes were 1-year risk of MACE (myocardial infarction [MI], ischemic stroke, or stent thrombosis) and bleeding (major and non-major). Secondary outcomes were components of MACE and any-cause dyspnea. These outcomes were identified using previously used International Classification of Disease Clinical Modification—tenth revision (ICD-10-CM) diagnosis codes. Stabilized inverse probability treatment weighting was applied, and Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate 1-year risk of primary and secondary outcomes. Results: The cohort included 6,662 prasugrel- and 25,452 ticagrelor-treated patients. Compared to ticagrelor, prasugrel was associated with lower risk of MACE (3.83 vs 5.61events per 100 person-years; adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67-0.94) and MI (3.43 vs 4.73 events per 100 person-years; aHR 0.83; 95% CI 0.69-0.99), numerically lower stent thrombosis rates (0.02 vs 0.07 events per 100 person-years) and any-cause dyspnea (7.84 and 12.62 events per 100 person-years; aHR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.67-0.86). Bleeding (2.85 vs 3.89 events per 100 person-years; aHR 0.92; 95% CI, 0.75-1.14) did not differ between prasugrel and ticagrelor. Conclusions: Real-world U.S. data from commercially insured ACS patients with PCI showed that prasugrel was associated with better ischemic effectiveness compared to ticagrelor, with no difference in bleeding risk. These findings align with clinical trial results and real-world data from other geographic regions supporting the preferential use of prasugrel over ticagrelor in ACS patients undergoing PCI.

appraisal.main_limitation: Claims-based outcome coding and treatment selection bias, with confounding by indication likely despite weighting.
appraisal.one_line: US claims cohort compared prasugrel with ticagrelor after PCI for ACS.

Bleeding (2.85 vs 3.89 events per 100 person-years; aHR 0.92; 95% CI, 0.75-1.14) did not differ between prasugrel and ticagrelor.

title: Abstract 13943: Comparative Effectiveness and Safety of Prasugrel versus Ticagrelor After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention - A Real-World Cohort Study

abstract: Background: In patients with recent myocardial infarction (MI), infarct-related artery (IRA) occlusions are generally crossed successfully using conventional guidewire techniques because the lesions are predominantly thrombotic. However, when lesion crossing fails, likely because of lesion complexity beyond simple thrombus accumulation and organization, operators face unique challenges. Unlike chronic total occlusions, MI-related IRA occlusions often lack well-developed collateral circulation, preventing visualization of the distal vessel and limiting procedural guidance. We report a novel real-time Hydro Dynamic Recanalization (HDR)-guided dual microcatheter strategy for crossing a wire-resistant IRA occlusion after recent MI. Case: A man in his 50s presented approximately 24 hours after the onset of chest pain and was diagnosed with inferior MI. Coronary angiography revealed total occlusion of the mid right coronary artery. Medical therapy was initially selected, and elective PCI was performed 10 days after symptom onset. At the time of PCI, no significant collateral circulation was observed, consistent with the findings at the index angiography. Decision-Making: Initial attempts using a workhorse guidewire and subsequently a polymer-jacketed guidewire failed to cross the lesion. Standalone HDR successfully visualized the distal vessel beyond the occlusion. However, guidewire crossing remained unsuccessful because the guidewire could not be advanced into the visualized distal vessel, suggesting that HDR-created channels were transient and unstable within a fragile thrombotic lesion with complex underlying architecture.To overcome this limitation, a second microcatheter carrying a guidewire was introduced. The first microcatheter was used for repeated HDR, while the second microcatheter was simultaneously used for guidewire manipulation. Real-time advancement of the guidewire toward the transient contrast pathway visualized by HDR enabled successful lesion crossing and restoration of distal vessel access. Intravascular ultrasound demonstrated a large thrombus burden, and definitive PCI was successfully completed. Conclusion: Recent MI-related IRA occlusions may occasionally exhibit complex lesion morphology that is resistant to conventional guidewire escalation. In the absence of collateral visualization, standalone HDR may permit distal vessel visualization but fail to provide a durable pathway for guidewire crossing. Real-time HDR guidance combined with a dual microcatheter technique enabled successful utilization of these transient pathways and may represent a useful bailout strategy for wire-resistant recent MI lesions.
title: Abstract 13953: Real-Time HDR Guidance Using a Dual Microcatheter Technique Enables Guidewire Crossing of a Wire-Resistant Infarct-Related Artery Occlusion After Recent Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Introduction: Although bleeding complications in cardiogenic shock (CS) are associated with worse outcomes, the relationship between baseline antithrombotic exposure, underlying shock phenotype, invasive management strategies, and bleeding risk remains poorly defined. We evaluated factors associated with increased bleeding risk in a large, contemporary multicenter CS registry. Methods: Adult patients (≥18 years) with CS enrolled in the AHA Cardiogenic Shock Registry were included. Patients with cardiac arrest prior to shock onset, transfer from an outside healthcare facility, durable left ventricular assist device, or unknown baseline antithrombotic status were excluded. Baseline characteristics, clinical presentation, markers of illness severity, and in-hospital management strategies, including MCS, were evaluated for their association with moderate/severe GUSTO bleeding. Results: A total of 3,070 patients (66±14 years, 36% female) with CS were included; 63% had a history of heart failure, 36% were receiving baseline anticoagulation, 44% were receiving baseline antiplatelet therapy, and 25% were managed with MCS during hospitalization (Table 1). Compared with patients managed without MCS, those with MCS were younger and more frequently presented with AMI-CS, advanced SCAI shock stages, and greater use of invasive therapies, including PCI, CABG, mechanical ventilation, and renal replacement therapy (RRT). Baseline anticoagulation was less common among patients managed with MCS than among those managed without MCS (26% vs 40%, Table 1).Overall, 339 patients (11.0%) experienced moderate/severe GUSTO bleeding. Bleeding rates increased significantly with higher SCAI shock stage, IV heparin and antiplatelet therapy at shock onset, PCI, CABG, RRT, and any MCS use (Figure 1 and 2). Specifically, patients with MCS had nearly 4-fold higher bleeding rates than those managed without MCS (24.2% vs. 6.7%, p<0.001). Baseline antithrombotic therapy was not independently associated with increased bleeding risk, with the exception of pre-admission warfarin. On multivariable analysis, MCS (adjusted OR 3.54, 95% CI 2.68-4.69), PCI (adjusted OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.31-2.81), and CABG (adjusted OR 3.56, 95% CI 2.34-5.38) were independently associated with moderate/severe bleeding. Among MCS devices, bleeding risk was highest among patients supported with VA-ECMO (Figure 1). Conclusion: In this large, multicenter CS registry, bleeding risk was heterogeneous and was associated with illness severity and invasive management strategies, including MCS, PCI and CABG, whereas baseline antithrombotic exposure was not independently associated with bleeding. Future studies should identify key drivers of bleeding, strategies to mitigate bleeding risk, and whether pre-admission antithrombotic therapy influences treatment selection, including the use of MCS.
title: Abstract 13965: What Drives Bleeding in Cardiogenic Shock? Insights from AHA Cardiogenic Shock Registry

abstract: Background: Myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) occurs in approximately 14% of at-risk surgical patients and is independently associated with serious adverse cardiovascular outcomes. However, individual risk varies widely among those affected, and optimal management remains uncertain. Although MINS is recognized as a clinically important condition requiring postoperative cardiovascular follow-up, risk stratification among affected patients remains poorly established. We therefore investigated predictors of adverse outcomes in patients who developed MINS. Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort study included patients undergoing noncardiac surgery at our institution between January 2020 and December 2022, who had a Revised Cardiac Risk Index ≥1 or ≥3 coronary risk factors (n=3,286). Postoperative high-sensitivity troponin I (hs-TnI) was measured on days 1 and 3, and all patients underwent a 12-lead electrocardiogram within one hour postoperatively. MINS was defined as an hs-TnI elevation ≥32 pg/mL within three postoperative days. Among patients who developed MINS, the primary outcome was defined as a composite of 30-day mortality or heart failure. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify predictors of adverse outcome, and a 3-factor risk score was developed based on the identified factors. Results: Among 3,286 patients, 447 (13.6%) developed MINS. The primary outcome occurred in 40 MINS patients (8.9%), including 30-day mortality in 26 (5.8%) and heart failure in 19 (4.3%). Multivariable logistic regression identified three independent predictors of adverse outcome: age ≥70 years (odds ratio [OR] 6.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.03-34.5, p=0.006), hs-TnI peak (per log unit, OR 1.82, 95% CI 1.45-2.32, p < 0.001), and emergency surgery (OR 3.46, 95% CI 1.67-7.29, p=0.001). A 3-factor risk score incorporating these variables (1 point each for age ≥70 years, hs-TnI peak ≥300 pg/mL, and emergency surgery) stratified primary outcome rates as follows: score 0, 0% (n=52); score 1, 5.0% (n=238); score 2, 12.5% (n=136); score 3, 55.0% (n=20) (area under the curve [AUC] 0.747). Cumulative incidence of adverse outcome increased significantly with higher scores (p < 0.0001). Conclusions: Risk stratification using a 3-factor risk score (age ≥70 years, hs-TnI peak ≥300 pg/mL, and emergency surgery) reveals high-risk patients among those with MINS, supporting risk-guided postoperative cardiovascular management.
title: Abstract 13987: Risk Stratification of Adverse Outcomes in Patients with Myocardial Injury After Noncardiac Surgery (MINS)

abstract: Introduction: Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) accounts for 10-20% of infective endocarditis cases and carries significant morbidity and mortality. Peri-annular abscess, conduction disturbances, and complex abnormal communication of the heart chambers with adjacent structures make early surgical outcome critical in advanced disease. Patient Information: A 70 year old male who had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement five years ago, presented with recurrent bacteremia but no visible vegetations in the echocardiogram. He was prescribed oral antibiotics. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Blood culture demonstrated Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae . The patient was discharged home with oral antibiotics because of negative echo findings. His systemic symptoms and recurrent bacteremia returned six weeks later. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning A repeat transoesophageal echocardiogram demonstrated Prosthetic valve vegetation with peri-annular abscess formation and mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. Multiple aortic root abscesses were confirmed by computed tomography (CT). Surgery was recommended at Heart Team Meeting and peri-annular expansion was evident. Therapeutic Intervention High-risk redo surgery was performed after multidisciplinary Heart Team reviewed. Extensive infection of the aortic root, anterior mitral leaflet, tricuspid annulus, and intervalvular fibrosa (IVF) was found. Aortic root-hemi-Commando operation was carried out comprising mechanical aortic root replacement, and rebuilding of the aorto-mitral continuity using bovine pericardium along with tricuspid valve repair, and anterior mitral valve repair. As the conduction pathway was found to be affected he had temporary pacemaker insertion in anticipation of permanent pacemaker. Follow Up, Outcomes and Adverse Events The patient had a gradual post-operative recovery . Permanent pacemaker implantation was required due to complete heart block. He completed six weeks of intravenous antibiotics as per the infectious disease recommendations. At follow-up, the patient was clinically well with prosthetic valve with no paravalvular leak. Discussion and Synthesis: PVE with IVF is a potentially fatal surgical emergency. Although risky and technically difficult, advanced reconstructive techniques like Commando and hemi-Commando surgeries can give optimal structural heart reconstructive outcome in highly specialised centre. Significance of timely diagnosis, interdisciplinary decision-making, access to sophisticated reconstructive surgical expertise is highlighted by this example. PATIENT perspective Patient gave informed consent after receiving thorough counseling about surgical risk and the expected postoperative course. He acknowledged that surgery was the sole potentially life-saving option and he was fully aware of dangers.
title: Abstract 13993: Surgical Salvage for Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis with Extensive Aortic Root Abscesses and Multivalvular Destruction: A Root-Hemi-Commando Procedure with Concomitant Tricuspid Valve Repair

abstract: Introduction: Advances in myocardial infarction (MI) treatment have drastically decreased acute mortality rates; however, delayed effects of MI remain fatal, with 1- and 5-year mortality rates remaining high. Despite advances in standard-of-care for MI, current treatment does not address excessive and prolonged inflammation at the infarct site, which, if untreated, can result in reperfusion injury, chronic heart failure, and possibly fatal arrhythmias. Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs) have displayed cardio-reparative properties post-MI, however, their clinical use is limited by their low accumulation/retention at the infarct site, often requiring highly invasive administration techniques. Thus, we have developed “Zippersomes”, MSC-EVs functionalized with leucine zipper proteins that heterodimerize with complementary partners, enabling layer-by-layer depot formation of subsequent doses at the infarct site. Through IV administration in a murine model of MI, we observed 7-fold more accumulation of MSC-EVs at the infract site, retention in the injured myocardium of 21 d, and a significant increase in cardiovascular functional recovery relative to MSC-EVs alone. Hypothesis/Research Questions: We hypothesize that Zippersomes will improve post-MI recovery in a porcine model relative to MSC-EVs or no treatment. Specifically, we’re studying whether Zippersomes will induce toxicity, and whether they improve functional recovery of cardiac tissue-post MI. Methods: Zippersomes were synthesized by appending leucine zipper proteins to porcine bone marrow (pBM) MSC-EVs via thiol-maleimide conjugation. MI was induced via permanent ligation of the LAD artery, with IV injections of either Zippersomes (4.46E9 EVs/kg), MSC-EVs, or 1X PBS occurring every 24 hours post-MI over 72 total hours (3 total injections). Pigs were monitored for 28 d post-MI, after which they were euthanized and the heart, liver, and kidneys were excised for histological analysis. Systemic toxicity caused by Zippersomes was determined via pig weight, white blood cell count, and liver/kidney histology (H&E stain). Functional recovery was determined via echocardiography at various timepoints post-MI, infarct size measurements 28-d post-MI and histological examination of LV tissue. Results: Zippersome treatment showed no systemic toxicity via weight loss and histological analysis. Recovery of cardiac function was improved in pigs that received Zippersomes, with end of study ejection fractions showing no significant differences from baseline levels (~60%), and significantly lower infarct sizes (~5%) relative to other groups (> 10%). Conclusions: This study showcases scale-up of Zippersomes to a clinically relevant porcine model, and the potential of this minimally invasive, long-lasting therapeutic platform for clinical studies in humans.
title: Abstract 13994: Sustained Local Delivery via Minimally Invasive Zippersome Treatment Improves Post-Myocardial Infarction Recovery in Swine

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock complicating heart failure without acute myocardial infarction accounts for the majority of CS hospitalizations and carries substantial in-hospital mortality. Frailty a state of increased vulnerability to physiologic stressors is highly prevalent among patients with acute cardiovascular disease and is associated with worse outcomes across a range of cardiac conditions. However, the relationship between frailty and clinical outcomes remains poorly understood. Methods: Using the NRD database (2018-2020), we identified (weighted N=203,272) Non-elective, non-AMI, heart failure-related cardiogenic shock (HF-CS) hospitalizations. HFRS stratified patients into low (<5; 12.9%), intermediate (5-15; 76.9%), and high (>15; 10.1%) categories. Survey-adjusted modified Poisson regression with robust variance was used to estimate adjusted risk ratios (aRR), preferred over logistic regression. Models were adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, and hospital characteristics, with low HFRS as reference. Results: High-HFRS patients were older (70.5 vs 62.1 years), more often female (44.7% vs 33.8%), and had greater CKD (62.8% vs 27.5%), prior stroke (21.4% vs 7.4%), and acute respiratory failure (80.8% vs 34.7%;p<0.001). In-hospital mortality rose across HFRS strata (16.3%, 34.5%, 37.1%); both intermediate and high HFRS independently predicted 1.9-fold higher mortality compared with low HFRS (intermediate aRR 1.92 [1.84-2.01]; high aRR 1.94 [1.84-2.05]). Compared with low HFRS, high HFRS was associated with greater AKI (aRR 2.41; p<0.001), dialysis need (aRR 4.30; p<0.001), and non-routine discharge (aRR 1.42; p<0.001). RHC use fell from 28.5% to 11.5% across strata; high HFRS independently predicted lower RHC use (aRR 0.52; p<0.001), yet among RHC recipients, adjusted mortality was 49% lower than in those receiving neither RHC nor MCS (aRR 0.51; p<0.001). Despite modest overall 30-day readmission differences (21.2% to 25.0%), high HFRS independently predicted death during 30-day readmission (aRR 2.36; p<0.001), non-index hospital readmission (aRR 1.74; p<0.001), and sepsis/infection readmission (aRR 3.26; p<0.001) compared with low HFRS. Heart failure-specific readmission paradoxically decreased among high-HFRS patients (aRR 0.78; p<0.001). Conclusion: In a nationally representative HF-CS cohort, frailty independently doubled in-hospital mortality, reduced hemodynamic assessment. Among survivors, post-discharge risk was characterized by death during readmission, non-index hospital readmission, sepsis and not recurrent heart failure decompensation. The paradoxical decrease in HF-specific readmission likely reflects competing mortality rather than improved cardiac recovery. These data support systematic frailty assessment to guide hemodynamic monitoring decisions and post-discharge care planning in HF-CS.
title: Abstract 13996: Frailty, Treatment Intensity, and Outcomes in Non-Ischemic Cardiogenic Shock: Evidence from the National Readmission Database

abstract: Introduction: The CHAMPION-AF and CLOSURE-AF trials have yielded conflicting results regarding the non-inferiority of left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) versus oral anticoagulation (OAC) for ischemic stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Stroke mechanisms, however, were not systematically examined in either trial. Hypothesis: Atherothrombotic (vascular/large artery) stroke risk, which is reduced by OAC but not by LAAO, may contribute to differential stroke/bleeding outcomes in AF patients. Methods: In this modeling study, 3-year risk of a composite outcome (ischemic stroke + major bleeding) was estimated separately for LAAO and OAC strategies. Ischemic stroke risk was partitioned into LAA-embolic, non-LAA embolic (assumed 10% of total embolic risk), and atherothrombotic (large artery) stroke components. Annual LAA-embolic stroke risk (0.5%-5.0%) and annual atherothrombotic stroke risk (0%-2.25%) were varied independently across clinically plausible ranges. Based on published literature, OAC was assumed to reduce embolic stroke risk by 63% and atherothrombotic stroke risk by 40%. LAAO-related reduction in LAA-embolic stroke risk, along with major bleeding, device-related thrombosis, and procedural complication rates, were informed by CHAMPION-AF and CLOSURE-AF in separate trial-specific models. Results were visualized as grid plots of the difference in 3-year composite event risk (LAAO minus OAC) across embolic and atherothrombotic stroke risk values. Results: The optimal strategy shifted toward LAAO with increasing LAA-source embolic risk and toward OAC with increasing atherothrombotic stroke risk. In the CHAMPION-AF-informed model, LAAO demonstrated lower composite event risk across most modeled scenarios. The annual atherothrombotic stroke risk threshold at which OAC became the preferred strategy ranged from 0.74% (at 0.5% annual LAA-embolic risk) to >2.25% (at ≥3.0% annual LAA-embolic risk). In contrast, the CLOSURE-AF-informed model favored OAC across a greater proportion of scenarios, with corresponding thresholds ranging from 0.19% (at 0.5% annual LAA-embolic risk) to >2.25% (at ≥3.5% annual LAA-embolic risk). Conclusions: The relative benefit of LAAO vs. OAC may depend on the patients’ differential embolic vs. atherothrombotic stroke risk profile. Future clinical trials should attempt to quantify source-specific ischemic stroke risk in AF patients.

appraisal.design_and_n: Modelling study estimating 3-year composite risk (ischemic stroke + major bleeding), with inputs from CHAMPION-AF and CLOSURE-AF in separate trial-specific models.
appraisal.main_limitation: Scenario analysis with assumed risk partitions and published-literature inputs, with no patient-level data and no uncertainty or value-of-information quantification in the abstract.
appraisal.one_line: Decision-model analysis suggests LAAO versus OAC preference depends on embolic versus atherothrombotic stroke risk, reconciling CHAMPION-AF and CLOSURE-AF.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: The annual atherothrombotic stroke risk threshold at which OAC became the preferred strategy ranged from 0.74% (at 0.5% annual LAA-embolic risk) to >2.25% (at ≥3.0% annual LAA-embolic risk) in the CHAMPION-AF-informed model.
appraisal.why_it_matters: Offers a mechanistic explanation for conflicting LAAO trials and points to source-specific stroke risk as an effect modifier worth testing in IPD or trial-level synthesis.

title: Abstract 14004: Atherothrombotic Stroke Risk as a Missing Piece in Understanding Left Atrial Appendage Closure Clinical Trials: A Modeling Study

abstract: Background: PCSK9-targeting therapies and bempedoic acid both lower LDL cholesterol after myocardial infarction (MI), but the two have not been compared head-to-head for clinical outcomes. We assessed whether either offers an advantage in secondary prevention. Methods: Using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (172 healthcare organizations), we identified adults with MI or unstable angina recorded between 2020 and 2025 who began lipid-lowering therapy at least one day after the event. Patients on a PCSK9-targeting agent (evolocumab, alirocumab, or inclisiran) were compared with those on bempedoic acid; patients receiving both were excluded. Groups were balanced 1:1 by propensity score matching on demographics, comorbidities, concomitant medications, and baseline LDL (1,858 per group). Outcomes were assessed at 1 and 3 years using risk ratios and Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results: After matching, cohorts were well balanced (standardized differences <0.05 for nearly all covariates). Event rates were low and closely overlapping throughout follow-up. At 1 year, the PCSK9 and bempedoic acid groups did not differ in MACE (2.2% vs 1.8%; HR 1.15, 95% CI 0.70-1.89; p=0.572), all-cause death (2.6% vs 2.9%; HR 0.86, 0.58-1.26; p=0.430), heart failure (4.2% vs 4.0%; HR 1.01, 0.69-1.48; p=0.945), new-onset type 2 diabetes (3.8% vs 2.9%; HR 1.27, 0.81-2.00; p=0.300), or gout/hyper uricemia (0.9% vs 1.2%; HR 0.71, 0.37-1.39; p=0.319). This pattern held at 3 years, with comparable MACE (3.6% vs 3.3%; HR 1.04, 0.71-1.50), death (4.6% vs 4.3%; HR 1.03, 0.76-1.40), and heart failure (7.5% vs 6.4%; HR 1.13, 0.84-1.51), and no endpoint reaching significance. Two metabolic signals widened over time but remained non-significant: new-onset diabetes was higher with PCSK9 therapy (5.9% vs 4.2%; HR 1.39, 0.96-2.02; p=0.079), while gout/hyper uricemia was higher with bempedoic acid (2.1% vs 1.4%; HR 0.65, 0.39-1.10; p=0.104). Conclusions: In this large, real-world post-MI cohort, PCSK9-targeting therapy and bempedoic acid produced comparable rates of MACE, mortality, and heart failure through 3 years, suggesting either is a reasonable option and that choice can rest on tolerability, access, and cost. Given the observational design and reliance on coded data, randomized confirmation is warranted.
title: Abstract 14031: Comparative Effectiveness of PCSK9 Inhibitors and Bempedoic Acid in Secondary Prevention After Myocardial Infarction: A Global Real-World Study

abstract: Background: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) causes profound metabolic reprogramming and severe cardiac dysfunction. Although cell division cycle 20 homolog (CDC20) is a well-known regulator of the cell cycle, its pathophysiological role in ischemic cardiac injury remains unclear. This study investigated the impact of CDC20 on cardiac fatty acid metabolism post-AMI. Methods: CDC20 expression profiles were analyzed using Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets and validated in AMI mice and hypoxic cardiomyocytes. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors were utilized to achieve cardiac-specific CDC20 overexpression or knockdown in vivo. Molecular pathways and the therapeutic efficacy of Lomitapide, a small-molecule inhibitor of CDC20, were subsequently evaluated. Results: CDC20 was significantly upregulated in the ischemic myocardium. At 28 days post-AMI, cardiac-specific CDC20 overexpression markedly exacerbated adverse cardiac remodeling and significantly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) (P &lt; 0.05). Conversely, CDC20 knockdown successfully preserved cardiac function and reduced infarct size. Mechanistically, CDC20 directly bound to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα), promoting its ubiquitin-mediated degradation and consequently impairing cardiac fatty acid metabolism. Crucially, pharmacological inhibition of CDC20 with Lomitapide restored PPARα expression, leading to a significant improvement in LVEF and a marked reduction in myocardial fibrosis in AMI mice (P &lt; 0.05). Conclusions: CDC20 aggravates post-AMI injury by driving ubiquitin-mediated PPARα degradation and disrupting fatty acid metabolism. Minimizing this effect via targeted inhibition of CDC20 with Lomitapide rescues cardiac function, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for myocardial infarction.
title: Abstract 14046: Cell Division Cycle 20 Homolog Exacerbates Myocardial Infarction Injury by Promoting Peroxisome Proliferator Activated Receptor Alpha Degradation

abstract: Introduction: Patients with a history of cancer increasingly undergo complex coronary interventions, yet the impact of prior malignancy on the outcomes of chronic total occlusion (CTO) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains poorly characterized. We examined the association of cancer history with procedural and in-hospital outcomes in a large multicenter registry. Methods: We analyzed 13,970 patients who underwent CTO PCI in the Prospective Global Registry for the Study of Chronic Total Occlusion Intervention (PROGRESS-CTO; NCT02061436). Patients were stratified by history of cancer. Baseline, angiographic, and procedural characteristics and in-hospital outcomes were compared. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the independent association of cancer history with technical success, procedural success, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and coronary perforation, adjusting for clinical and angiographic confounders. Results: A history of cancer was present in 1,161 patients (8.3%). Compared with patients without cancer, those with prior malignancy were older (70.8 ± 9.2 vs 63.9 ± 10.6 years; p<0.001) and had a higher prevalence of hypertension, dyslipidemia, heart failure, cerebrovascular and peripheral arterial disease, and greater lesion complexity (J-CTO 2.55 ± 1.18 vs 2.33 ± 1.23; CASTLE 2.36 ± 1.30 vs 1.86 ± 1.20; moderate/severe calcification 56.8% vs 44.7%; all p<0.001). Cancer patients had higher crude rates of MACE (3.4% vs 1.6%), perforation (6.9% vs 4.4%), and pericardiocentesis (2.2% vs 0.9%) (all p<0.001), with lower technical (84.6% vs 87.9%; p=0.001) and procedural success (82.5% vs 86.7%; p<0.001). After multivariable adjustment, cancer history remained independently associated with MACE (adjusted OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.07-2.55; p=0.024) and perforation (adjusted OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.22-2.21; p=0.001). In contrast, the lower technical and procedural success observed on unadjusted analysis was no longer significant after adjustment (both p>0.3), indicating it was largely attributable to greater patient and lesion complexity rather than cancer history itself. Conclusions: Among patients undergoing CTO PCI, a history of cancer was independently associated with higher risk of MACE and coronary perforation, whereas technical success was comparable after accounting for clinical and angiographic complexity. These findings support the feasibility of CTO PCI in carefully selected cancer patients while underscoring the need for heightened periprocedural vigilance for perforation and adverse events.
title: Abstract 14077: Impact of Prior Cancer History on the Outcomes of Chronic Total Occlusion Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Insights from the PROGRESS-CTO Registry

abstract: Introduction: Anesthetic induction is a period of hemodynamic vulnerability in cardiac patients; hypotension or pressor responses may precipitate myocardial ischemia, arrhythmia, or circulatory collapse. Whether alternative intravenous induction agents offer hemodynamic advantages over propofol remains uncertain. Hypothesis: Alternative intravenous induction agents preserve heart rate (HR) and mean arterial pressure (MAP) better than propofol during induction in adults undergoing cardiac interventions. Methods: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Embase for randomized controlled trials comparing propofol with alternative intravenous induction agents (etomidate, ketamine, midazolam, dexmedetomidine, ciprofol, remimazolam) in adults undergoing cardiac surgical or interventional procedures (coronary artery bypass grafting, valve surgery, or transcatheter aortic valve interventions). Co-primary outcomes were HR and MAP, extracted at serial timepoints (1, 2, 3, 5, 10 min) across predefined phases: post-induction/pre-intubation, post-intubation, surgical stimulation, cardiopulmonary bypass, end-of-bypass, and end-of-surgery. Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using random-effects models. Results: Twelve trials (2007-2025; 2,780 patients) met eligibility. Post-induction, alternative agents maintained higher MAP than propofol at 1 min (MD 7.90 mmHg, 95% CI 0.57-15.23), 2 min (MD 6.34 mmHg, 95% CI 1.80-10.87), and 3 min (MD 8.70 mmHg, 95% CI 3.87-13.53). Post-intubation, MAP remained higher with alternative agents at 1 min (MD 13.25 mmHg, 95% CI 8.47-18.03), 3 min (MD 12.98 mmHg, 95% CI 6.04-19.93), 5 min (MD 4.95 mmHg, 95% CI 0.62-9.28), and 10 min (MD 11.00 mmHg, 95% CI 1.67-20.33). HR showed no consistent direction: it was higher with alternative agents at 3 min post-induction (MD 5.49 bpm, 95% CI 0.91-10.08) and 3 min post-intubation (MD 5.18 bpm, 95% CI 1.48-8.87), and lower at 15-60 min post-induction (MD –6.06 to –7.44 bpm). Conclusions: Alternative intravenous induction agents better preserved MAP than propofol during early induction and through the first 10 min after intubation, whereas HR showed no consistent between-group difference. These time-dependent profiles support individualized induction-agent selection based on baseline cardiac function, circulatory reserve, and perioperative hemodynamic goals
title: Abstract 14083: Hemodynamic Effects of Different Intravenous Anesthetic Induction Agents versus Propofol in Patients Undergoing Cardiac Interventions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: The optimal arterial access strategy for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in bifurcation lesions remains uncertain. Research question: To compare procedural and clinical outcomes of radial access versus femoral access in patients undergoing bifurcation PCI. Methods: This retrospective and prospective observational cohort study included patients enrolled between 2013 and 2026 across eight centers in the United States, Russia, and Turkey within the PROGRESS-BIFURCATION registry (NCT05100992). Procedural characteristics and clinical outcomes were compared between radial and femoral access for bifurcation PCIs. Primary endpoints were technical and procedural success. Secondary endpoints included in-hospital major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and procedural complications. Results: Among 2,504 patients undergoing 2,710 bifurcation PCIs, 1311 (48.4%) procedures utilized radial access and 1399 (51.6%) femoral access. Patients in the femoral group were older (66.8 ± 12.2 vs. 64.2 ± 17.7 years; p=0.01) and had a higher prevalence of comorbidities, including dyslipidemia, heart failure, and current smoking, and more frequently presented with acute coronary syndromes. The femoral group also presented with more complex lesions, with higher prevalence of Medina 1,1,1 lesions (44.0% vs. 30.1%; p<0.001), left main disease (26.5% vs. 20.6%; p<0.001), and severe calcification (18.6% vs. 11.6%). Two-stent techniques were more commonly used in the femoral access group (34.9% vs. 22.9%; p<0.001). As compared with radial access, femoral access had longer procedural time (67 [45-110] vs. 60 [35-100] minutes), higher contrast volume (185 [150-250] vs. 170 [120-240]; p=0.005), and higher air kerma radiation dose (1.58 [1.02-2.78] vs. 1.35 [0.87-2.24] Gray; p<0.001). Femoral access had similar technical success (95.66% vs 96.56%; p=0.15) but higher in-hospital MACE (3.37% vs. 2.14%; p=0.03) and procedural complications (6.85% vs 9.27%; p=0.03) compared with radial (Figure 1). Over a median follow-up of 29 months, multivariable adjusted cox regression showed no significant difference between radial and femoral access in follow-up MACE incidence (aHR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66-1.08; p=0.18; Figure 2). Conclusion: In bifurcation PCI, radial access was associated with comparable technical success, but lower rates of in-hospital MACE compared with femoral access. These results support the preferential use of radial access in bifurcation PCI when feasible.
title: Abstract 14085: Radial versus Femoral Access in Bifurcation Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Insights from PROGRESS-BIFURCATION

abstract: Introduction: High circulating levels of aminothiols cystine and low levels of glutathione (GSH) are estimates of extracellular and intracellular oxidative stress (OS), respectively, and a high ratio of cystine/GSH is a predictor of mortality. Whether cystine/GSH ratio is associated with incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in coronary artery disease (CAD), and whether this is independent of established prognostic biomarkers reflecting inflammation, myocardial injury, neurohormonal stress, and immune activation, is unknown. Hypothesis: Cystine/GSH is associated with incident MACE independently of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), high-sensitivity troponin I (hs-TnI), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), and soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) levels. Methods: We studied 1,390 participants undergoing angiography and enrolled in the Emory Cardiovascular Biobank with concurrent measurement of cystine/GSH and four established biomarkers (hsCRP, hs-TnI, NT-proBNP, suPAR). The primary outcome was MACE (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke). Cause-specific Cox models were adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, LDL, heart failure history, eGFR, statin use, acute myocardial infarction, ACE/ARB use, β-blocker use, Gensini score, and ejection fraction. Cystine/GSH was first added to this base model alone, then with all four established biomarkers entered simultaneously. Results: Over a median follow-up of 7.1 years, 305 (22%) MACE occurred. Median age was 65 years; 67% were male, 33% had diabetes, and 44% had obstructive CAD. Added to the base model, higher cystine/GSH, reflecting higher OS, was associated with MACE (HR 1.2 per SD; 95% CI, 1.1-1.3; P=0.004). Individuals in the highest tertile of OS had an 83% relative increase in the cumulative MACE rate (30.4% vs. 16.6%) compared to those within the lowest tertile (Figure). This association persisted after further adjustment for all four aforementioned biomarkers (HR 1.1 per SD; 95% CI, 1-1.3; P=0.03). Conclusions: In patients with CAD, OS is associated with incident MACE independent of established risk pathways of inflammation, myocardial injury, neurohormonal stress, and immune activation, indicating that OS captures a distinct, non-redundant axis of cardiovascular risk. OS profiling may therefore have prognostic value complementary to established biomarkers, warranting further evaluation and specific therapeutic interventions.
title: Abstract 14098: Oxidative Stress is Independently Associated with Incident Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events Beyond Established Biomarkers in Coronary Artery Disease

abstract: Background: Despite growing use of hemodynamic monitoring in cardiogenic shock (CS), the real-world association of right heart catheterization (RHC) with post-discharge outcomes and advanced therapy referral remains poorly characterized. We examined RHC use and outcomes in a contemporary national CS cohort. Methods: We analyzed a nationally representative weighted cohort of 262,598 non-elective CS hospitalizations from the Nationwide Readmissions Database 2018-2020. Patients were classified into four exposure phenotypes: No RHC/No MCS (71.3%), RHC only (9.9%), MCS only (12.4%), and RHC+MCS (6.4%). Given the NRD’s design as a readmission database, primary outcomes were 30-day unplanned readmission, death-related readmission, and LVAD/orthotopic heart transplant (OHT) readmission. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, stroke, dialysis, and non-home discharge among survivors. Adjusted Risk ratios (aRR) were estimated using survey-weighted modified Poisson regression with stabilized inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting (IPTW) and doubly robust estimation to address treatment-selection bias. Formal interaction testing assessed effect modification by AMI status; E-values quantified residual confounding sensitivity. Results: RHC was used in 16.3% of admissions. After multivariable adjustment, RHC was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (aRR 0.770, 95% CI 0.752-0.788), stroke (aRR 0.756, 0.712-0.802), and dialysis (aRR 0.755, 0.723-0.788); non-home discharge was null (aRR 0.994, p=0.404). Unplanned 30-day readmission (aRR 1.008, p=0.562) and death-related readmission (aRR 0.996, p=0.928) were null. RHC was associated with a 6.4-fold higher LVAD/OHT readmission rate (aRR 6.39, 95% CI 5.15-7.94; crude rate 1.1% vs 0.1%). AMI status significantly modified the mortality association (interaction p<0.001): non-AMI CS showed a substantially larger benefit (aRR 0.609, 0.588-0.631) than AMI CS (aRR 0.941, 0.917-0.966). IPTW-adjusted estimates were consistent (aRR 0.797, 0.777-0.818); E-value was 1.92. Conclusions: In a nationally representative CS cohort, RHC was associated with lower in-hospital mortality, null unplanned readmission, and markedly higher advanced therapy referral. Mortality benefit was substantially larger in non-AMI CS, suggesting RHC adds greatest value when shock etiology is diagnostically uncertain. These associations warrant prospective validation.
title: Abstract 14102: Right Heart Catheterization in Cardiogenic Shock: Outcomes, Readmission, and Advanced Therapy Referral Insights from the Nationwide Readmissions Database

abstract: Introduction: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but devastating cause of acute viral cardiopulmonary failure. While extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is increasingly employed in severe disease, contemporary evidence remains sparse and largely confined to small institutional cohorts. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to define survival and clinical outcomes among ECMO-supported HCPS patients. Methods: This prospectively registered systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD420261416336 ) searched PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar from inception through May 2026. Observational studies and case series were included. Quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Survival to hospital discharge was pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, while ECMO candidacy criteria, deployment strategies, complications, healthcare utilization, and long-term outcomes were qualitatively synthesized. Results: Eight studies met inclusion criteria. Three independent cohorts contributed to quantitative synthesis, yielding a pooled analysis of 71 ECMO-supported patients , a substantial evidence base for a disease in which institutional experience is often limited to single-digit cases. Overall survival following ECMO was 70.4% (50/71; 95% CI 58.9-79.9%; P<0.001) . A striking temporal improvement emerged across three decades of practice, with survival increasing from 14/26 (53.8%) in the earliest cohort to 20/25 (80.0%) and 14/17 (82.3%) in contemporary series. Survival gains paralleled a shift from rescue ECMO to earlier physiology-guided initiation. Even among survivors, recovery remained resource-intensive, requiring mean ECMO support of 127.35 hours. and mean hospital stays of 23.4 days . Major complications included bleeding, limb ischemia, vascular injury, and amputation. Long-term follow-up demonstrated substantial post-discharge morbidity despite survival. Collectively, the literature suggests that improved HCPS outcomes have paralleled a transition from salvage ECMO to a planned physiology-guided strategy, while revealing a significant survivorship burden beyond hospital discharge. Conclusions: HCPS has traditionally been defined by the moment of catastrophic cardiopulmonary collapse. Our findings suggest it may be determined by what happens before it. The consistent improvement in survival observed across successive ECMO eras points toward early recognition of physiologic decline and progressively earlier deployment of mechanical circulatory support as a potentially modifiable determinant of outcome. In a disease measured in hours rather than days, the most important ECMO decision may not be how to run it—but when to start it.

Abstract 14113: The Window Before Collapse: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome -
                    A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Myocardial perfusion depends on myocardial blood flow and myocardial blood volume (MBV). Ninety percent of MBV resides in the microvasculature, making capillary recruitment a key determinant of MBV. The loss of microvasculature is associated with reduced regional fractional myocardial blood volume (fMBV); whereas, ischemia causes an increase in fMBV due to autoregulatory responses, including capillary recruitment. Ferumoxytol, a blood-pool MRI contrast agent with high r1 relaxivity, sensitizes intravascular T1 signal to MBV changes, enabling quantification of fMBV (%), the fraction of myocardium occupied by blood. Pre-clinical studies have shown fMBV as a promising complementary biomarker in ischemic heart disease (IHD). Hypothesis: Low fMBV in patients with IHD is associated with major adverse cardio-cerebrovascular events (MACCE) and improves risk discrimination. Methods: Healthy volunteers (n=31, 30.9±4.5 y) and patients with IHD and abnormal stress PET (n=61, 66.6±9.9 y) underwent 3T ferumoxytol-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance. Basal, mid, and apical MOLLI T1 maps were acquired pre-contrast and after incremental ferumoxytol doses up to 4.0 mg/kg. After non-rigid registration, fMBV maps were generated using a validated two-compartment water-exchange model and segmented by the 16-segment AHA model. For each AHA segment in the healthy cohort, the reference limit was defined as the 10th percentile of the segmental fMBV value. To establish the low fMBV threshold, ROC analysis was performed using data from healthy and IHD subjects. Accordingly, low fMBV in the IHD cohort was defined as either having a severe focal reduction (≥1 segment with fMBV >1.05% below the reference limit) or having a multi-segment reduction (≥4 segments below segmental references). MACCE included all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular events, revascularization, and heart failure admission. Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression assessed the association between low fMBV and MACCE (unadjusted and adjusted for age, sex, and left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF]). ROC analysis evaluated the discriminatory value of low fMBV beyond age, sex, and LVEF. Results: Representative fMBV maps from a healthy volunteer and a patient with IHD are shown in Fig. 1. During a median follow-up of 30.1 (15.4-43.1) months, 14 MACCEs occurred. Low fMBV (n=46/61) showed a trend towards higher MACCE hazard (adjusted hazard ratio, 4.35 [0.89-21.29]; P=0.069). At 24 months, adding low fMBV increased AUC from 0.799 to 0.924 (ΔAUC=0.125; DeLong P=0.049), with 90.9% sensitivity and 79.1% specificity (Fig 2). Conclusions: In this exploratory study, low fMBV in the IHD cohort showed a trend toward higher MACCE hazard and improved risk discrimination. These findings support fMBV as a complementary non-invasive marker for in IHD, warranting validation in large cohorts.
title: Abstract 14119: Fractional Myocardial Blood Volume and Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Ischemic Heart Disease

abstract: Case Presentation: Yearly in the United States, ~200,000 people are diagnosed with Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) and 1-2% of cases are occult without a primary lung tumor. Diagnosis can be delayed which may increase morbidity and emotional distress. A 54-year-old male with tobacco and alcohol use disorder presented to the ED with constipation and progressive dyspnea. He was diagnosed with an unprovoked left lower extremity DVT two months prior and was started on anticoagulation. On admission, he was found to be tachycardic, hypoxic, with elevated troponin, BNP, and white blood cell count. CT chest showed mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, pericardial effusion, and renal cortical hypodensities concerning for cardioembolic phenomena. He underwent TEE revealing severe aortic regurgitation with a mobile left coronary cusp echodensity consistent with vegetation. Blood cultures were negative prompting consideration of noninfective etiologies such as cardiac tumor or thrombosis. Subsequent CT head identified bilateral acute embolic infarcts from likely cardioembolic source. After multidisciplinary team discussion, surgical aortic valve replacement (AVR) was offered given borderline cardiac function (CI 2.86) and active embolization. He underwent bioprosthetic AVR and left atrial appendage clipping. Intraoperatively, a large 800 cc hemorrhagic pericardial effusion causing cardiac tamponade was drained. Aortic valve pathology demonstrated fibrinous material consistent with thrombotic endocarditis. Periaortic tissue immunohistochemistry was positive for CK OSCAR, TTF-1, and Napsin A establishing lung adenocarcinoma as the underlying diagnosis. His postoperative course was complicated by new bilateral DVTs with pulmonary emboli despite taking therapeutic anticoagulation and developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure; an IVC filter was placed. Subsequent cervical lymph node biopsy confirmed metastatic disease. He improved in the ICU and was discharged home on POD #8. Six weeks later, he represented to the ED with acute chest pain found to have ST elevations in leads V4-V6 and ischemic cardiomyopathy. Coronary angiography showed abrupt cutoff of distal LAD status post thrombectomy retrieval of fibrinous material and thrombus without evidence of malignancy. Once hemodynamically stabilized, chemoimmunotherapy with carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab was initiated in the outpatient setting. PET/CT at three months demonstrated complete metabolic response with resolution of all FDG-avid disease. LVEF recovered. Discussion and Conclusion: Metastatic malignancy may mimic infective endocarditis. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of culture-negative valvular disease with systemic embolization. Multimodality imaging and multidisciplinary evaluation prevent delays in diagnosis and significantly alter management and outcomes.
title: Abstract 14180: Occult Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Exhibited by Thrombotic Endocarditis with Systemic Embolization

abstract: Background: Guidelines recommend oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and additional risk factors (class 1: risk ≥2% per year, class 2a: risk ≥1 but <2% per year). Percutaneous left atrial appendage (LAA) occlusion has been introduced as a potential alternative to oral anticoagulation. Research Question: What is the residual risk of ischemic stroke following percutaneous LAA occlusion? Methods: We performed a preregistered (CRD420251181525) systematic review of MEDLINE and Embase to May 18, 2026, to identify randomized trials of percutaneous LAA occlusion in patients with AF. We included trials with ≥100 participants assigned to percutaneous LAA occlusion and ≥6 months of follow-up. We excluded trials exclusively testing this treatment as a concomitant procedure or within ≤180 days of catheter ablation. We derived annualized event rates from individual trials and pooled them using random-effects meta-analysis in R. Results: From 6,034 citations, we identified nine eligible trials that included 5,533 participants randomized to percutaneous LAA occlusion. Five trials compared percutaneous LAA occlusion with oral anticoagulation (2,878 device recipients), one with single antiplatelet/no antithrombotic therapy (320 device recipients), and three compared occlusion devices head-to-head (2,335 device recipients). Three trials only included patients unsuitable for oral anticoagulation, and no trial studied percutaneous LAA occlusion in addition to oral anticoagulation. The mean age of study participants ranged from 69.4-78.5 years, 28.8%-42.4% were female and the mean CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score ranged from 3.4-5.2. The proportion of patients with persistent/permanent AF ranged from 30.7%-73.6%, while prior stroke/transient ischemic attack ranged from 7.9%-40.5%. Eight trials including 5,297 device recipients reported on ischemic stroke following percutaneous LAA occlusion. During a weighted mean average follow-up of 3.4 years, the pooled annualized rate of ischemic stroke following percutaneous LAA occlusion was 1.5% (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.3%-1.7%) per year (I 2 =0%) (Figure). Event rates were similar in trials testing WATCHMAN 2.5 (1.5% per year), WATCHMAN FLX (1.6% per year) and Amplatzer Amulet (1.6% per year) (p=0.96). Rates of ischemic stroke were similar in trials that enrolled patients suitable (1.4%, 95% CI 1.1%-1.8%) and unsuitable for oral anticoagulation (1.6%, 95% CI 1.4%-1.9%) (p=0.34). Due to insufficient data, we were unable to perform prespecified subgroup analyses according to CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score, AF pattern, and prior stroke. Conclusions: A sizeable proportion of percutaneous LAA occlusion recipients have a residual risk of stroke that exceeds the current threshold for a class 2a recommendation for oral anticoagulation. Published data were insufficient to identify higher-risk subgroups.
title: Abstract 14196: Residual Risk of Ischemic Stroke in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation Following Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials

abstract: Introduction: Conduction disturbances requiring permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation are one of the most consequential complications following TAVR. While baseline RBBB is recognized as a significant risk for post-TAVR PPM, its impact on length of stay (LOS) and implications on periprocedural management have not been fully characterized. Research Question: We assessed whether preprocedural EKG conduction abnormalities, particularly RBBB, identify patients at increased risk for post-TAVR PPM implantation and increased LOS. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 309 patients undergoing TAVR at an academic medical center. After excluding 16 patients with pre-existing PPM, 293 patients were included in this analysis. Pre-procedural EKGs were used as baseline parameters for PR interval, QRS duration, and type of conduction block. The primary outcome was new PPM implantation within 12 months following TAVR. Secondary outcomes included LOS, all-cause mortality, and major adverse cardiac events (MACE) at 6 and 12 months. Baseline characteristics and clinical outcomes were compared using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate. Regression analyses were used to evaluate baseline EKG parameters and conduction abnormalities as predictors of PPM implantation and LOS. Results: Among 293 patients (mean age 76 ± 11 years, 73% male), the overall PPM rate was 7.8% (n=23). Baseline RBBB was present in 7.5% of the cohort (n=22) and was associated with a higher PPM rate compared with patients without RBBB (32% vs 5.9%, p<0.001). RBBB was associated with an elevated odds of PPM implantation (OR 7.44, 95% CI 2.54 - 20.5, p<0.001). Although no patient with baseline LBBB (n=10) required PPM, the composite presence of any baseline conduction abnormality (RBBB, LBBB, or IVCD) was independently associated with PPM implantation (OR 2.69, 95% CI 1.13-6.44, p=0.024). PPM recipients experienced significantly longer LOS compared to those without PPM (5.4 ± 3.1 vs. 2.5 ± 3.4 days, p<0.001). No significant associations were identified between other baseline ECG parameters and 6 or 12-month mortality or MACE, though event rates were limited. Conclusion: Baseline RBBB was strongly associated with post-TAVR PPM implantation and more than a two-fold increase in LOS. These findings identify RBBB as a marker of a high-risk subgroup that may benefit from tailored periprocedural monitoring and management strategies, such as early electrophysiology consultation and pre-procedural patient counseling.
title: Abstract 14198: Warning, Warning: Baseline Right Bundle Branch Block and Permanent Pacemaker Implantation After TAVR

abstract: Background: Autoimmune rheumatic diseases (AIRDs) are associated with chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, endothelial dysfunction, and accelerated atherosclerosis, contributing to excess cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Prior studies have suggested worse outcomes following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in patients with AIRDs; however, contemporary evidence remains heterogeneous. We performed an updated systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating long-term outcomes after PCI among patients with AIRDs. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar was conducted from inception through May 2026 in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Cochrane Risk of Bias. Studies comparing PCI outcomes in patients with and without AIRDs were included. AIRDs comprised rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren syndrome, spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, mixed connective tissue disease, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and systemic vasculitis. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction (MI), repeat revascularization, in-hospital mortality, and readmission. As the MACE definitions varied across studies; study-reported composite cardiovascular endpoints were pooled as reported. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.4.1. Results: Twelve studies comprising 7,104,017 patients undergoing PCI were included, including 40,667 patients with AIRDs and 6,963,350 without AIRD. Compared with patients without AIRDs, those with AIRDs had a higher risk of all-cause mortality (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.09-1.70; p=0.007; I 2 =99%) and MACE outcomes (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.05-1.27; p=0.002; I 2 =74%). No statistically significant differences were observed in recurrent MI (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.98-1.79; p=0.07) or repeat revascularization (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.00-1.71; p=0.05). In-hospital mortality was similar between groups (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.69-2.14; p=0.50). However, AIRD patients had a significantly greater risk of readmission after PCI (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.09-1.42; p=0.001). Conclusions: In this updated meta-analysis of more than 7.1 million patients undergoing PCI, AIRDs were associated with a higher risk of long-term mortality, MACE, and hospital readmission. These findings should be interpreted in the context of heterogeneous AIRD phenotypes, variable MACE definitions, and potential residual confounding. Future studies should determine whether disease activity, inflammatory burden, and immunomodulatory therapies modify cardiovascular risk after PCI.
title: Abstract 14211: Long-Term Mortality, MACE, and Readmission After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases: A Meta-Analysis of 7.1 Million Patients

abstract: Background: Ascending aortic and aortic arch replacement carries high perioperative risk. Temporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS) is increasingly used in high-risk cardiac surgery, but device-specific outcomes in this population remain limited to case reports and small series. Research Question: What is the association between temporary MCS strategies and in-hospital outcomes among hospitalizations for ascending aortic or aortic arch replacement? Methods: Using the National Inpatient Sample (2019-2023), adult hospitalizations undergoing ascending aorta or aortic arch replacement were identified. MCS was categorized as no MCS, intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) only, temporary ventricular assist device (VAD) only, veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) only, or multiple devices. Survey-weighted multivariable regression models estimated adjusted associations with in-hospital mortality, stroke, acute kidney injury requiring dialysis, red blood cell transfusion, length of stay, total hospital charges, and a composite adverse event, adjusting for demographics, comorbidities, cardiogenic shock, invasive mechanical ventilation, acute dissection, and concomitant cardiac procedures. Results: The analytic cohort included 87,215 weighted hospitalizations (17,443 unweighted), of which 2,705 (3.1%) received temporary MCS. IABP was most common (1.8%), followed by VA-ECMO (0.7%), temporary VAD (0.3%), and multiple devices (0.3%). After adjustment, all MCS categories were associated with higher in-hospital mortality compared with no MCS: IABP (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.20; 95% CI, 3.65-7.40), temporary VAD (aOR 10.80; 95% CI, 5.29-22.06), VA-ECMO (aOR 19.20; 95% CI, 11.61-31.75), and multiple devices (aOR 21.89; 95% CI, 9.18-52.15). VA-ECMO was associated with higher odds of any stroke (aOR 2.94; 95% CI, 1.73-5.00) and ischemic stroke (aOR 2.15; 95% CI, 1.22-3.81). Temporary VAD and VA-ECMO were associated with hemorrhagic stroke. All MCS categories were associated with higher dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury and total hospital charges. Conclusion(s): Temporary MCS during ascending aortic surgery was associated with higher in-hospital mortality, adverse events, and costs, with the greatest risk observed for VA-ECMO and multiple-device support. These findings support selective, risk-based MCS use and underscore the need for prospective studies distinguishing preemptive from rescue device placement.
title: Abstract 14220: Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support During Ascending Aortic and Aortic Arch Replacement

abstract: Background: Previous meta-analyses suggested improved short-term outcomes with culprit-vessel only (CV) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) compared with multivessel (MV) PCI in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) complicated by cardiogenic shock (CS). However, more recent studies have reported conflicting findings regarding the magnitude of benefit observed with CV-PCI. Therefore, we performed an updated systematic review and meta-analysis comparing clinical outcomes between MV-PCI and CV-PCI in patients with AMI and CS. Methods: PubMed and Google Scholar were systematically searched from inception through March 2026 for randomized and observational studies comparing MV-PCI and CV-PCI in patients with AMI complicated by CS. Data were pooled as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using a random-effects model. Outcomes of interest included all-cause mortality at ≤30 days and >30 days, reinfarction, renal replacement therapy, repeat revascularization, cardiac death, rehospitalization, stroke, and bleeding. Results: A total of 23 studies comprising 47,759 patients treated with MV-PCI and 120,303 treated with CV-PCI were included. Compared with CV-PCI, MV-PCI was associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality at ≤30 days (RR 1.07; 95% CI 1.01-1.12; p=0.018), hemorrhagic stroke (RR 1.24; 95% CI 1.01-1.52; p=0.04), and unspecified stroke (RR 1.15; 95% CI 1.03-1.28; p=0.01). No significant differences were observed between strategies in all-cause mortality at >30 days (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.95-1.09), cardiac death (RR 0.90; 95% CI 0.68-1.19), reinfarction (RR 1.10; 95% CI 0.91-1.34), renal replacement therapy (RR 1.14; 95% CI 0.92-1.43), repeat revascularization (RR 0.75; 95% CI 0.55-1.02), or rehospitalization (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.82-1.20). Bleeding outcomes were also similar between groups, including major bleeding (RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.96-1.13), minor bleeding (RR 1.15; 95% CI 0.83-1.59), and unspecified bleeding (RR 1.11; 95% CI 0.74-1.67). Conclusions: Compared with CV-PCI, MV-PCI was associated with increased short-term mortality and stroke in patients with AMI complicated by cardiogenic shock, with otherwise comparable long-term outcomes. These findings further support CV-PCI as the preferred initial revascularization strategy, although additional contemporary randomized data are warranted.
title: Abstract 14226: Contemporary Outcomes of Multivessel versus Culprit-Only PCI in Acute Myocardial Infarction Complicated by Cardiogenic Shock: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Leadless pacemakers have emerged as an effective alternative to conventional transvenous systems, eliminating lead and pocket related complications. However, real-world data across multiple leadless platforms remain limited. Objective: To characterize real-world procedural outcomes, technical challenges, and complications associated with leadless pacemaker implantation across contemporary platforms at a high-volume tertiary referral center. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of consecutive leadless pacemaker device implantation procedures performed at a large-volume tertiary referral center between January 2015 and December 2025. Baseline clinical characteristics, implantation indications, procedural success, technical difficulty, and short-term procedural complications were evaluated. Procedures involving leadless devices from 3 manufacturers, Medtronic, Abbott/St. Jude, and Boston Scientific were included. Results: A total of 570 patients underwent 685 leadless device implantation procedures. Mean age was 67.4±17.4 years (39.8% females). The most frequent indications were atrioventricular block (55.9%), severe symptomatic bradycardia (23.1%), sinus node dysfunction (6.9%), prior device complications or limited venous access (9.5%), and prior device infection or elevated infection risk (4.6%). Overall implantation success was 99.4% (681/685) and remained high across manufacturers, ranging from 99.2% to 100%. Four failures occurred due to extensive fibrosis (n=1), poor signal quality (n=2), and pericardial effusion requiring intervention (n=1). Technical difficulty was encountered in 23 procedures (3.3%), most related to challenging anatomy (n=18), followed by morbid obesity (n=2), extensive fibrosis (n=2), and severe chamber dilation (n=1). Procedural complications occurred in 19 procedures (2.8%), including cardiac perforation/tamponade (n=6), device embolization/dislodgement (n=5), death (n=2), stroke/transient ischemic attack (n=1), infection (n=1), and other complications (n=4). Two deaths occurred: one due to cardiogenic shock in a patient who was found to have RCA stent thrombosis and intraprocedural LAD thrombus formation, and one due to hemopericardium with tamponade refractory to intervention. Conclusions: Leadless pacemaker implantation demonstrated excellent procedural success and a low complication rate (2.8%) across multiple device platforms, substantially lower than the 5-10% immediate complication rates historically reported with conventional transvenous pacemakers.
title: Abstract 14231: Leadless Pacemakers in Clinical Practice: A Decade of Experience

abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have been linked to atrial fibrillation (AF), but the roles of thyroid dysfunction and subclinical immune-cardiotoxicity remain uncertain. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using Clalit Health Services electronic health records from 2012-2024. Adult patients with lung, breast, melanoma, renal, or bladder cancer receiving ICIs were compared with chemotherapy-treated patients. Patients with prior AF/flutter, thyroid dysfunction, or myocarditis were excluded. Multivariable Cox models evaluated incident AF over 0-1, 1-3, and 0-3 years, with thyroid dysfunction, sex-stratified, landmark, competing-risk proxy, and biomarker sensitivity analyses, including systemic immune-inflammation index (SII). Results: The cohort included 13,023 patients: 3,682 treated with ICIs and 9,341 with chemotherapy. ICI exposure was associated with higher incident AF risk over 3 years (HR 1.89, 95% CI 1.21-2.94), with the strongest signal in the first year (HR 1.72, 95% CI 1.04-2.85). This pattern persisted in thyroid-naïve patients (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.22-3.19) and after excluding early events (HR 1.84, 95% CI 1.11-3.07). Incident thyroid dysfunction was not a significant population-level mediator. Female ICI-treated patients showed the strongest early AF signal. Peri-AF analyses showed higher SII in ICI-treated than chemotherapy-treated patients, together with ferritin elevation, troponin rise, and sex-specific subclinical thyroid changes. Conclusions: ICI exposure was associated with increased AF risk, particularly during the first year, without clear mediation by overt thyroid dysfunction. ICI-associated AF may reflect a subclinical immune-cardiotoxic phenotype characterized by systemic inflammation, macrophage activation, myocardial injury, and sex-specific thyroid changes
title: Abstract 14257: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Associated Atrial Fibrillation and Subclinical Immune-Cardiotoxicity
