abstract: Introduction/Background: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) has high morbidity and mortality with lipoprotein a (Lp(a)) being associated with increased atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk and PAD severity. Major adverse limb events (MALE) are four times higher in patients with elevated Lp(a) and elevated levels are independently associated with incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and MALE in patients with PAD treated with revascularization, irrespective of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol level and statin administration. Previous studies have demonstrated risk reduction in MACE and percutaneous coronary intervention in those with elevated Lp(a) with use of aspirin or ticagrelor. However, no studies currently evaluate the effect of various antithrombotic regimens in those with elevated Lp(a) and PAD. Evaluation of these agents, which are readily available, may provide an accessible option to reduce associated MALE in patients with elevated Lp(a) levels. Methods/Approach: Retrospective data was gathered for patients age >18 years that had an Lp(a) level resulted with known PAD (ABI <0.9 or ≥1.4) and a minimum of 3 years follow-up. The analysis included 623 patients on anticoagulation (AC), antiplatelets (AP), or combination AC/AP therapy between 2010 and 2025. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was developed to quantify the risk associated with Lp(a) level (<30 vs. >30 mg/dL) after adjusting for the prescribed antithrombotic regimen. The model included a formal test for a statistical interaction between Lp(a) level and therapy type to determine if the effect of Lp(a) differed across treatment strategies. Results/Data: Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that a high Lp(a) level was significantly associated with a higher incidence of MACE (p=0.038) and MALE (p=0.040), but not all-cause mortality. In the multivariable Cox model, the type of antithrombotic therapy was a powerful predictor of events (p<0.001), with patients on combination AC/AP therapy having the highest risk, likely reflecting significant confounding by indication. After adjusting for the prescribed therapy, high Lp(a) remained an independent and significant predictor of MALE (Hazard Ratio: 1.37; 95% CI: 1.04-1.80; p=0.024). No significant interaction was found between Lp(a) level and the type of antithrombotic therapy (p=0.25). Conclusion(s): The correlation between antithrombotic strategy and Lp(a) prothrombotic effects does not appear pronounced in this cohort though several limitations need to be taken into account. Thus, there is not currently a clear reason based on Lp(a) level that one antithrombotic regimen should be chosen over another.
title: Abstract 17405: Outcomes Across Antithrombotic Regimens in Peripheral Artery Disease and the Influence of Lipoprotein(a)

abstract: Background: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has fundamentally altered the treatment landscape for severe aortic stenosis (AS), particularly among elderly patients at elevated surgical risk. However, the population-level impact of TAVR expansion on national AS mortality trends remains incompletely defined. Methods: We analyzed mortality data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-Ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) Multiple Cause of Death database from 1999-2024. Deaths related to nonrheumatic aortic valve stenosis were identified using ICD-10 code I35.0. National age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) were calculated annually. Temporal trends were evaluated using Joinpoint regression to identify significant changes in mortality trajectories and estimate annual percent changes (APCs). Age-stratified analyses were performed among adults aged 65-74 years, 75-84 years, and ≥85 years. Results: A total of 318,984 AS-related deaths were identified during the study period. Joinpoint regression identified a single significant inflection point in 2013 (95% CI, 2012-2015). From 1999-2013, AS mortality increased significantly (APC +0.84%/year; 95% CI 0.47-1.22; p<0.001). Following 2013, mortality declined significantly through 2024 (APC –2.59%/year; 95% CI –3.09 to –2.10; p<0.001). Age-adjusted mortality peaked at 4.07 deaths per 100,000 population in 2007 and subsequently reached a historic low of 2.97 deaths per 100,000 population in 2024. Age-stratified analyses demonstrated that mortality reductions were concentrated among older adults. Mortality remained relatively stable among individuals aged 65-74 years, while substantial declines were observed among those aged 75-84 years and ≥85 years, the populations most likely to undergo transcatheter valve intervention Conclusions: National aortic stenosis mortality in the United States underwent a significant reversal in trend beginning in 2013, transitioning from increasing mortality to sustained annual declines through 2024. Mortality improvements were predominantly observed among adults aged 75 years and older. The timing and age-specific distribution of these findings parallel the expansion of TAVR and suggest a potential population-level association between transcatheter valve therapy and improved outcomes in patients with AS.
title: Abstract 17407: Reversal of National Aortic Stenosis Mortality Trends During the Expansion of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in the United States, 1999-2024

abstract: Background: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a neglected female-predominant arteriopathy characterized by stenosis and aneurysms in medium-sized arteries, without atherosclerosis. FMD is often diagnosed in middle-aged women in the context of resistant hypertension, stroke, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD). We aimed to explore molecular signatures of FMD lesions to delineate their specific arterial remodeling. Methods: Paraffin-embedded arterial samples were immune-stained to check for RNA quality and diagnosis of FMD lesions. We used 10x Visium spatial transcriptomic sequencing (Illumina NextSeqTM 500). FASTQ files were processed using Space Ranger (v3.0.0) and differential expression analyses using Seurat (v5.0.3) in R (v4.3.3). Cell types were inferred using public single-cell datasets. Pseudotime trajectory analyses were performed using the monocle 3 package (v1.3.7), enrichment analyses using clusterProfiler (v4.10.1), and gene co-expression network analyses using hdWGCNA (v0.3.03). We integrated GWAS summary statistics and spatial transcriptomics via gsMap method (v1.70). Immunofluorescence was performed according to standard protocols. Results: Quality control prioritized 4 affected samples and 2 controls. UMAP clustering identified 4 medial (M1-M4) and five adventitial (A1-A5) populations. M1-M4 were enriched for smooth muscle cell (SMC) markers, with M4, unique to FMD lesions, displaying SMCs with a macrophage-like signature, which we confirmed using immunofluorescence for two immunity markers: CD68+ and CD163+, and the absence of macrophage infiltration. Collagen-rich M3 cluster was markedly enriched in FMD lesions compared to controls. Differential gene expression and pseudo-time analyses suggested a gene expression trajectory first through downregulation of contractile markers in SMCs, followed by upregulation of collagens, and finally the development of an inflammatory signature of the media as the most advanced lesional state. We identified five spatial co-expression modules (SMs): SM1 predominant in normal media, SM2 almost exclusive to FMD lesions, and SM3/SM4 as intermediate networks, representing potential transitional remodeling states. SM5 was non-specific. The integration of GWAS data showed that SMC-dominant spatial niches expressed several risk genes for FMD, SCAD, and blood pressure traits, without reaching significant enrichment. Conclusions: Leveraging spatially resolved molecular data, we show a distinct gene-expression program involving SMC phenotypic evolution from contraction toward a pro-fibrotic state, and an immune signature at an advanced stage of FMD lesions. We provide original insights into FMD-specific arterial remodeling, involving inflammation for the first time, with distinct features from atherosclerotic inflammation involving macrophages.
title: Abstract 17408: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveal Gene Expression Signatures in Arterial Fibromuscular Dysplasia Lesions

abstract: Introduction: Blood pressure control is key to the management of high-risk patients with hypertension and coronary artery disease (CAD). Current guidelines recommend a blood pressure target of <130/80 mmHg regardless of sex. Research Question: What is the association between blood pressure control and cardiovascular outcomes in women and men with CAD undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)? Methods: We included consecutive patients with hypertension undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) between January 2012 and December 2024 at a large US tertiary center. Patients with cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock, active cancer, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)<30 ml/min/1.73m 2 , or left ventricular ejection fraction ≤30% were excluded. Blood pressure control was defined per 2025 American guidelines as mean systolic blood pressure (SBP)<130 mmHg and mean diastolic blood pressure (DBP)<80 mmHg, averaged from cuff measurements obtained during hospitalization. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) at 1 year, defined as a composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), non-fatal stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, or hospitalization for hypertensive emergency. The association between blood pressure control and MACE was assessed using a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for age, race/ethnicity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and prior MI. Results: Among the 21,636 patients included, 6,300 (29.1%) were women and mean age was 67±11 years. Women had a higher prevalence of uncontrolled hypertension than men (69% vs 61%, p<0.001), were of similar age, had a higher prevalence of diabetes, and had a lower prevalence of prior MI. Blood pressure levels were similar in women and men with uncontrolled hypertension (mSBP 148±13 mmHg and mDBP 72±7mmHg in women; mSBP 145±12mmHg and mDBP 76±8 mmHg in men). MACE occurred in 7.8% of women and 5.9% of men at 1 year. Uncontrolled hypertension was associated with the occurrence of MACE in men (HR 1.34 [95%CI 1.17-1.53], p<0.001) but not in women (HR 0.92 [95%CI 0.77-1.10], p=0.36) ( Figure ). After adjustment, uncontrolled hypertension was not associated with higher MACE in men (aHR 1.08[0.93-1.25], p=0.31). These findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses using the previously recommended blood pressure target of<140/90 mmHg and a stricter target of <120/70 mmHg. Conclusions: In patients with CAD undergoing PCI, blood pressure control defined per current guidelines was associated with MACE in men but not in women, suggesting the need to investigate sex-specific blood pressure thresholds in patients with CAD.
title: Abstract 17416: Association Between Blood Pressure Control and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Women and Men Undergoing Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

abstract: Background: Stress hyperglycemia is a well-characterized risk factor in critically ill patients, including those with myocardial infarction. However, its incremental risk over chronic glycemic dysregulation—measured via glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)—remains poorly established. The stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) has emerged as a novel prognostic tool to isolate the impact of acute stress hyperglycemia, but its utility in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) warrants further investigation. Research Question: Can the SHR enhance early risk stratification for in-hospital major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with STEMI? Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study at a tertiary reference center, enrolling patients aged > 18 years admitted with STEMI between July 2024 and December 2025. All included patients underwent initial serum glucose and HbA1c testing during the index hospitalization. Exclusion criteria were a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state at admission, type 1 diabetes, or chronic steroid use. The primary outcome was in-hospital MACE, a composite of reinfarction, stroke, cardiogenic shock, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation, and all-cause death. Results: Of the initial 800 patients, 650 met the eligibility criteria (mean age 61 ± 11 years; 77.5% male). Comorbidities included diabetes in 49% (n=319) and hypertension in 55% (n=358). In-hospital MACE occurred in 162 patients (25%). Patients who experienced MACE had a significantly higher median SHR compared to those without MACE (1.15 [IQR 0.47] vs. 1.01 [IQR 0.36], p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression analysis, SHR emerged as a powerful independent predictor of in-hospital MACE (OR: 2.97; 95% CI:1.86-4.85; p < 0.001). Adding SHR to the baseline clinical risk model substantially enhanced risk discrimination and reclassification, yielding a NRI of 0.391 (p < 0.001) and IDI of 0.038 (95% CI: 0.020-0.057; p < 0.001). Furthermore, in a multivariable model targeting the hard endpoint of isolated in-hospital mortality, SHR remained a robust independent predictor (OR: 3.24; 95% CI: 1.46-7.01; p = 0.002). Conclusions: The SHR is a robust, independent predictor of in-hospital MACE and mortality in STEMI patients. Incorporating SHR into baseline clinical assessments significantly improves risk discrimination and reclassification, highlighting its value as a practical tool for early risk stratification.
title: Abstract 17423: Stress Hyperglycemia Ratio Predicts In-Hospital MACE and Enhances Risk Reclassification in Patients with STEMI

abstract: Background: Coronary artery disease coexists with severe aortic stenosis in 30-80% of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Altered coronary hemodynamics in severe AS, including left ventricular hypertrophy and microvascular dysfunction, may reduce the accuracy of angiographic lesion assessment. Whether physiology-guided coronary assessment improves outcomes over angiography-guided assessment, and whether percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of significant lesions reduces events compared with conservative management, remain unsettled. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL (January 2010-April 2026) for studies of invasive coronary physiology (FFR, iFR, RFR, other non-hyperemic pressure ratios) in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR. Two prespecified modules were analyzed: Module A pooled studies comparing physiology- vs angiography-guided strategy; Module B addressed PCI vs conservative management. DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman small-sample sensitivity was performed in R. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB2 and full seven-domain ROBINS-I; GRADE was applied to each outcome. Results: Five clinical studies (~2,146 unique patients after cohort-overlap correction) met inclusion criteria; three contributed event-level data to quantitative synthesis. Module A: physiology-guided revascularization was associated with lower MACCE compared with angiography-guided assessment (pooled OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.25-0.76; HKSJ 95% CI 0.07-2.62; I 2 =0%; P=0.003; ARR 8.8%; NNT ≈12; GRADE Low). Module B (NOTION-3): PCI of significant lesions reduced the composite of CV death, MI, and urgent revascularization (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.51-0.99, P=0.04; derived OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.97; ARR 9.1%; NNT ≈11; GRADE Moderate), offset by higher bleeding (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.03-2.22; NNH ≈12). Mechanistic studies (n=7) demonstrated relative stability of hyperemic indices (FFR) after TAVR while resting indices (iFR, RFR) showed greater post-procedural variability and reclassification; reclassification of treatment indication occurred in approximately 6% of lesions despite stable mean FFR (Pesarini), and AS-specific cutoffs of FFR ≤0.83 and RFR ≤0.85 (COMIC-AS) have been proposed. Conclusions: Physiology-guided coronary assessment is associated with improved outcomes in patients undergoing TAVR. The near-equivalence of NNT for benefit and NNH for bleeding underscores the need for individualized risk assessment. A stepwise NHPR → FFR workflow using AS-specific thresholds may guide clinical decision-making. Module A's small evidence base (k=2) is reflected in the wide HKSJ sensitivity interval, transparently reported as small-sample uncertainty; prospective validation is needed.
title: Abstract 17449: Physiology-Guided Coronary Assessment in Severe Aortic Stenosis Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Alternate access (AA) routes, e.g., transapical and transaxillary, are usually employed in patients with heavily calcified iliofemoral arteries requiring a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), unlike the gold standard transfemoral route, due to the increased procedural morbidity associated with their anatomy. However, comparative data for newly developed intravascular lithotripsy (IVL)-assisted transfemoral TAVR for these patients remained limited. Methods: A systematic search of major electronic databases from inception to May 2026 evaluated studies comparing IVL-TAVR with non-IVL TAVR (alternate access routes or standard transfemoral route without IVL assistance). A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted using RevMan version 5.4, providing pooled estimates as risk ratios (RRs) or mean differences (MDs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, with most studies having a moderate risk. Heterogeneity was analyzed using the I 2 statistic, and prespecified sensitivity analyses were performed by sequential exclusion of studies. Results: Data from five studies, including 5097 individuals (IVL-TAVR: n=1,305; non-IVL TAVR: n=3,792), were pooled. IVL-TAVR was associated with reduced use of general anesthesia (RR 0.36; p=0.0001) and intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (RR 0.15; p=0.0001).Furthermore, IVL-TAVR increased the duration of hospital stay (MD +0.33 days; p=0.0004) and showed a borderline increase in the risk of readmission (RR 1.23; p=0.05). No significant differences existed in the rates of freedom from in-hospital mortality (RR 0.99), overall mortality (RR 1.27), strokes (RR 0.59), major vascular complications (RR 1.18; p=0.80, I 2 =66%), need for pacemaker insertion (RR 1.07), and major bleeding (RR 0.74). The composite efficacy endpoint showed no significant difference between groups (RR 1.32; I 2 =95%; p=0.25); the high heterogeneity was driven by differences between studies in how the endpoints were defined. Sensitivity analyses excluding the registry study, Imran et al., resolved the heterogeneity for major vascular complications (I 2 =0%), yielding a higher risk for the IVL-TAVR group compared to non-IVL TAVR (RR 2.75, 95% CI 2.14-3.53). Conclusion: IVL-assisted transfemoral TAVR has similar outcomes in terms of mortality and safety as non-IVL TAVR. This supports the potential role of this approach to allow access in patients with severe calcification of the iliac and femoral arteries. Advantages include decreased need for general anesthesia and invasive monitoring, which can't be offset by small increases in hospital stays and higher rates of readmission. To determine the definitive role of IVL-assisted TAVR, further adequately sized and powered prospective comparative trials will be necessary.
title: Abstract 17453: Intravascular Lithotripsy (IVL)-Assisted Transfemoral Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) versus Non-IVL-Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients with Peripheral Artery Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Although transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the management of severe aortic stenosis, accurately identifying patients at risk of post-procedural futility and adverse clinical outcomes remains a major unmet need. Conventional risk scores may fail to capture the complex interactions among clinical and procedural variables. Machine learning (ML) approaches offer a data driven strategy for more precise and individualized risk stratification. Methods: Eligible studies including adult patients undergoing TAVR for severe aortic stenosis were included. We evaluated ML-based models, including random forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost, neural networks, support vector machines, deep learning, and ensemble approaches. Conventional comparators included STS score, EuroSCORE II, logistic EuroSCORE, and traditional regression based models. The primary outcome was model discrimination measured by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary outcomes included all cause mortality, futility, heart failure hospitalization, conduction disturbances, permanent pacemaker implantation, and technical failure. Random effects models were used to pool AUROC estimates and direct differences in AUROC between ML and conventional prediction models. Results: Twelve studies were included in the primary AUROC analysis. Between diverse populations and endpoints, ML models demonstrated robust predictive performance for post-TAVR futility and adverse clinical outcomes, achieving a pooled AUROC of 0.772 (95% CI, 0.743-0.799). In direct comparative analyses, ML consistently outperformed conventional risk scores, with a pooled ΔAUROC of 0.165 (95% CI, 0.084-0.246; p=0.0001), representing a clinically meaningful improvement in risk discrimination. Diagnostic accuracy analyses yielded a pooled sensitivity of 73.1%, specificity of 73.3%, and diagnostic odds ratio of 7.48. For mortality related outcomes, ML models achieved excellent discrimination (AUROC 0.819; 95% CI, 0.767-0.871), while maintaining good performance for non-mortality outcomes, including futility and major postprocedural complications (AUROC approximately 0.770), with no significant subgroup differences. Between study heterogeneity reflected variations in algorithms, outcome definitions, patient characteristics, and validation methodologies. Conclusions: ML models provide superior discrimination for identifying patients at risk of futility and adverse clinical outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of ML driven risk stratification to advance precision medicine in structural heart interventions and improve patient selection beyond traditional scoring systems. Further prospective studies with rigorous external validation are warranted before widespread clinical implementation.
title: Abstract 17460: Machine Learning versus Conventional Risk Models for Predicting Futility and Adverse Clinical Outcomes Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock (CS) carries a mortality exceeding 40%. Valvular heart disease (VHD) represents a distinct and potentially reversible etiology of CS, yet its relationship to shock severity at presentation, as defined by the SCAI shock stage classification, remains poorly characterized. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that VHD-related CS presents at less advanced shock stages compared to non-valvular CS, with implications for early intervention strategies. Methods: We analyzed 1,232 consecutive CS patients classified by SCAI stage (A/B=early, C=classic, D=deteriorating, E=extremis) and VHD etiology: no VHD (n=310), isolated mitral regurgitation (MR, n=230), isolated tricuspid regurgitation (TR, n=245), and multi-valve VHD (n=447; comprising MR+TR 72.5%, MR+TR+AS 17.9%, AS+TR 4.9%, MR+AS 2.7%, AS alone 2.0%). Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc tests and ordinal logistic regression (reference: no VHD) were performed, with multinomial logistic regression as sensitivity analysis. Results: SCAI stage distribution differed significantly across VHD groups (Kruskal-Wallis H=30.35, p<0.001). Advanced shock (SCAI D/E) was present in 31.9% of non-VHD patients versus 19.1% in isolated MR, 28.6% in isolated TR, and 14.5% in multi-valve VHD. On ordinal logistic regression, isolated MR (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.39-0.74, p=0.0002) and multi-valve VHD (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.40-0.69, p<0.001) were independently associated with lower odds of presenting at an advanced SCAI stage versus no VHD. Isolated TR was not significantly associated with shock stage (OR 0.90, p=0.499). On multinomial sensitivity analysis, multi-valve VHD patients had 69% lower odds of SCAI E versus A/B compared to non-VHD patients (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.19-0.52, p<0.001). Conclusions: In 1,232 CS patients, VHD (particularly isolated MR and MR+TR) was independently associated with significantly lower odds of advanced SCAI shock stage at presentation (OR ~0.53-0.54, p<0.001), with multi-valve patients showing 69% lower odds of SCAI E extremis (OR 0.31, p<0.001). These findings suggest VHD-related CS may be identified at an earlier, more actionable shock stage, underscoring the need for valve-specific CS protocols.
title: Abstract 17469: Valvular Heart Disease and Its Association with SCAI Shock Stages at Presentation in Cardiogenic Shock: A Registry Analysis of 1,232 Patients

abstract: Introduction: Four genomic, lipid, and inflammatory biomarkers can identify individuals with adverse atherosclerotic biology. A single measurement of coronary artery disease polygenic risk score (CAD PRS), lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)], low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) in midlife can predict first cardiovascular event. Whether a combination of these four biomarkers measured in people with known CAD can also predict recurrent CAD events remains unknown. Hypothesis: Among individuals with established CAD, a single measurement of four biomarkers capturing atherosclerotic biology can predict CAD recurrence. Methods: We studied 13,509 middle aged individuals with prevalent CAD, and available CAD PRS, LDL-C, Lp(a) and hs-CRP measurements in the Mass General Brigham Biobank. CAD recurrence was identified through diagnostic and procedural codes. LDL-C levels were corrected according to lipid lowering medication use. Elevated biomarkers are determined as a values above clinical threshold for each biomarker which is defined by CAD PRS ≥ 80th percentile or top quintile, LDL-C ≥ 130 mg/dL, hs-CRP ≥ 2 mg/L and Lp(a) ≥ 125 nmol/L. Age and sex adjusted logistic regression models were used to estimate odds ratio (OR) of individual and additive effects of elevated biomarkers on CAD recurrence. Discrimination was assessed through calculating the C statistic of age and sex augmented by the four biomarkers and also clinical risk factors including current smoking, history of myocardial infarction (MI), MI in the past 12 months, prior percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass graft, ischemic stroke, congestive heart failure, and peripheral artery disease, current type 2 diabetes, and estimated glomerular filtration fraction <60 mL/min/1.73m2. Results: Of 13,509 individuals with established CAD (mean age 68.1 years, 86.7% white, 40.7% females), 4044 (29.9%) individuals had CAD recurrence over a median follow up of 15 years. Each biomarker was individually associated with CAD recurrence. The OR for CAD recurrence of each elevated individual biomarker in a model adjusted for age and sex was 1.82 (95% CI 1.59-2.07) for CAD PRS in top quintile, 1.48 (95% CI 1.34-1.63) for hs-CRP ≥ 2 mg/L, 2.46 (1.85-3.28) for Lp(a) ≥ 125 nmol/L and 1.53 (1.39-1.69) for LDL-C ≥ 130 mg/L.The ORs for recurrent CAD by the number of elevated biomarkers compared to none was 1.63 (95% CI 1.50-1.77), 2.42 (95% CI 2.09-2.81), and 4.70 (95% CI 3.06-7.31) for one, two and three or four elevated biomarkers, respectively. A model consisting of age, sex, and the four biomarkers discriminated recurrent CAD with C-statistic of 0.607, while the same model with added clinical biomarkers discriminated recurrent CAD with C-statistic of 0.762. Conclusion: A single measurement of four biomarkers, CAD PRS, hs-CRP, Lp(a) and LDL-C, strongly predicted recurrent CAD events.
title: Abstract 17478: Genomic, Inflammatory, and Lipid Biomarker Profiles and Their Association with Coronary Artery Disease Progression

abstract: Background: Patients with bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) have historically been excluded from pivotal transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) trials. Despite increasing TAVR use in patients with BAV, contemporary nationwide data evaluating 30-day readmission outcomes and healthcare burden remain limited. Research Question: How does 30-day all-cause readmission affect clinical outcomes and healthcare utilization, and what factors independently predict readmission in patients with BAV undergoing TAVR? Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study utilizing the National Readmissions Database (NRD) from 2019-2022. Adult hospitalizations undergoing index TAVR with concurrent BAV diagnosis were identified. Index TAVR procedures were identified using the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10), Procedure Coding System codes: 02RF37H, 02RF37Z, 02RF38H, 02RF38Z, 02RF3JH, 02RF3JZ, 02RF3KH, 02RF3KZ, 02RF47Z, 02RF48Z, 02RF4JZ, and 02RF4KZ. BAV disease was identified using ICD-10 Clinical Modification diagnosis codes Q21.x and Q23.x. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause readmission. Secondary outcomes included major bleeding, acute kidney injury (AKI), stroke, acute myocardial infarction (MI), length of stay (LOS) at hospital, and inflation-adjusted hospitalization charges. Multivariable logistic and linear regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of outcomes. Results were reported as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. Results: A total of 9,356 hospitalizations for TAVR in patients with BAV were identified, of whom 593 (6.3%) experienced 30-day all-cause readmission. 30-day readmission was independently associated with higher odds of acute MI (OR 1.80 [1.03-3.14], p=0.039), prolonged LOS at hospital (β 1.4 [0.57-2.2], p<0.001), and increased inflation-adjusted hospitalization charges (β $35,548 [$11,576-$59,519], p=0.004) compared with those who were not readmitted. However, 30-day readmission was not independently associated with major bleeding (OR 1.15 [0.74-1.79], p=0.5), AKI (OR 1.56 [0.99-2.45], p=0.058), or stroke (OR 1.36, [0.60-3.08], p=0.5). In addition, higher Charlson comorbidity index independently predicted 30-day readmission (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.14-1.26, p < 0.001), major bleeding (OR 1.21), AKI ((OR 1.43), stroke (OR 1.40), acute MI (OR 1.42), increased LOS (β 0.43) and higher hospitalization charges (β 7,585). Conclusion: Among patients with BAV undergoing TAVR, 30-day all-cause readmission occurred in a small proportion of patients but was associated with prolonged LOS, higher hospitalization charges, and increased risk of acute MI. A higher Charlson Comorbidity Index was found to be an independent predictor of adverse outcomes, highlighting the importance of comprehensive risk stratification in this complex patient population.
title: Abstract 17496: Predictors and Outcomes of 30-Day Readmission Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients with Bicuspid Aortic Valve: A Nationwide Readmissions Database Analysis

abstract: Coronary artery bypass grafting may be performed with cardiopulmonary bypass (on-pump CABG [ONCAB]) or on the beating heart without bypass (off-pump CABG [OPCAB]), however evidence comparing long-term outcomes remains inconsistent. Therefore, we assessed clinical outcomes associated with OPCAB versus ONCAB in a large contemporary real-world cohort by conducting a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network of adults undergoing CABG from January 2015 to December 2025. Patients were stratified by operative technique. Missing continuous variables were imputed using Bayesian Ridge multiple imputation by chained equations. Propensity score matching used 1:1 greedy nearest-neighbor matching without replacement and included age, sex, race, prior stroke/transient ischemic attack, anemia, anticoagulant use, systolic blood pressure, serum creatinine, HbA1c, and AST; all matched variables achieved excellent balance. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were ischemic stroke, acute kidney injury (AKI), acute myocardial infarction (AMI), major bleeding, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and heart failure decompensation, defined as hospitalization for heart failure or cardiogenic shock with intravenous loop diuretic use. Doubly robust Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) with 97.5% confidence intervals (CIs). After matching, 43,772 patients were included (21,886 OPCAB; 21,886 ONCAB), with all standardized mean differences below 0.10. During follow-up, 2,640 verified heart failure decompensation events occurred. OPCAB was associated with lower risk of heart failure decompensation versus ONCAB (HR 0.71, 97.5% CI 0.64-0.80), but higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.21, 97.5% CI 1.14-1.28) and ischemic stroke (HR 1.13, 97.5% CI 1.07-1.19). Risks of AKI (HR 0.98, 97.5% CI 0.93-1.04), AMI (HR 0.98, 97.5% CI 0.91-1.05), major bleeding (HR 1.08, 97.5% CI 0.99-1.19), and subsequent PCI (HR 1.05, 97.5% CI 0.97-1.12) did not differ significantly. In conclusion, OPCAB was associated with reduced long-term heart failure decompensation, but increased mortality and ischemic stroke compared with ONCAB in this large propensity-matched real-word patient population. These findings highlight divergent long-term outcomes between surgical strategies and may inform patient selection and operative decision-making.
title: Abstract 17506: Long-Term Clinical Outcomes Following Off-Pump versus On-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Papillary muscle rupture (PMR) is a rare (<1%) but catastrophic mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction (AMI), causing acute severe mitral regurgitation (MR), pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock. The posteromedial papillary muscle is disproportionately vulnerable due to exclusive perfusion by the posterior descending artery. Without prompt intervention, mortality approaches 80%. A 73-year-old man with no prior cardiac history presented after six days of untreated chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis. Admission (day 6): hypotension (66/50 mmHg), complete atrioventricular block, troponin I 9,454 ng/L, NT-proBNP 28,929 pg/mL. Initially SCAI stage C, the patient deteriorated to stage D despite escalating vasoactive support. Echocardiography confirmed posteromedial PMR with acute severe MR, biventricular dysfunction, and pulmonary artery systolic pressure 57 mmHg. Coronary angiography showed three-vessel disease (SYNTAX score 11) and distal right coronary artery thrombus with TIMI 1 flow. Norepinephrine, dobutamine, and amiodarone were initiated. On day 9, urgent surgery included coronary artery bypass grafting (left internal mammary artery to left anterior descending artery, radial artery to intermediate branch, saphenous vein graft to posterior descending artery with thrombectomy) and mitral valve replacement with a 27 mm bioprosthesis. Postoperative course was refractory: dual vasopressor-inotrope dependence, mechanical ventilation, and re-exploration for hemorrhage. The patient sustained cardiac arrest and died on postoperative day 1. Two converging factors drove surgical futility. First, a six-day delay allowed irreversible biventricular remodeling and SCAI stage D progression before intervention. Second, the MCS dilemma in acute severe MR: given the risk of afterload augmentation with available devices, MCS was deferred in favor of expedited surgery — yet myocardial injury precluded recovery. Whether preoperative ventricular unloading (Impella CP or TandemHeart) might have improved postoperative hemodynamics remains an open question. Perioperative mortality for PMR repair is 24-27% even in optimal candidates; advanced age, six-day ischemic time, and stage D shock compounded risk here. Post-infarction PMR requires immediate echocardiographic diagnosis and transfer to centers with cardiac surgery and MCS capabilities. Diagnostic delay and SCAI stage D shock are independent mortality determinants. The optimal MCS strategy in acute severe MR warrants prospective evaluation.
title: Abstract 17526: Posteromedial Papillary Muscle Rupture Complicating Late-Presenting Inferior Myocardial Infarction: Refractory Cardiogenic Shock and the Limits of Surgical Salvage

abstract: Introduction: Infectious endocarditis, especially in prosthetic heart valves, is a life-threatening condition and can lead to a plethora of complications including embolic events, perivalvular extension, and valvular destruction causing heart failure. Diagnosing Prosthetic valve endocarditis can be challenging on echocardiography due to the stent frame shadows in the perivalvular space, with combined sensitivities of TTE & TEE generally dropping to 67.8%. Patient findings: A 74-year-old gentleman with a recent transcatheter aortic valve replacement and a prior prosthetic knee replacement developed methicillin - sensitive staphylococcus aureus bacteremia seeding from left knee septic arthritis resulting in new, progressive conduction block resulting in complete heart block with ventricular standstill, with no obvious vegetations or aortic root thickening noted on the TTE and TEE. Diagnoses, Interventions, Outcomes: The patient had a temporary pacing wire placed to undergo removal of the infected knee hardware. Given the new high grade AV block, an FDG - PET/CT was performed and showed aortic valve and root heterogenous radiotracer activity confirming the diagnosis of infective endocarditis with aortic abscess. Cardiac surgery demonstrated an aortic annular abscess with left main arterial involvement, treated with Bentall procedure and left main reconstruction. He subsequently had Micra leadless permanent pacemaker placed. Following the procedure, the patient had an aspiration event requiring intubation for acute hypoxic respiratory failure and transient vasopressor support with course being complicated by renal failure and heparin- induced thrombocytopenia. After achieving hemodynamic stability, the patient was subsequently discharged on post-operative day 30 with an extended course of antibiotics. Conclusion: New conduction block in a patient with bacteremia is a relatively specific marker of perivalvular abscess and should trigger additional diagnostic investigations including metabolic imaging modalities and surgical consultation even when echocardiography is negative.
title: Abstract 17527: Progressive Heart Block Guiding Diagnosis of Aortic Root Annular Abscess of Prosthetic Aortic Valve Despite Negative Echocardiography in Staphylococcus Bacteremia

abstract: Background: Mitral annular calcification (MAC) complicates the management of mitral regurgitation (MR) and is associated with increased procedural complexity and surgical risk. Although mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) is increasingly used in high-risk patients, comparative real-world outcomes of M-TEER versus surgical mitral valve intervention in patients with MR and MAC remain limited. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using a multicenter real-world data network. Adults with MR and MAC who underwent M-TEER were compared with those who underwent surgical mitral valve repair or replacement. The index date was defined as the date of mitral valve intervention. Propensity-score matching was performed using demographics and baseline comorbidities, and covariate balance was assessed using standardized mean differences. The primary outcomes were 1-year all-cause mortality and 1-year stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA). A sensitivity analysis restricted to patients aged 65 years or older was performed. Results: Before matching, 452 patients underwent M-TEER and 1,469 underwent surgical mitral intervention. After propensity-score matching, 297 matched pairs were analyzed. At 1 year, mortality was similar between M-TEER and surgery, occurring in 42 patients in each cohort (14.1% vs 14.1%; HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.61-1.43; p=0.736). Stroke/TIA also did not differ significantly between groups (9.4% vs 12.5%; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.43-1.14; p=0.147). In the age 65 years or older sensitivity analysis, 1-year mortality remained similar between groups (14.6% vs 14.2%; HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.60-1.49; p=0.807), as did Stroke/TIA (6.9% vs 9.9%; HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.35-1.17; p=0.144). Conclusion: Among patients with MR and MAC, M-TEER demonstrated similar 1-year mortality and cerebrovascular outcomes compared with surgical mitral intervention, despite its frequent use in higher-risk patients. These findings support M-TEER as a viable alternative treatment strategy in appropriately selected patients with MAC-associated MR. Findings were consistent in an age ≥65 years sensitivity analysis
title: Abstract 17528: Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair versus Surgery in Patients with Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Annular Calcification: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Radiation heart disease (RHD) is a progressive, multisystem complication of mediastinal radiation that may not manifest clinically for decades. The full phenotypic spectrum, encompassing coronary artery disease, polyvalvular disease, conduction system disease, and cardiomyopathy, is rarely documented in a single patient over a complete longitudinal course. Patient Information: A 72-year-old man with Hodgkin lymphoma treated with mediastinal radiation in 1973 presented with acute decompensated heart failure. His cardiac history was notable for prior CABG, surgical aortic valve replacement and mitral valve repair in 2007, sick sinus syndrome requiring permanent pacemaker implantation, and pulmonary hypertension. He had no established cardiologist and had been managed across multiple institutions without longitudinal coordination. Clinical Timeline: Admission echocardiography demonstrated LVEF 42% representing new HFrEF, severe mitral stenosis with mean gradient 14 mmHg at 115 bpm, moderate-severe mitral regurgitation, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, severe pulmonary hypertension with PASP 63 mmHg, and dilated right ventricle with reduced systolic function. Septal bounce and respirophasic septal shift raised concern for concomitant constrictive physiology. BNP was 6,592 pg/mL. Evaluation: Cardiac CT demonstrated an incomplete mitral annuloplasty ring, neo-LVOT of greater than 400 mm 2 , ascending aortic calcification, and absence of pericardial calcification. Constrictive physiology was confirmed hemodynamically. The constellation of polyvalvular disease, CAD, conduction system disease, and new cardiomyopathy occurring 53 years after mediastinal radiation was consistent with advanced RHD. Interventions: Following aggressive IV diuresis and volume optimization, the patient underwent bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement with pacemaker generator exchange via right thoracotomy in May 2026. Follow-up and Outcomes: The postoperative course was complicated by vasoplegic shock, aspiration pneumonia, ARDS, gram-negative bacteremia, acute renal failure requiring continuous renal replacement therapy, and multiorgan failure. Goals of care were transitioned to comfort-focused measures. The patient died on postoperative day five. Discussion: This case documents the full cardiotoxic legacy of mediastinal radiation over five decades, culminating in a surgical intervention of prohibitive risk that nonetheless represented the only remaining therapeutic option. The absence of longitudinal cardio-oncology surveillance allowed progressive valvular and myocardial disease to reach an irreversible threshold. Recognition of RHD as a multisystem, lifelong condition requiring structured follow-up is essential to prevent the diagnostic and therapeutic odyssey illustrated by this case.
title: Abstract 17531: Post-Radiation Heart Disease: Polyvalvular Pathology, Coronary Artery Disease, and Conduction System Failure 53 Years After Mediastinal Radiation for Hodgkin Lymphoma

abstract: Background: The Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) shock classification stratifies cardiogenic shock (CS) severity at a single timepoint. However, CS is a dynamic syndrome and whether changes in trajectory of SCAI stage during the first 72 hours provide independent prognostic information beyond the admission stage remains unknown. Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of 1,079 CS patients admitted to Mayo Clinic in Arizona between 2021 and 2025. SCAI stage was prospectively assigned at presentation and serially reassessed every 24 hours over the subsequent 72 hours. Patients were classified into six trajectory phenotypes based on their dynamic pattern: “stable”, ”worsening”, “improving”, “worsening/improving ”, “improving/worsening ”, and “died within 72 hours”. The primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality. A Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for initial SCAI stage was used to assess the independent prognostic value of trajectory. Results: Overall, in-hospital mortality was 19.6% (n=212). By initial SCAI stage, in-hospital mortality increased stepwise from 14.6% (Stage A/B, n=508) to 17.8% (Stage C, n=360), 28.9% (Stage D, n=90), and 39.7% (Stage E, n=121). Importantly, 17% and 18% of Stage D and E patients died within the first 72 hours, reflecting the extreme early lethality of this phenotypes, Figure 1 . Phenotypic trajectory stratified outcomes independent of initial stage. Among patients who survived beyond 72 hours, those with a “stable” trajectory had the lowest in-hospital mortality (11.9%), while “worsening” (17.5%), “improving” (16.0%), and “worsening/improving” (18.4%) groups carried progressively higher risk, Figure 2 . On multivariable Cox regression, “worsening” was the only trajectory independently associated with in-hospital mortality after adjusting for initial SCAI stage (HR 1.81, 95% CI 1.14-2.86, p=0.011), Figure 3 . Conclusions: In a large contemporary CS cohort, serial SCAI staging over the first 72 hours reveals clinically meaningful trajectory phenotypes that provide independent prognostic value beyond admission classification alone. Worsening trajectory independently predicted an 81% increase in mortality hazard, supporting dynamic hemodynamic re-assessment as a tool to guide timely therapeutic escalation in CS.
title: Abstract 17534: Dynamic SCAI Stage Trajectory During the First 72 Hours Provides Prognostic Value Beyond Initial Shock Classification in Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Background: Breast cancer (BC) is the most common malignancy among women worldwide. As advances in cancer treatment have improved survival; cardiovascular disease has emerged as an important cause of morbidity and mortality among BC survivors. Coronary artery calcifications (CAC) and calcifications in the aorta (CA) are established markers of cardiovascular risk, but their prognostic significance with Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)—defined as acute myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome/ischemic heart disease requiring revascularization, stroke, and cardiovascular death—remains incompletely understood. Purpose: Determine if the presence of CAC or CA on baseline PET/CT (Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography) or chest CT predicts MACE. Methods: Retrospective cohort study of female patients diagnosed with BC between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2015, and followed until 12/31/2025. Treatment included surgery, hormone therapy, chemotherapy (CTX) or radiation (RTX) therapy. CTX (anthracycline +/-trastuzumab). Baseline PET/CT or chest CT were reviewed for the presence of CAC+/-CA. Patients were excluded if they lacked baseline imaging or had experienced a MACE before treatment. Univariate and multivariate adjusted Cox regression models were used to evaluate associations between CAC/CA and MACE. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were performed to assess event-free survival. Results: 896 female patients with BC were included (mean age: 74 years, IQR: 65-84), Follow up median 15.1 years (IQR: 10.3-17.1), white (826 [92.2%]). Estrogen receptor (ER+) was identified in 894 (98.3%) patients and progesterone receptor (PR+) in 890 (99.3%). Surgery in 885 (98.3%), RTX in 100%, CTX in 359 (40.1%), and hormone therapy in 618 (69.0%). CAC was identified in 311 (34.7%) patients and CA in 194 (21.7%). The presence of CAC was significantly associated with MACE (HR: 1.52 [95% CI: 1.2-2.0], p=0.0016) (Fig. a). On multivariable analysis, CAC remained the strongest predictor of MACE after adjusting for age, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, estrogen receptor status, and progesterone receptor status (HR: 1.40 [95% CI: 1.1-1.9], p<0.001) (Fig. c). No significant association was found between CA and MACE (p>0.05) (fig. b). Conclusion: These findings support the value of CAC as a non-invasive cardiovascular risk marker for MACE in BC patients and identify individuals who could benefit from closer cardiovascular surveillance during and after cancer treatment.
title: Abstract 17549: Predictive Value of Coronary Artery Calcification on the Baseline PET/CT or Chest CT for MACE in Female Patients with Breast Cancer

abstract: Background: The purinergic signaling CD39-CD73 axis generates immunosuppressive adenosine and shapes T cell responses. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) have been shown to be associated with CD39 cell surface expression in immune cell subsets. The functional impact of the ENTPD1 variant rs3814159 in those immune subsets remains unclear. We have also observed genotype-associated differential clinical outcomes in patients following ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). We examined whether SNP genotype influences stimulated immune cell gene expression and the circulating serum cytokine response post-STEMI. Methods: PBMCs from 11 healthy donors stratified by rs3814159 variant (n=6 AA, n=5 GG) were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 beads for 6 h paired with unstimulated controls and profiled using scRNA-seq (~243,000 cells after QC and doublet removal). Differential expression used subject-level pseudobulk (DESeq2), within and between genotype, condition and genotype x condition effect modeling; P values were FDR-adjusted per cell type. Serum from STEMI patients (n=5 AA, n=5 GG) was assayed using the Meso Scale Discovery (MSD) platform measuring 32 cytokine/chemokines at six timepoints (0,6,12,24,48 h and 30 days) and compared using mixed-effects modeling. Results: ENTPD1 was the top genotype-associated gene, significantly lower in GG than AA subjects and concentrated in the T cell subsets; Activated CD4 + T cells (log 2 FC -3.53, padj=9e-56), Tregs (-3.00, padj=3e-26), and CD8 + effector-memory T cells (-3.25, padj=3e-14). There was no genotype x condition interaction effect observed, indicating a constitutive, stimulation independent difference when PBMCs were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 beads, which are highly specific for T cell activation. In an independent cohort of STEMI patients, serum analysis showed significantly increased IL-4 levels (genotype effect p=0.044) in AA patients than GG patients across all measured timepoints post-STEMI. Conclusion: SNP rs3814159 genotype is associated with preserved stimulated transcriptomic profiles highlighted by substantially reduced, constitutive ENTPD1/CD39 expression in Tregs and effector subsets in GG subjects. In the post-STEMI cohort, AA patients showed significantly higher serum IL-4 levels, consistent with genotype-linked skewing toward a Th2/immunoregulatory phenotype. These convergent findings across stimulated immune cells, post-infarction serum and clinical outcomes implicate rs3814159 as a modulator of purinergic immunoregulation warranting further validation.
