title: Abstract 17722: Comparative Effectiveness of Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Repair, Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement, Surgical Intervention, and Medical Therapy for Severe Tricuspid Regurgitation: A Grade-Assessed Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) remains a leading cause of emergency hospitalization in the United States. However, contemporary national trends in respiratory and hemodynamic support utilization and their associated outcomes remain underexplored. Methods: The National Inpatient Sample (2018-2023) was queried for adult emergency hospitalizations with acute or acute-on-chronic heart failure as the primary diagnosis. HCUP-provided discharge weights were applied to generate nationally representative weighted estimates. Patients were stratified according to escalation of respiratory and hemodynamic support: no support, NIV, IMV, cardiogenic shock without MCS, and cardiogenic shock requiring MCS. Survey-weighted analyses evaluated temporal trends, in-hospital outcomes, and multivariable predictors of mortality. Results: Among 104,132 emergency ADHF hospitalizations, NIV utilization increased from 7.7% in 2018 to 9.8% in 2023, while IMV utilization declined from 2.4% to 2.1% (Figure 1A). Cardiogenic shock demonstrated the largest temporal increase, rising from 4.6% to 8.1% (+77%), accompanied by increased MCS utilization from 1.0% to 1.7%. A marked mortality gradient was observed across escalating support strata (Figure 1B). In-hospital mortality was 1.8% among unsupported admissions, increasing to 5.4% with NIV, 14.7% with cardiogenic shock without MCS, 19.8% with cardiogenic shock requiring MCS, and 33.5% among patients requiring IMV.After multivariable adjustment, mortality risk remained significantly elevated with NIV (aOR 3.11, 95% CI 2.74-3.54), cardiogenic shock without MCS (aOR 9.26, 95% CI 8.12-10.56), cardiogenic shock requiring MCS (aOR 11.80, 95% CI 9.35-14.89), and IMV (aOR 26.77, 95% CI 22.85-31.37) compared with unsupported admissions (Figure 1C). Resource utilization increased substantially with escalating support requirements, with the highest burden observed among patients requiring MCS (median LOS 22 days; median cost $651,489) (Figure 1D). Conclusion: Emergency ADHF hospitalizations are increasingly characterized by hemodynamic instability, with cardiogenic shock rates rising by 77% nationally between 2018 and 2023. Escalating support requirements are associated with progressively higher mortality and resource utilization, while IMV identifies a particularly high-risk population. These findings suggest a contemporary shift in ADHF severity toward advanced circulatory failure and highlight opportunities for earlier recognition and intervention.
title: Abstract 17730: Ventilation Over Circulation: Invasive Mechanical Ventilation, Not Mechanical Circulatory Support, Marks the Peak-Mortality Phenotype in Emergency Acute Decompensated Heart Failure

abstract: Background: Valve disease guidelines recommend treating hypertension (systolic blood pressure [BP] >140 mmHg) in chronic aortic regurgitation (AR), as systolic hypertension increases left ventricular (LV) afterload. However, control of hypertension in AR can be difficult. The prevalence of suboptimal BP control and its association with LV remodeling and outcomes in AR are not well defined. Current hypertension guidelines recommend BP <130/80 mmHg. Methods: We studied asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic patients with moderate or severe chronic AR on cardiac MRI, preserved LV function, and ≥2 clinical BP measurements after the index study. Exclusions were >mild concomitant valvular disease, prior valve intervention, and congenital disease or shunts. Mean systolic/diastolic BP were calculated from available BP measurements. Suboptimal BP control was defined by mean BP thresholds of ≥140/90 and ≥130/80 mmHg. Associations with LV hypertrophy were evaluated by linear regression. The primary outcome was a composite of death, heart failure hospitalization, or referral for aortic valve replacement (AVR); the secondary outcome was AVR referral. Results: Among 299 patients (median age 67 [55-77] years; 80% male), the median number of BP measurements per patient was 17 [5-41]. Mean BP was ≥140/90 mmHg in 110 (37%) and ≥130/80 mmHg in 198 (66%). Medications were renin-angiotensin inhibitors in 181 (61%), calcium channel blockers in 83 (28%), beta blockers in 125 (42%), and diuretics in 61 (20%); 56 (19%) were on ≥3 agents. Compared with optimal BP, suboptimal BP was associated with higher AR regurgitant volume [43 (33-60) vs 37 (30-51) mL, p=0.002], LV end-diastolic volume index [114 (99-133) vs 108 (83-127) mL/m 2 , p=0.047], and LV mass index (LVMi) [85 (74-98) vs 72 (61-90) g/m 2 , p<0.001]. Suboptimal BP was associated with higher LVMi in univariable analysis (β=11.07 [5.77-16.36], p<0.001) and after adjustment for regurgitant volume, age, sex, NYHA class, EuroScore II, and LVESV index (β=7.58 [3.28-11.89], p<0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower event-free survival with suboptimal BP for both outcomes (log-rank p≤0.007) (Figure 1). In Cox regression, suboptimal BP was associated with higher composite outcome risk in univariable analysis (HR 1.86, 95% CI 1.23-2.81, p=0.003) and remained independently associated after adjustment for age, sex, NYHA II symptoms, EuroScore II, AR regurgitant volume, LVESV index, and LVMi (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.13-2.70, p=0.012). Findings were consistent for the AVR referral outcome and using the 140/90 mmHg threshold. Conclusion: In chronic AR, 1 in 3 patients had suboptimal BP control using the 140/90 mmHg target, and 2 in 3 had uncontrolled hypertension using 130/80 mmHg. Suboptimal BP control was associated with greater LV hypertrophy and risk of adverse outcomes including progression to AVR. Further studies of BP-control strategies in AR are warranted.
title: Abstract 17741: Suboptimal Hypertension Control and Adverse Outcomes in Chronic Aortic Regurgitation

abstract: Introduction: Microvascular obstruction (MVO) following percutaneous coronary intervention is a frequent complication that results in worse clinical outcomes and has no consistently effective therapy. We are developing a novel treatment, termed ‘sonoreperfusion’, to restore microvascular patency following acute myocardial infarction. This entails ultrasound-targeted microbubble cavitation (UTMC) of an intravenously administered clinical-grade microbubble (MB) contrast agent, Definity ® , to induce microbubble oscillations which disrupt and clear obstructive microthrombi to restore microvascular perfusion. In our prior rat hindlimb model of MVO, we demonstrated that UTMC restored microvascular patency using our custom-made microbubbles. In the present porcine model of myocardial MVO, we evaluated the efficacy of Definity ® MBs (Lantheus Medical Imaging) and tested the hypothesis that clinically used ultrasound contrast MBs could serve as theranostic agents for both imaging and treatment of MVO Methods: Following a 20-min complete balloon occlusion of the mid-left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) in pigs, post-ischemic myocardial MVO was induced by injecting freshly prepared microthrombi into the LAD microvasculature. Following 10 min. of stable MVO, Definity ® MBs were infused through the ear vein or femoral vein for contrast-enhanced ultrasound imaging (CEUS) and 20 min of UTMC treatment. A clinical ultrasound transducer was positioned vertically above the myocardium to deliver therapeutic US for 20 min (Philips SONOS 7500, S3 probe, ultraharmonic mode, 1.3 MHz, MI=1.6, 7 frames per burst, 1 burst per second), with concomitant administration of Definity ® MBs, in the treatment group. In the control group, all steps were identical except for therapeutic US delivery on day 1. On day 2, cardiac MRI was performed. On day 3, angiography and echocardiography were performed. Finally, Evan’s blue was administered simultaneously into the coronary arteries for risk area measurement, before sacrificing the pig Results: UTMC significantly increased MCE-derived blood volume in the LAD myocardium, compared with the untreated control at 48 hrs (10.4 ± 4.1 dB vs. 1.1 ± 1.0 dB, p =0.001). Similarly, following UTMC, MRI-derived left ventricular (LV) function, including ejection fraction (74.6 ± 7.7% vs. 54.2 ± 5.1%; p =0.19) and LV stroke volume (77.9 ± 5.1 cm 3 vs. 48.2 ± 14.2 cm 3 ; p =0.02), was improved compared to control. Finally, we found that UTMC with Definity ® MBs resulted in a smaller infarct area (4.1 ± 2.9% vs. 13.7 ± 3.4%; p =0.02) Conclusions: UTMC with Definity ® MBs achieved rapid reperfusion of MVO compared to untreated controls. This was associated with smaller infarcts and improved LV systolic performance compared to untreated controls. This technique provides a potential adjunctive therapy for post-ischemic MVO, with the ultimate goal of improving clinical outcomes
title: Abstract 17757: Ultrasound Targeted Microbubble Cavitation for the Treatment of Myocardial Microvascular Obstruction: A Porcine Study

abstract: Background: Resistant hypertension (RH) — uncontrolled BP on ≥3 maximally dosed agents including a diuretic — affects 12-15% of hypertensive adults and carries disproportionate MACE risk. Catheter-based renal denervation (RDN) has re-emerged after sham-controlled trials demonstrated significant ambulatory BP reductions. Whether these hemodynamic gains translate into long-term hard cardiovascular outcomes has not been pooled. This is the first meta-analysis restricted to sham-controlled RDN trials reporting MACE data beyond 12 months. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, we searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov through March 2025. Eligible studies were randomized sham-controlled trials of RDN in confirmed RH with ≥12-month follow-up and MACE reporting. Primary outcomes: MACE (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) and 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP (ASBP) reduction. Secondary outcomes included antihypertensive pill burden, renal function, and procedural safety. Pooled MDs and RRs used random-effects models; ASBP-MACE dose-response assessed by meta-regression. Results: Sixteen sham-controlled trials (n=5,892; baseline ASBP 165.4 ± 14.2 mmHg; median follow-up 28 months) were included. RDN significantly reduced 24-hour ASBP (MD –8.7 mmHg, 95% CI –11.2 to –6.2; p<0.0001; I 2 =31%). MACE was significantly lower with RDN (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64-0.90; p=0.002); stroke was reduced by 34% (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.49-0.88; p=0.005). Meta-regression confirmed a significant ASBP-MACE dose-response (β=–0.021; p=0.003). Antihypertensive burden decreased by 0.8 agents (p<0.0001). Procedural serious adverse events occurred in 1.2%. Conclusions: Renal denervation produces durable BP reduction that translates into significant MACE and stroke reduction in sham-controlled trials. The ASBP-MACE dose-response confirms hemodynamic mediation of cardiovascular benefit. Current AHA resistant hypertension guidelines do not include RDN as a therapeutic option; this sham-controlled pooled evidence base supports formal guideline consideration as an adjunctive strategy in true RH. An adequately powered, outcomes-primary RDN trial is now the logical next step.
title: Abstract 17759: Renal Denervation versus Optimal Medical Therapy for Resistant Hypertension: Long-Term Cardiovascular Outcomes — A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Sham-Controlled Trials

abstract: Background: High vascular shear stress and turbulence can cause acquired von Willebrand syndrome (AVWS) and Heyde syndrome, as demonstrated in aortic valve stenosis (AS). Increased breakdown of von Willebrand factor (VWF) high-molecular-weight multimers (HMWM) increases bleeding risk. Whether the turbulent jet of mitral valve regurgitation (MR) also induces AVWS remains unclear. AVWS in MR could reduce thrombotic risk in patients with concomitant atrial fibrillation (AF), while MR reduction therapy may reduce bleeding risk. Hypothesis: MR disrupts the VWF pathway similarly to AS, and this effect can be reversed by mitral valve surgery or mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER). Methods: Between June 2023 and September 2025, we prospectively enrolled 45 patients with severe MR undergoing MR reduction therapy. Biomarkers of thrombogenicity, including the VWF pathway (Table 1), were assessed at baseline and after a mean follow-up of 10 months following MR surgery or M-TEER. Clinical thrombotic and bleeding events were recorded for one year before and after MR intervention. Statistical analyses were performed using paired Student’s t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: All patients (age 65 ± 12 years; 58% male) had severe MR (EROA 0.6 ± 0.1 cm 2 , RVol 60.4 ± 6.1 mL, RF 54.5 ± 4.2%). MR etiology was degenerative in 38%, functional in 16%, and mixed in 46%. AF was present in 36% of patients. Following MR intervention (11% M-TEER, 82% annuloplasty, 7% bioprosthetic valve replacement), 80% showed no-mild and 20% mild-moderate residual MR. VWF activity (GPIbM or CB)/antigen (Ag) ratio of <0.7, indicative of AVWS, was present in 9 patients (20%). MR reduction significantly increased VWF:GPIbM/Ag ratio (+0.15 ± 0.02; p <0.001) and VWF:CB/Ag ratio (+0.12 ± 0.04; p = 0.005). We also observed a significant increase in factor VIII (+11.83 ± 4.45%; p = 0.011), which is linked to the VWF pathway. Finally, reduced baseline VWF HMWM (<40%) were observed in 10 patients (22%). Following MR reduction, HMWM increased significantly (+7.37 ± 1.02%; p <0.001) (Figure 1). All patients with impaired VWF activity/Ag ratios and reduced HMWM showed complete recovery after MR reduction. No significant changes were observed in other coagulation pathways. During follow-up, four patients (9%) experienced TIA/stroke (vs. only one patient in the year prior to the procedure). Mild bleeding symptoms (e.g., epistaxis, ecchymoses) occurred in 21 patients (47%), with improvement or resolution in 18 patients (86%) after MR reduction. Conclusion: Our data show an association between MR and AVWS, which resolves after mitral valve repair. In addition, MR was associated with lower thromboembolic risk and higher bleeding risk. These findings suggest that MR could be a modifier of thromboembolic risk assessment in AF patients and may help individualize anticoagulant treatment and guide timing of MR reduction therapy.
title: Abstract 17819: Mitral Valve Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Repair Influence Thrombotic and Bleeding Risk, Including the von Willebrand Factor Pathway: The MITRATAB-VWF Study

abstract: Background: Secondary atrial fibrillation (AF) occurs in acute reversible conditions such as acute myocardial infarction (AMI), sepsis, postoperative states, hyperthyroidism and acute pulmonary disease. Current anticoagulation recommendations are largely extrapolated from primary AF populations and the effectiveness of oral anticoagulation (OAC) across different secondary AF etiologies remains uncertain. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of anticoagulation in secondary AF and determine whether outcomes vary by precipitating condition. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted per PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies included adult patients with secondary AF who received oral anticoagulation compared with no anticoagulation. Adjusted effect estimates were extracted and pooled using random-effects generic inverse-variance models. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 and Tau 2 statistics. Analyses were performed using RevMan 5.4. Primary efficacy outcomes included thromboembolic events (stroke, transient ischemic attack, or systemic embolism) and all-cause mortality. Major bleeding was the primary safety outcome. Prespecified subgroup analyses were performed by AF etiology. Results: Ten studies comprising more than 30,000 patients with secondary AF were included. Anticoagulation was associated with lower thromboembolic risk (adjusted effect 0.76, 95% CI 0.58-1.00; I 2 =55%) and all-cause mortality (adjusted effect 0.56, 95% CI 0.38-0.84; P=0.004). Significant variation in mortality benefit was observed across etiologies (P for subgroup interaction <0.00001), with the greatest reduction in sepsis-associated AF (0.31, 95% CI 0.25-0.38), followed by postoperative AF (0.45, 95% CI 0.40-0.51) and AMI-associated AF (0.73, 95% CI 0.61-0.89). Hyperthyroidism-associated AF demonstrated the largest reduction in thromboembolic events (0.27, 95% CI 0.12=0.62). Anticoagulation was associated with increased major bleeding risk (adjusted effect 1.26, 95% CI 1.13-1.40; I 2 =41%). Conclusions: Oral anticoagulation in secondary AF is associated with lower risks of thromboembolic events and all-cause mortality, but higher major bleeding risk. Benefits varied significantly across secondary AF etiologies, with the greatest gains seen in hyperthyroidism- and sepsis-associated AF. These findings suggest secondary AF should not be treated as a single condition and that anticoagulation decisions may need to be tailored to the underlying etiology. Further prospective studies are needed to identify which patients are most likely to benefit.
title: Abstract 17831: Etiology-Specific Outcomes of Oral Anticoagulation in Secondary Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Migraine is a highly prevalent headache disorder responsible for significant morbidity and millions of global years lost to disability. An underutilized migraine treatment approach is prevention through medications, such as propranolol, valproic acid, and topiramate, which focuses on addressing migraine burden and patient comorbidities. Because migraines are strongly associated with a higher risk for stroke and other major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events (MACCE), identifying the prophylactic therapy that most effectively protects the vulnerable migraine patient population from these events and migraine episodes would be especially valuable. Hypothesis: Preventive therapy with propranolol is associated with lower rates of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), and MACCE compared with other first-line therapies in patients with chronic migraine. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX health research network, querying data across 112 healthcare organizations. Adult patients (≥18 years) with a diagnosis of chronic migraine with or without aura (ICD-10-CM: G43.7x and G43.Ex) were split into 3 cohorts based on their prescription: propranolol (n=17,553), topiramate (n=48,421), or valproate (n=4,093). The cohorts underwent 1:1 propensity score matching based on factors such as age, race, ethnicity, BMI, smoking, and notable indications for propranolol. The primary outcome was any stroke or TIA within 5 years. Secondary outcomes included other major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events during 5-year follow-up. Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each outcome. Results: Relative to valproate and topiramate, propranolol exposure was associated with lower odds of stroke or TIA, MACCE, and several cardiovascular secondary outcomes. Compared with valproate, propranolol was associated with lower odds of MACCE (OR 0.867, 95% CI 0.768-0.978), acute coronary syndrome (OR 0.633, 95% CI 0.414-0.970), death (OR 0.573, 95% CI 0.389-0.845), any stroke or TIA (OR 0.571, 95% CI 0.459-0.710), and the composite of other cardiovascular endpoints (OR 0.715, 95% CI 0.626-0.816). When compared with topiramate, propranolol was associated with lower odds of MACCE (OR 0.917, 95% CI 0.861-0.978), any stroke or TIA (OR 0.875, 95% CI 0.775-0.994), decompensated heart failure (OR 0.923, 95% CI 0.859-0.991), and new-onset heart failure (OR 0.922, 95% CI 0.860-0.989). Conclusion: In propensity-matched cohorts of patients with chronic migraine, propranolol use was associated with lower odds of stroke or TIA and several cardiovascular outcomes compared with topiramate and valproate. These findings support further investigation into the potential cerebrovascular and cardiovascular benefits of propranolol among patients receiving migraine prophylaxis.
title: Abstract 17851: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Outcomes Associated with Propranolol, Topiramate, and Valproate in Patients with Chronic Migraine

abstract: Background: Surgical tricuspid valve (TV) repair or replacement can be complicated by post-operative bradyarrhythmias requiring permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation. Traditional transvenous PPMs can worsen TR, interfere with prosthetic valves, or cause structural complications such as leaflet impingement. We present a case series describing successful dual- and single-chamber leadless PPM placement in three patients following TV surgery. Case 1: A 60-year-old man with severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation underwent mitral valve replacement and TV repair complicated by tachy-brady syndrome and sinus node dysfunction. A dual-chamber leadless pacemaker implantation was performed and the ventricular device was safely passed through the repaired TV with successful deployment and uncomplicated post-operative course. Case 2: A 50-year-old woman with a prior bioprosthetic TV replacement developed complete heart block requiring biventricular PPM implantation, which was complicated by phrenic nerve stimulation. Her BiV system was extracted and dual-chamber leadless PPMs were successfully implanted with no significant tricuspid regurgitation on post-operative echocardiography. Case 3: A 67-year-old woman with severe TR underwent extraction of a dual-chamber ICD due to TV impingement, followed by bioprosthetic TV replacement. Persistent junctional rhythm with hemodynamic compromise necessitated single-chamber leadless PPM implantation. Conclusion: When placed with meticulous catheter manipulation, leadless systems offer a safe alternative for patients requiring pacing after TV surgery.
title: Abstract 17872: Leadless Pacemaker Implantation Following Surgical Tricuspid Valve Replacement: A Case Series

abstract: Introduction: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an important cause of acute coronary syndrome in young women and may occur during the postpartum period. Diagnosis can be challenging when electrocardiographic abnormalities are subtle and ventricular function is preserved. Patient Information and Clinical Findings: A 35-year-old G4P4 woman presented 12 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with sudden substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm while carrying groceries. Blood pressure was 150/94 mmHg, and heart rate was 56 beats/min. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus bradycardia with ST-segment depression in leads II and V5. High-sensitivity troponin increased from 951 ng/L to a peak of 3,729 ng/L. Diagnostic Assessment: The differential diagnosis included non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, pregnancy-associated SCAD, pulmonary embolism, stress cardiomyopathy, and peripartum cardiomyopathy. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 60-65%) without regional wall motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography revealed a 2.5-cm spontaneous dissection of the mid-left anterior descending artery with preserved TIMI III distal flow and no flow-limiting stenosis, confirming SCAD. Therapeutic Intervention and Outcomes: The patient was initially treated with aspirin and anticoagulation for acute coronary syndrome. Following angiographic diagnosis, conservative management was pursued, given preserved coronary flow and hemodynamic stability. She was discharged on guideline-directed medical therapy with cardiology follow-up, cardiac rehabilitation referral, and planned repeat coronary imaging. Discussion: Pregnancy-associated SCAD most commonly presents during the early postpartum period and may occur in patients without traditional cardiovascular risk factors. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by significant myocardial injury despite subtle electrocardiographic findings and preserved ventricular function. Normal ventricular function and minimal ECG abnormalities should not reassure clinicians when postpartum patients present with ischemic chest pain and elevated cardiac biomarkers. Recognition of SCAD is critical because management differs from atherosclerotic acute coronary syndrome, and conservative treatment is generally preferred in stable patients. Conclusion: SCAD should remain a key consideration in postpartum patients presenting with chest pain and elevated cardiac biomarkers, even when electrocardiographic changes are minimal and ventricular function is preserved.
title: Abstract 17874: Postpartum Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection Presenting as NSTEMI Despite Preserved Ventricular Function Twelve Days After Vaginal Delivery

abstract: Introduction: Increased abdominal aortic diameter has been associated with cardiovascular disease and mortality, but its role as a predictor of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) remains unclear. No previous meta-analysis has specifically evaluated this association. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically review and synthesize the available evidence on this association. Research Question: Is increased abdominal aortic diameter associated with a higher incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults compared with normal aortic diameter? Methods: Searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, LILACS, and Google Scholar until May 2026 using a traditional and Consensus approach. Study selection was performed in Rayyan. Eligible observational studies in adults compared individuals with increased versus normal abdominal aortic diameter and reported at least one cardiovascular outcome. Outcomes included cardiovascular mortality, stroke, myocardial infarction, and unstable angina. Data were pooled using random-effects models. Statistical analyses were performed in Stata 19. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic and clinical evaluation, while sensitivity analyses explored sources of variability. Results: Among 11,260 records identified, 70 articles underwent full-text review and 14 studies comprising more than 200,000 participants met the inclusion criteria. Seven studies evaluated cardiovascular mortality; heterogeneity decreased from I 2 =85.2% to 0% after sensitivity analysis, while the association remained significant (RR 1.76; 95% CI 1.63-1.90) (Figure 1). Six studies evaluated stroke and showed high heterogeneity (I 2 =86.4%) with no significant association in the primary analysis; after sensitivity analysis, heterogeneity decreased to I 2 =0% and a significant association was observed (HR 1.63; 95% CI 1.45-1.82) (Figure 2).Ten studies assessed myocardial infarction; heterogeneity decreased from I 2 =89.5% to 0% after sensitivity analysis, with significant risk estimates of 1.73 (95% CI 1.51-1.97) (Figure 3). Three studies evaluated unstable angina; heterogeneity decreased from I 2 =11.2% to 0%, and the association remained significant (RR 1.88; 95% CI 1.48-2.38). Conclusions: Increased abdominal aortic diameter was associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and unstable angina. These findings support the potential role of abdominal aortic diameter as an indicator of increased cardiovascular risk.
title: Abstract 17877: Abdominal Aortic Diameter as a Predictor of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Adult Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Invasive physiological assessment using fractional flow reserve (FFR) and instantaneous wave-free ratio (iFR) is routinely used to guide deferral of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in intermediate coronary stenoses. However, the long-term safety of deferring non-culprit lesions with negative physiological indices, particularly in patients with multivessel disease, remains unclear. Methods: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 randomized and observational studies evaluating adults with multivessel coronary artery disease in whom PCI was deferred for intermediate non-culprit lesions based on negative invasive physiology (FFR >0.80 and/or iFR >0.89). Studies with ≥12 months follow-up reporting lesion-level and patient-level outcomes were included. Pooled event rates (proportions per 100 observations) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using Generalized Linear Mixed Models with a random-effects framework. Results: Lesion-level outcomes were low (Figure 1): acute myocardial infarction 1.40% (95% CI: 0.73 to 2.67), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) 5.26% (95% CI: 2.88 to 9.40), target lesion revascularization 6.61% (95% CI: 3.49 to 12.16), target vessel revascularization 4.09% (95% CI: 2.39 to 6.92), target lesion failure 10.76% (95% CI: 7.77 to 14.71), cardiovascular death 1.37% (95% CI: 0.68 to 2.72), and a combined outcome of cardiac death and MI at 0.64% (95% CI: 0.07 to 5.61). Patient-level outcomes (Figure 2) reflected higher residual risk: MACE 10.55% (95% CI: 7.67 to 14.34; I2=99%), all-cause death 4.24% (95% CI: 2.73 to 6.52), cardiovascular death 1.52% (95% CI: 0.99 to 2.33), acute myocardial infarction 1.95% (95% CI: 1.26 to 3.00), overall revascularization 8.86% (95% CI: 6.17 to 12.56), target vessel revascularization 4.82% (95% CI: 3.05 to 7.52), target lesion revascularization 4.94% (95% CI: 3.44 to 7.05), and target lesion failure 9.35% (95% CI: 5.07 to 16.58). Additional patient-level events included unstable angina at 4.63%, stable angina at 7.46%, PCI at 5.76%, CABG at 1.52% (95% CI: 0.86 to 2.68), and a combined outcome of cardiac death and MI at 3.03% (95% CI: 0.91 to 9.57). Longer follow-up was associated with increased patient-level MACE and lesion-level TLR; subgroup analyses by clinical presentation and physiological index showed no significant differences. Conclusion: Deferral of PCI for intermediate non-culprit lesions with negative physiology is associated with low lesion-level events, supporting physiology-guided safety. Persistent patient-level risk underscores the need for complementary risk stratification beyond ischemia alone, incorporating plaque vulnerability, clinical context, and longitudinal monitoring.
title: Abstract 17899: Safety of Deferring Physiology-Negative Intermediate Non-Culprit Lesions in Multivessel Coronary Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock (CS) may arise from the interaction of rhythm disturbances, valvular disease, and impaired diastolic reserve, and management should be guided by underlying physiology. Case: A 75-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure (EF<10%) was referred to the emergency department after labs revealed markedly elevated liver enzymes (>1000 U/L). She reported one month of abdominal pain, bloating, dyspnea, and fatigue. She was hypotensive (103/63 mmHg) and tachycardic (151 bpm in AF) with elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasilar crackles, cool extremities, and bilateral lower-extremity edema. Labs demonstrated lactic acidosis (9.1 mmol/L), elevated high-sensitivity troponin T (3,942 ng/L), NT-proBNP (18,953 pg/mL), severe transaminitis, and acute kidney injury. Chest radiography showed pulmonary edema. She developed worsening hypoxemia and altered mentation, necessitating ICU transfer and intubation, vasoactive support, and eventual intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) placement. Invasive hemodynamic revealed elevated filling pressures (PA 46/26/31 mmHg, CVP 12 mmHg, PCWP 23 mmHg) and low cardiac output (1.47 L/min). TTE demonstrated rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS), which appeared to be moderate at a controlled heart rate (70 bpm) but became functionally severe during tachycardia (97 bpm), with markedly elevated transmitral gradient (8.5 mm Hg). Notably, inotropic therapy exacerbated tachycardia and hemodynamic instability, whereas mechanical circulatory support facilitated improved rhythm control, resulting in recovery of systolic function and resolution of shock. Discussion: This case illustrates dynamic functional severe MS as a reversible driver of CS in AF with RVR on a background of diastolic vulnerability and multivessel coronary disease. Tachycardia shortened diastole, converting moderate MS into functionally severe obstruction with abrupt rises in left atrial pressure and profound low output, while mechanical afterload reduction and rhythm control reversed shock and allowed reassessment of true valve severity. In high-risk patients with complex valve and coronary disease, early invasive hemodynamic profiling, temporary mechanical circulatory support, and multidisciplinary decision-making can enable stabilization and staged revascularization/valve strategies rather than emergent high-risk combined intervention. Conclusion: Dynamic worsening of MS during AF with RVR is an under-recognized, physiology-driven cause of CS in which targeted rate control and temporary mechanical support can be lifesaving.
title: Abstract 17909: Is it the Valve, the Vessel, or the Rate? Dynamic Mitral Stenosis Related Cardiogenic Shock in Atrial Fibrillation

abstract: Introduction: After contemporary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), short-duration dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) followed by P2Y12 monotherapy may reduce bleeding without increasing ischemia versus standard DAPT. Methods: A systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Central identified randomized controlled trials. Bayesian network meta-analysis was performed in R using the ‘meta’ package. Risk of bias was assessed with ROB 2.0. Random-effects models estimated major bleeding and major adverse cardiovascular events. Results: The Bayesian network meta-analysis included 12 randomized controlled trials (48,732 patients). Short-duration DAPT (1-3 months) followed by P2Y12 monotherapy significantly reduced major bleeding versus standard DAPT (OR 0.58, 95% CrI 0.42-0.79) without increasing major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; OR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.78-1.13). Short-duration DAPT ranked highest for bleeding safety (SUCRA 0.92) and similar for MACE (SUCRA 0.54). Myocardial infarction (OR 0.97, 95% CrI 0.79-1.19), stent thrombosis (OR 0.89, 95% CrI 0.61-1.28), all-cause death (OR 0.91, 95% CrI 0.70-1.17), and stroke (OR 1.02, 95% CrI 0.74-1.38) showed no significant differences. Net adverse clinical events favored short-duration DAPT (OR 0.69, 95% CrI 0.53-0.89). Node-splitting indicated no inconsistency. ROB 2.0 showed low bias in 8 trials. Ticagrelor monotherapy yielded the lowest bleeding risk (OR 0.51, 95% CrI 0.34-0.72). Conclusion: Short-duration DAPT followed by P2Y12 monotherapy significantly reduces major bleeding without increasing ischemic events compared to standard DAPT after contemporary PCI. This strategy offers an optimal balance of safety and efficacy, supporting abbreviated DAPT as a preferred approach, particularly in high-bleeding-risk patients.
title: Abstract 17917: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Short-Duration Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Followed by P2Y12 Monotherapy versus Standard Dual Antiplatelet Therapy After Contemporary PCI: A Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

abstract: Background: Patients undergoing veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) require systemic anticoagulation but remain at high risk for bleeding and thrombotic complications. Unfractionated heparin is commonly used, while bivalirudin has emerged as an alternative; however, comparative real-world outcome data remain limited. We evaluated short-term outcomes associated with bivalirudin versus heparin among adults undergoing VA-ECMO. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Adults aged ≥18 years who underwent VA-ECMO between January 1, 2015 and April 30, 2025 and received bivalirudin or heparin within 3 days of ECMO initiation were identified. Patients were compared after 1:1 propensity score matching for demographics, comorbidities, markers of illness severity, vasopressor use, antiplatelet therapy, and baseline laboratory parameters. Outcomes were assessed from day 3 through day 14 after ECMO initiation. Time-to-event outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and hazard ratios were estimated using Cox proportional hazards regression. Outcomes included all-cause mortality, bleeding composite (hemoptysis, melena, hematemesis, other gastrointestinal bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage), blood product transfusion, ECMO-related/postprocedural hemorrhage, and thrombotic composite (cerebral infarction, intracardiac thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or acute extremity embolism). Results: Before matching, 1,178 patients received bivalirudin and 5,278 received heparin. After propensity score matching, 1,158 patients were included in each group. All-cause mortality did not differ significantly between bivalirudin and heparin groups (22.6% vs 24.1%; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.09; p=0.339). The bleeding composite was also similar between groups (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.86-1.29; p=0.603). Bivalirudin was associated with a lower hazard of transfusion (20.5% vs 26.1%; HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64-0.90; p=0.001), but a higher hazard of ECMO-related/postprocedural hemorrhage (4.6% vs 2.7%; HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.10-2.66; p=0.017). There were no significant differences in thrombotic events (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.91-1.35; p=0.306). Conclusion: In this large multicenter propensity-matched cohort of adults undergoing VA-ECMO, bivalirudin and heparin were associated with similar short-term mortality, bleeding composite, and thrombotic events. Bivalirudin was associated with lower transfusion hazard but higher ECMO-related/postprocedural hemorrhage, highlighting a nuanced safety profile that warrants further prospective evaluation.
title: Abstract 17924: Bivalirudin versus Heparin in Patients Undergoing Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: A Multicenter Propensity-Matched Analysis

abstract: Primary cardiac sarcomas are exceedingly rare malignancies, with intimal sarcomas comprising an aggressive subset. Delayed diagnosis is common due to nonspecific symptoms mimicking more prevalent cardiopulmonary conditions. A 43-year-old male with a history of hypertension presented with sudden-onset chest pain, pink frothy productive cough, exertional near-syncope, unintentional weight loss, and night sweats over several months. Upon presentation to the emergency department, he was hemodynamically stable but noted to have tachycardia (HR 124 bpm) and hypoxia (SpO2 75% on room air). The physical exam revealed a loud S1 and S2 but no obvious murmurs. Concern for pulmonary embolism (PE) prompted computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the chest, which was negative for PE but revealed a large left atrial (LA) mass causing both inflow and outflow obstruction. TTE was performed, confirming a large, mobile LA mass with extension across the mitral valve. He was referred to cardiac surgery and taken for an urgent excision. Final pathology confirmed primary cardiac intimal sarcoma. Systemic chemotherapy with doxorubicin was initiated 4 weeks postoperatively. Adjuvant radiation commenced 5 months after diagnosis and was completed 2 months later. Initial brain MRI showed no intracranial metastases. However, 10 months after the initial presentation, the patient developed dizziness, confusion, and visual changes. MRI revealed a new left temporal lobe lesion. Left parieto-occipital craniotomy was performed and confirmed high-grade sarcoma metastasis. Paclitaxel was initiated 11 months after initial diagnosis. He recently developed dyspnea, and TTE noted progressive, now severe, mitral regurgitation. He is currently undergoing evaluation for surgical and transcatheter valve replacement. This case illustrates the presentation of primary cardiac intimal sarcoma, where constitutional signs, near-syncope, and pulmonary edema can be misattributed to deconditioning or infectious etiologies. We highlight the multidisciplinary management of a left atrial (LA) intimal sarcoma presenting with obstructive physiology as well as a remarkable response to treatment despite a median survival of 6-12 months. Prompt surgical resection is essential, though prognosis remains poor due to propensity for rapid systemic and intracranial metastasis. A high index of suspicion and early imaging are critical for prompt diagnosis. The patient maintained excellent functional status (ECOG 0) and remained highly active throughout his treatment course.
title: Abstract 17942: Primary Cardiac Intimal Sarcoma Presenting as Acute Cardiopulmonary Decompensation

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock (CS) has historically carried in-hospital mortality of 40-60%. Beginning in 2022, our quaternary center implemented a structured CS program including a multidisciplinary shock team, standardized escalation pathways, and 24/7 surgical availability for Impella 5.5 mechanical circulatory support. Whether these systems-of-care changes have been associated with improving patient outcomes over time has not been formally characterized. Hypothesis: Risk-adjusted in-hospital mortality among CS admissions has declined over time since program implementation. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of consecutive adults with manually adjudicated CS admitted to a single quaternary center from July 2022 through November 2025. The primary outcome was index-hospitalization mortality. Secondary outcomes were discharge home and a composite of death. Temporal trends were assessed with logistic regression using admission year as a continuous predictor, with and without adjustment for age, sex, and admission Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. A per-quarter trend and Cochran-Armitage test were also performed. Results: A total of 1,019 admissions were analyzed (median age 63 years, 30% female, median SOFA 1); 55 (5.4%) received concurrent durable LVAD or heart transplant. Annual in-hospital mortality declined from 26.9% (2022) to 26.6% (2023), 20.7% (2024), and 21.3% (2025; through November). The unadjusted odds of in-hospital death decreased 4% per calendar quarter (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.93-1.00, p=0.033). After adjustment for age, sex, and SOFA, the per-year reduction was significant (adjusted OR 0.85 per year, 95% CI 0.74-0.98, p=0.029). The composite of death or hospice discharge also decreased (OR 0.87 per year, 95% CI 0.76-0.99, p=0.036). Discharge home increased from 36.5% to 44.9% (OR 1.13 per year, 95% CI 1.00-1.27, p=0.053). Conclusions: Over 3.5 years following implementation of a structured 24/7 cardiogenic shock program with surgical mechanical circulatory support availability, in-hospital mortality at a single quaternary center fell by approximately 22% in relative terms, with a statistically significant per-year reduction after risk adjustment and an accompanying rise in discharge-home rates. These findings support a coordinated systems-of-care approach to CS and warrant multicenter confirmation.
title: Abstract 17948: Temporal Trends in In-Hospital Mortality Following Implementation of a Structured 24/7 Cardiogenic Shock Program at a Quaternary Center

abstract: Introduction/Background: The SMART-CHOICE 3 trial demonstrated improved ischemic outcomes with clopidogrel versus aspirin monotherapy following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in Korean patients. However, the generalizability of these findings to a diverse United States population, especially among females, elderly (>75 years old), and minority races, remains uncertain. Research Question/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that clopidogrel monotherapy would be associated with lower rates of major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) without increased bleeding compared with aspirin monotherapy among high-risk US patients following PCI. Methods/Approach: Using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we conducted a retrospective target-trial emulation of adults undergoing PCI who completed dual antiplatelet therapy for 6months-1year and subsequently transitioned to clopidogrel or aspirin monotherapy. High ischemic risk was defined by prior myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus, or chronic kidney disease. Patients receiving oral anticoagulation, alternative P2Y12 inhibitors, active malignancy, or prior intracranial hemorrhage were excluded. 1:1 propensity score matching was performed using demographic, clinical, and treatment-related variables (Table 1). The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), defined as all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke/transient ischemic attack, or cardiac arrest. Secondary outcomes included major bleeding and all-cause mortality. Results/Data: After propensity score matching, 10,712 patients were included in each treatment group. Clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with a lower risk of MACCE compared with aspirin monotherapy (29.8% vs. 32.9%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84-0.92; log-rank p<0.001; Figure 1). Major bleeding occurred less frequently with clopidogrel (4.1% vs. 8.0%; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.43-0.54; p<0.001). All-cause mortality was also lower among patients receiving clopidogrel (5.5% vs. 8.6%; HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.57-0.70; p<0.001). Directionally consistent reductions in MACCE, bleeding, and mortality were observed among women (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.84-0.96; p=0.002), patients aged >75 years (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.78-0.91; p<0.001), and patients with chronic kidney disease (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.78-0.87; p<0.001). Conclusion: In a large, diverse US population-based real-world target-trial emulation, clopidogrel monotherapy following 6-12 months of DAPT in patients undergone PCI was associated with lower risks of MACCE, major bleeding, and all-cause mortality compared with aspirin monotherapy among high-risk patients. These findings extend the external validity of SMART-CHOICE 3 and support further evaluation of clopidogrel as a long-term antiplatelet strategy following PCI.

appraisal.design_and_n: After propensity matching, 10,712 patients in each treatment group.
appraisal.main_limitation: Retrospective EHR data with residual confounding; the 29.8% vs 32.9% event rates imply broad outcome definitions including all-cause mortality.
appraisal.one_line: Target trial emulation in TriNetX of clopidogrel versus aspirin monotherapy after PCI, testing external validity of SMART-CHOICE 3.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Clopidogrel was associated with a lower risk of MACCE than aspirin (29.8% vs. 32.9%; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.84-0.92).

title: Abstract 17953: External Validation of SMART-CHOICE 3: Clopidogrel versus Aspirin Monotherapy Following Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in a Diverse US Population

abstract: Background: Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a high-risk thromboembolic substrate driven by atrial arrhythmias and amyloid-related atrial mechanical dysfunction. In practice, anticoagulation status guides the need for thrombus-exclusion imaging before cardioversion or other rhythm-control strategies. However, intracardiac and left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombi have been reported despite oral anticoagulation, raising concern that anticoagulation alone may be insufficient to exclude thrombus risk in CA. Objective: To evaluate the prevalence of intracardiac and LAA thrombus in adults with CA and characterize thrombus detected despite oral anticoagulation. Methods: We performed a PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for adult studies of confirmed CA reporting imaging- or pathology-confirmed intracardiac, left atrial, or LAA thrombus with extractable event counts and denominators. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was performed for imaging-based studies. Pre-cardioversion cohorts were analyzed as a prespecified subgroup. Thrombus despite anticoagulation and autopsy/pathology cohorts were summarized separately. Study quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Results: Five imaging-based studies including 631 CA patients assessed for thrombus were included. Intracardiac/LAA thrombus was identified in 92 patients, with a pooled prevalence of 16.7% (95% CI, 9.8%-27.2%; I 2 =89.9%). In pre-cardioversion cohorts, pooled prevalence was 19.9% (95% CI, 13.6%-28.2%; I 2 =43.6%). Sensitivity analysis excluding a procedure-level cohort yielded a similar pooled prevalence of 16.1%. In studies with extractable anticoagulated denominators, thrombus was detected in 12.8% of anticoagulated patients undergoing assessment. Among studies reporting anticoagulation status of thrombus cases, at least 49.1% occurred despite documented anticoagulation. Imaging-based studies were generally at low to moderate risk of bias, mainly due to selective thrombus assessment and clinical-setting heterogeneity. Conclusion: Intracardiac and LAA thrombi are clinically common in CA, occurring in anticoagulated patients and pre-cardioversion settings where a missed thrombus may alter management. These findings support amyloid atrial myopathy as a distinct thrombotic substrate not reliably mitigated by conventional anticoagulation strategies. A lower threshold for imaging-based thrombus exclusion before cardioversion/rhythm-control procedures may be warranted in selected CA patients, even when anticoagulation appears adequate. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal thrombus-exclusion strategies, identify predictors of thrombus despite anticoagulation, and test whether CA-specific anticoagulation or rhythm-control pathways reduce thromboembolic events.
title: Abstract 17954: Intracardiac and Left Atrial Appendage Thrombus in Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Prevalence and Occurrence Despite Anticoagulation

abstract: Introduction: Sotorasib is a KRAS G12C inhibitor used in advanced non-small cell lung cancer, with cardiovascular complications remaining poorly characterized. We describe a probable sotorasib-associated myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries phenotype presenting with acute heart failure shortly after treatment initiation. Patient Information: An 80-year-old man with metastatic KRAS G12C-mutated non-small cell lung cancer presented with progressive dyspnea and acute hypoxic respiratory failure six days after initiation of sotorasib therapy. Pre-treatment transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% without regional wall motion abnormalities. Clinical Findings and Timeline: High-sensitivity troponin showed a marked dynamic rise from 4,840 to 6,565 to 9,797 to 9,924 ng/L. B-type natriuretic peptide was 1,607 pg/mL. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm with anterolateral ischemic changes, including ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in leads V2 to V4. Repeat echocardiography revealed newly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% to 40%, grade II diastolic dysfunction, moderate aortic stenosis, atrial septal aneurysm, and new lateral and apical wall akinesis. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Coronary angiography demonstrated non-obstructive coronary artery disease without a culprit lesion. The combination of myocardial injury, ischemic electrocardiographic abnormalities, new systolic dysfunction, new regional wall motion abnormalities, and absence of obstructive coronary disease was consistent with a myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries-like presentation. Infectious evaluation, including viral testing, was unrevealing, and no alternative trigger adequately explained the abrupt deterioration. Therapeutic Intervention and Outcome: Given the close temporal relationship between sotorasib initiation and symptom onset, drug-associated cardiotoxicity was suspected. Sotorasib was discontinued and supportive management was initiated. The patient subsequently died, precluding assessment of ventricular recovery. Discussion and Synthesis: This case highlights a probable early signal of sotorasib-associated cardiotoxicity. Although causality cannot be established from a single case and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging could not be completed, before-and-after imaging, objective myocardial injury, non-obstructive coronary angiography, and absence of an alternative explanation support a probable drug-associated cardiovascular event. As use of KRAS G12C inhibitors expands, clinicians should maintain awareness for new cardiac symptoms, biomarker elevation, or ventricular dysfunction shortly after treatment initiation.
title: Abstract 17964: Sotorasib-Associated MINOCA Phenotype Presenting with Acute Heart Failure: A Probable Early Pharmacovigilance Signal

abstract: Introduction: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a rare but increasingly recognized cause of acute coronary syndrome, most commonly affecting women with few traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Although chest pain is the typical presenting symptom, SCAD can rarely manifest with neurologic or systemic phenomena. We present a case in which multivessel SCAD initially presented with an episode of transient global amnesia (TGA). Patient Information: A 69 year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hyperlipidemia, prior myopericarditis, and a prior TGA episode presented as a code stroke activation. Her husband noted she had awakened with acute amnesia, disorientation, and an inability to retain new information. He reported the episode as strikingly similar to her TGA three years prior. Clinical Findings and Timeline: She denied chest pain and dyspnea on presentation. Troponin rose to a peak of 8,376 ng/L. Initial EKG showed nonspecific ST changes. CT head and CT perfusion were unremarkable. CTA head showed vertebral artery beading consistent with fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). Brain MRI was negative for stroke. EEG during the amnestic episode excluded seizure. TGA was confirmed as the neurologic diagnosis. On the third day of hospitalization she developed nausea and substernal chest discomfort. Repeat EKG showed new T wave inversions in inferior leads. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Echocardiogram showed preserved LVEF (65%) with no wall motion abnormalities. Cardiac MRI demonstrated anterolateral delayed enhancement, raising concern for myocarditis versus infarction. Coronary angiography revealed multivessel SCAD: 99% stenosis of the right posterior descending and posterolateral arteries, 70% distal LAD stenosis, and 80% third marginal stenosis. Therapeutic Interventions: Conservative management was pursued given hemodynamic stability and preserved LVEF. Clopidogrel was started. She was continued on rosuvastatin, metoprolol succinate and dapagliflozin. Anticoagulation was continued for atrial fibrillation. Follow-up and Outcomes: The patient was referred to vascular surgery and a tertiary FMD specialist at outpatient follow-up and remained clinically stable. Discussion and Synthesis: TGA is considered a once-in-a-lifetime event in the vast majority of patients. Recurrence is estimated at under 10% and should prompt consideration of an alternative or concurrent etiology. When a patient presents with cardiac biomarker elevation and incidental imaging findings concerning for systemic arteriopathy, SCAD should be on the differential. The absence of chest pain does not exclude an acute coronary etiology, and acute coronary syndrome can present with neurological manifestations.
title: Abstract 17987: Multivessel Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection in a Patient with Fibromuscular Dysplasia Presenting as Transient Global Amnesia

abstract: Background: HIV infection is associated with cardiovascular disease, including coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, and heart failure. As survival has improved in the modern antiretroviral era, HIV-positive patients are increasingly presenting with acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF). Whether HIV independently affects in-hospital outcomes in this population remains incompletely understood. Research Question: Is HIV infection independently associated with worse in-hospital outcomes among patients hospitalized with ADHF? Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (2016-2020). Adult hospitalizations with a primary diagnosis of ADHF were identified using ICD-10 codes and stratified by HIV status. Propensity-score matching (1:1) yielded 5,463 hospitalizations in each group. Continuous variables were compared using two-sample t-tests and categorical variables using chi-square tests. Multivariate logistic regression, adjusting for demographics, comorbidities, and disease severity, evaluated associations between HIV and clinical outcomes including acute kidney injury (AKI), acute respiratory failure, hemodialysis initiation, mechanical circulatory support (MCS) use, and in-hospital mortality, as well as length of stay, charges, and discharge disposition. Results: The matched groups were well balanced in age, sex, and most comorbidities. HIV-positive patients had higher rates of AKI (41.17% vs 37.32%, p<0.001), acute respiratory failure (28.65% vs 25.24%, p<0.001), and hemodialysis initiation (18.78% vs 16.95%, p=0.013), and lower MCS use (1.19% vs 1.79%, p=0.009). Rates of mechanical ventilation and in-hospital mortality were similar. After adjustment, HIV was associated with higher odds of AKI (aOR 1.22; 95% CI 1.13-1.33), acute respiratory failure (aOR 1.18; 95% CI 1.08-1.29), and hemodialysis initiation (aOR 1.20; 95% CI 1.02-1.42), and lower odds of MCS use (aOR 0.65; 95% CI 0.47-0.90). HIV was not independently associated with in-hospital mortality (aOR 1.12; 95% CI 0.95-1.33). Length of stay (8.63±11.15 vs 8.27±12.70 days, p=0.116) and total charges ($114,961 vs $111,983, p=0.499) were similar, whereas HIV-positive patients were less frequently discharged home (15.58% vs 18.20%, p<0.001). Conclusion: Among ADHF hospitalizations, HIV infection is associated with greater end-organ complications without higher in-hospital mortality, and with lower MCS use, underscoring the need for vigilant monitoring and equitable escalation of care.
title: Abstract 17996: Impact of HIV on In-Hospital Outcomes in Patients Hospitalized with Acute Decompensated Heart Failure: A Propensity-Matched Nationwide Analysis

abstract: Background: Regionalized surgical programs centralize procedural expertise but may fragment post-discharge care, particularly as community-care options expand. Non-index readmission after cardiac surgery, including SAVR, is common and associated with worse outcomes. We tested whether referral catchment was associated with documented readmission after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) at a regional VA cardiac surgery center. Methods: We studied 347 consecutive veterans undergoing SAVR from 2009 to 2024. Patient ZIP code centroids were geocoded to the nearest VA medical center in the regional network and collapsed into index-center local and three non-local referral catchments. The primary endpoint was 30-day documented VA readmission; any-time documented VA readmission was a sensitivity endpoint. Seven readmitted patients without classifiable timing were retained only in any-time analyses. Logistic regression adjusted for STS predicted morbidity/mortality (PROMM), age, and TAVR availability; sex was excluded due to zero readmissions among 9 women. Results: Thirty-day documented VA readmission occurred in 24/340 (7.1%). Baseline predicted STS PROMM was similar locally versus non-locally (median 8.2% [6.3-12.6] vs 8.5% [6.2-13.6]; p=0.802). Non-local referral catchment had lower 30-day documented readmission than the index-center local catchment (index-center local 12/88 (13.6%) vs non-local 12/252 (4.8%); OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.14-0.74; p=0.008). Results were similar for any-time documented VA readmission (index-center local 20/91 (22.0%) vs non-local 27/256 (10.5%); OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22-0.80; p=0.008). Four-region 30-day rates showed a similar gradient (p=0.052). Among 30-day readmissions, leading documented reasons were infection/wound 46%, pericardial effusion/tamponade-related 21%, heart failure 8%, arrhythmia/PPM 4%, other 21%; cause distribution did not differ by local vs non-local catchment (p=0.800). Observed operative mortality (index-center local 1/91 (1.1%) vs non-local 7/256 (2.7%); p=0.686) and observed STS major morbidity (index-center local 20/91 (22.0%) vs non-local 44/256 (17.2%); p=0.393) were similar locally versus non-locally. Bleeding, LOS, ICU LOS, and VARC-3 composites did not significantly differ by catchment. Conclusions: In a regional VA surgical network, non-local referral catchments were associated with lower documented VA readmission after SAVR despite similar operative risk and clinical outcomes. Although readmissions were documented within VA records, the specific VA facility of readmission was unavailable, therefore, this gradient is consistent with differential post-discharge pathways and readmission capture across VA sites rather than true differences in surgical quality. Post-discharge surveillance across VA referral catchments warrant investigation as VA community-care options expand.
title: Abstract 17997: Readmission Capture Across Referral Catchments After Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement in a Regional Veterans Affairs Network

abstract: Introduction Fluoropyrimidines, including 5-fluorouracil, are widely used in gastrointestinal malignancies and are among the most common non-anthracycline chemotherapies associated with cardiotoxicity. We present a case of fluorouracil-associated vasospastic angina presenting as a STEMI mimic. Patient Information A 71-year-old man with locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma and no prior cardiac history began first-cycle modified FLOT with fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel, and durvalumab. He received fluorouracil through a 46-hour infusion pump. Near completion, he developed intermittent substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm with dyspnea, diaphoresis, and nausea. Clinical Findings and Diagnostic Assessment In the emergency department, he was asymptomatic. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ischemic changes (figure 1), and high-sensitivity troponin T was 27 ng/L (normal <=15 ng/L). CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism. During observation, he developed severe chest pain with sinus tachycardia to the 130s. Repeat ECG showed anterolateral and inferior ST elevations (figure 2), and troponin increased to 44. The temporal association with fluorouracil, episodic symptoms, multi-territory ST elevations, and modest troponin elevation raised concern for coronary vasospasm. Therapeutic Intervention A STEMI alert was activated, and he received aspirin 324 mg and clopidogrel 600 mg. Given suspected vasospasm, IV nitroglycerin and diltiazem were initiated, with intracoronary nitroglycerin considered. His chest pain resolved, and repeat ECG 30 minutes later demonstrated resolution of ST-segment elevations, prompting cancellation of the STEMI alert. He was admitted for telemetry monitoring and continued on IV nitroglycerin. TTE demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function, ejection fraction of 57%, and no regional wall motion abnormalities. He had no recurrent angina or ischemic telemetry changes and was transitioned to oral isosorbide mononitrate. Follow-up and Outcomes He was discharged on oral isosorbide mononitrate with close cardio-oncology follow-up. Amlodipine was added for additional prophylaxis. After multidisciplinary discussion, fluorouracil rechallenge was planned with antianginal prophylaxis and close monitoring. Discussion Fluoropyrimidine-associated coronary vasospasm is an important STEMI mimic. Reported mortality ranges from 2.2-13% and recurrence after rechallenge has been reported in up to 90% of cases. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by temporal proximity to exposure, episodic angina, dynamic ischemic ECG changes, limited troponin rise, and rapid response to vasodilators. Although fluorouracil rechallenge has traditionally been discouraged, it may be considered in carefully selected patients when oncologic benefit is substantial, and alternatives are limited.
title: Abstract 18009: Fluorouracil-Associated Coronary Vasospasm Presenting as a Reversible STEMI Mimic

abstract: Purpose: Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) are among the most common findings on exercise treadmill testing (ETT). They are usually benign, but exercise-induced PVCs, particularly frequent or recovery-phase ectopy, have been linked in other populations to increased cardiovascular risk and mortality. In tactical athletes, such findings can affect fitness-for-duty decisions and health. We examined whether overall or stage-specific PVC incidence was associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in tactical athlete candidates. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 596 tactical athletes undergoing occupational ETT at a single center from 2016 to 2025. PVC incidence was defined as one or more PVCs during the duration of the test. MACE was a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation, ascertained from clinical records. PVC-positive and PVC-negative candidates were compared using chi-square and Fisher exact tests, with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). A secondary analysis compared MACE among candidates with recovery-phase PVCs, other-stage PVCs, and no PVCs. Results: Among 596 candidates, PVCs were present in 189 (31.7%) and MACE in 26 (4.4%). MACE was similar in PVC-positive and PVC-negative candidates (3.2% vs 4.9%; OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.25-1.61; p=0.40). A broader definition counting any documented cardiovascular diagnosis was concordant (6.3% vs 8.8%; OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.35-1.38; p=0.34). By PVC timing (n=520), MACE was similar across recovery-phase PVCs (2.6%), other-stage PVCs (4.9%), and no PVCs (6.4%; p=0.48). No comparison reached statistical significance. Conclusion: In this tactical athlete cohort, neither PVC incidence nor timing on ETT was associated with MACE. These findings suggest that PVCs identified on occupational screening may not, in isolation, justify automatic disqualification or reflexive downstream cardiac testing, supporting a more individualized, risk-factor-based approach that could help identify at risk-patients. Given the retrospective, single-center design and modest event count, prospective multi-center studies with longitudinal follow-up are needed to define which PVC characteristics carry prognostic weight in tactical athletes.
title: Abstract 18012: Incidence and Timing of Premature Ventricular Contractions on Exercise Treadmill Testing and Cardiovascular Events in Tactical Athletes

abstract: Background: Sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) is commonly attributed to ischemic scar in patients with obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). However, concomitant CAD may create diagnostic anchoring and obscure additional arrhythmogenic substrates. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) can differentiate ischemic from nonischemic myocardial injury and identify coexisting cardiomyopathies. Case: A 70-year-old man with hypertension presented with chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, and near-syncope. Electrocardiography demonstrated sustained monomorphic VT (>200 bpm), successfully terminated with direct-current cardioversion. Subsequent ECGs revealed alternating left anterior and left posterior fascicular block. Troponin peaked to 25.5 ng/mL. Echocardiography showed EF 40-45% with inferolateral hypokinesis. Coronary angiography demonstrated severe distal LAD disease and moderate circumflex/obtuse marginal disease with negative physiologic assessment (iFR 0.98). The distal LAD was successfully stented.Given the severity of VT and conduction abnormalities, CMR was obtained. EF was 44% with three distinct late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) patterns: transmural inferolateral enhancement consistent with ischemic infarction; extensive mid-myocardial enhancement involving the basal-mid septum; and subepicardial enhancement of the apical lateral wall. These latter findings did not conform to a coronary distribution. No edema, pericardial disease, or mediastinal lymphadenopathy was present. Decision-Making: Although obstructive CAD and elevated troponin provided an apparent explanation for presentation, CMR identified both ischemic and nonischemic scar patterns. The coexistence of transmural, mid-myocardial, and subepicardial LGE, together with VT and alternating fascicular block, suggested a second arrhythmogenic substrate. Cardiac sarcoidosis was considered the leading diagnosis, and FDG-PET was recommended. Conclusion: CMR revealed concurrent ischemic and nonischemic myocardial injury despite an apparently sufficient ischemic explanation for VT. Recognition of dual scar pathology prevented diagnostic anchoring and redirected evaluation toward suspected cardiac sarcoidosis, highlighting the value of advanced tissue characterization in ventricular arrhythmias.
title: Abstract 18019: Beyond the Culprit Lesion: Cardiac MRI Revealing Concurrent Ischemic and Nonischemic Myocardial Injury Following Ventricular Tachycardia:

abstract: Background: Complete revascularization (CR) following percutaneous coronary intervention(PCI) is standard of care for patients presenting with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and multivessel coronary artery disease (CAD). However, the optimal timing of CR remains uncertain. This study examined clinical outcomes following immediate versus staged PCI among patients with STEMI and multivessel CAD without cardiogenic shock. Methods: We updated our March 2025 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing staged and immediate CR. MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to April 30, 2026. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) at ≥12 months. Secondary outcomes included individual components of MACE. Risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using random-effects models. We conducted two sensitivity analyses. First, we conducted a stratified analysis with trials categorized as 1) early staged CR (during index hospitalization) or 2) late staged CR (post-discharge). Second, we used meta-regression to examine timing to staged PCI and MACE. Results: We included nine reports from eight trials (n=4,129); four reports from three trials were published since our previous meta-analysis. Overall, no differences in MACE were observed between staged and immediate CR (11.5% vs 10.6%; RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.78-1.41). However, all-cause mortality was lower in the staged group (3.8% vs 5.0%; RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60-0.97). Pooled estimates for all outcomes are presented in Table 1 . The first sensitivity analysis indicated a lower risk of MACE in trials with early staged CR compared with immediate CR (9.3% vs 11.7%; RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.67-0.94) but not in trials with late staged CR (12.7% vs 10.0%; P-interaction=0.02) ( Table 2 ). There was no difference in all-cause mortality in trials with early or late staged CR compared to immediate CR. In the second sensitivity analysis, meta-regression suggested a trend toward lower MACE with shorter delays to staged PCI (β=0.0078 per day; 95% CI -0.0068-0.0224) ( Figure 1 ). Conclusion: Among patients with STEMI and multivessel CAD, a pooled analysis shows that staged PCI is associated with lower all-cause mortality compared to immediate CR. A reduction in overall MACE was only seen in a sensitivity analysis limited to trials of early staged CR. These results suggest improved clinical outcomes with early staged CR done during the index hospitalization.

appraisal.main_limitation: Few trials, and mortality difference arises from secondary outcomes with heterogeneous timing definitions.
appraisal.one_line: Updated meta-analysis of immediate versus staged complete revascularisation in STEMI with multivessel disease.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: MACE did not differ between staged and immediate complete revascularisation (11.5% vs 10.6%; RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.78-1.41); all-cause mortality was 3.8% vs 5.0% in the staged and immediate groups respectively.
